There is no key size argument, because each kind has one size. Only the two RSA kinds would need a size, and this method does not create them.

params.name: kind
params.descHtml: The kind of key to create. P256 agrees and signs, X25519 only agrees, and Ed25519 only signs. The two RSA kinds are only read, never created.

doc.returnHtml: The key pair, ready to sign or to agree. Its write method gives PKCS#8, which Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read reads back.

errors.descHtml: $kind is RsaPkcs1 or RsaPss. This method never creates an RSA key. You get an RSA key from whoever issued it, and Core\Crypto\KeyPair::read reads it.

doc.shortHtml: Computes a shared secret with ECDH, from your own key pair and the public key that the other side sent. The result is the raw shared value, and it is not a key. Pass it to expandKey with a context string to make the keys you need.

params.name: mine
params.descHtml: Your own key pair, of kind P256 or X25519. The other kinds can only sign.

params.name: theirs
params.descHtml: The public key of the other side. It must be of the same kind, because two keys on different curves cannot agree.

doc.returnHtml: 32 bytes as secret bytes. This is the x-coordinate for P-256 and the u-coordinate for X25519. WebCrypto's deriveBits returns the same value for the same two keys.

errors.descHtml: The two keys cannot agree. One key is of a kind that cannot agree: Ed25519 or an RSA kind. Or the two keys are on different curves.

The X25519 point of the other side adds nothing, so the secret would be all zeros for any private key. The sender chose that point. So the error is about the sender, and it is not a bug in your program.

doc.shortHtml: Signs $message with the private key of $key. There is no argument for the algorithm or the digest, because the kind of the key pair sets the scheme. RsaPkcs1 and RsaPss use SHA-256, P256 uses ECDSA with SHA-256, and Ed25519 uses Ed25519. So a call cannot choose a scheme that does not match the key.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: The whole bytes to sign. You cannot pass a hash of the message in its place. A signature over a hash means something different.

params.name: key
params.descHtml: The key pair to sign with. It can be of any kind except X25519, which can only agree.

doc.returnHtml: The signature. For P256, it is 64 bytes: the r ‖ s pair that JWS and WebCrypto use, never DER. For Ed25519, it is 64 bytes. For either RSA kind, it has as many bytes as the modulus. RsaPkcs1 and Ed25519 give the same signature for a message every time. P256 and RsaPss use randomness, so two signatures of one message differ, and both verify.

errors.descHtml: $key is an X25519 key pair, which cannot sign. The kind is set when the pair is generated or read, so this is a bug in your program.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $signature is a signature of $message by $key. If it is not, it throws an error. The algorithm comes from the key, as in sign. So nothing in the data you received chooses how it is checked.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: The bytes that the signature should cover. A tainted value is allowed, and it stays tainted. A valid signature tells you who sent the bytes. It does not tell you that their content is safe.

params.name: signature
params.descHtml: The signature as sign returns it: r ‖ s for P256, never DER.

params.name: key
params.descHtml: The public key to check against, of any kind but X25519.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. For a valid signature, it returns. For a wrong one, it throws an error. So there is no false result that a == check could read wrongly.

errors.descHtml: The signature is not by this key for this message. It was changed, it has the wrong length for the algorithm of the key, or another key made it. All these cases have the same message, so the error does not say which part was wrong.
$key is an X25519 key, which cannot verify. It is your program's own key, not data you received, so this is a bug in your program.

classes.summaryHtml:
Encryption, signatures and key derivation. Each algorithm is a case of an enum, so a wrong name does not compile. No method picks an algorithm for you.

Core\Crypto holds the primitives a Novis program shares with something that is not Novis: a browser's WebCrypto, an SDK, whoever issued its keys. It seals and opens under an authenticated cipher, stretches a password and spreads uniform material into keys, draws key pairs, agrees a shared secret over a curve, and signs and verifies a message. No algorithm is ever a string, and none has a default — a cipher, a key's kind and a key's encoding are each a case of a closed enum that the call names.

When a call takes the cipher as a string and the nonce from the caller, mistakes are easy. One file uses aes-256-ecb, another uses an all-zero IV, and neither authenticates the data. Here the enum is closed and every case authenticates. A misspelled cipher is a compile error, and no unauthenticated cipher exists to choose. The library chooses the mode, the padding and the nonce, as it chooses Core\Password's parameters. Prefer XChaCha20Poly1305 when both ends are Novis. A browser reads Aes256Gcm.

**A key is a secret bytes, and that is part of its type.** ::generateKey answers one, and the compiler will not let a program put it in a plain bytes — so a key cannot be echoed, logged, dumped or carried into a Throwable message by accident. No member here removes the mark: a secret key goes into ::seal and stays a secret, and the private half of a pair leaves its Core\Crypto\KeyPair only as the secret bytes of a PKCS#8.

Sealing a secret message is the deliberate act, and it looks like one: Core\Secret::revealBytes($token, "sealed under a key the store cannot read"). That reads like friction and is the mechanism — turning a secret into bytes that leave the process is the one event worth being able to grep for.

**::open answers the plaintext or it throws.** There is no false and no ?bytes. A message altered by a single octet — the cheapest tamper there is — is refused, where an unauthenticated mode would hand back whatever is left of the plaintext and let the program act on it. Every way of failing to be authentic produces one message: altered, truncated, under the wrong key, or under the other cipher are indistinguishable on purpose, because telling them apart tells a forger which half of the attempt landed.

Each ::seal draws its own nonce and prefixes it to the answer, so the same message under the same key seals differently every time and the caller never keeps a counter. Under XChaCha20Poly1305 a sealed message is exactly 40 octets longer than its plaintext; under Aes256Gcm it is 28, the shorter nonce being WebCrypto's own IV.

<?nvs
secret bytes $key = Core\Crypto::generateKey();
bytes $message = 'attack at dawn' as bytes;

// No mode, no padding, no IV — and 40 octets of overhead, flat.
bytes $sealed = Core\Crypto::seal($message, $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305);
if (Core\Bytes::length($sealed) == Core\Bytes::length($message) + 40) {
    echo "sealed, 40 octets over\n";
}

if (Core\Crypto::open($sealed, $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305) == $message) {
    echo "and it opens\n";
}

// The nonce is drawn per call, so the same message never seals the same way.
if (Core\Crypto::seal($message, $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305) != $sealed) {
    echo "a fresh nonce every time\n";
}

// One octet short is a forgery, and an authenticated mode says so.
bytes $tampered = Core\Bytes::slice($sealed, 0, (Core\Bytes::length($sealed) as int) - 1);
try {
    bytes $forged = Core\Crypto::open($tampered, $key, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305);
    echo "tamper accepted\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $refused) {
    echo "tamper refused\n";
}

// So is an intact message under a key that did not seal it.
secret bytes $other = Core\Crypto::generateKey();
try {
    bytes $wrong = Core\Crypto::open($sealed, $other, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305);
    echo "opened under the wrong key\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $notThisKey) {
    echo "the wrong key is refused\n";
}
sealed, 40 octets over
and it opens
a fresh nonce every time
tamper refused
the wrong key is refused

## Two derivations, and which one a value belongs to

A key comes from one of three places: it is drawn, it is stretched out of something a person chose, or it is spread out of something already uniform. ::generateKey draws, ::deriveKey stretches with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, and ::expandKey spreads with HKDF-SHA256. All three answer the same 32 octets, so whichever one produced a key, ::seal takes it.

They are not interchangeable, and the difference is what the input is. A password has little entropy and is guessed offline, so stretching it is slow on purpose: the iteration count is a required argument, refused below 100,000 and above 2,000,000, and the salt is at least 16 octets. Nothing about a Core\Crypto::expandKey call is slow — it is two HMAC runs — because the secret going into it is already uniform, which a password is not. No type tells the two apart, so this is the one choice here a program makes for itself.

$info is what makes one root secret into as many keys as a program has uses for. Two calls over one secret with different context strings answer unrelated keys, which is how a service stops reusing one secret at two call sites without storing a second one.

<?nvs
// A password is stretched. The count is the call's, because whoever wrote a
// derived key down is the one who chose what it was derived under.
bytes $salt = Core\Random::bytes(16);
secret bytes $fromPassword = Core\Crypto::deriveKey('correct horse battery staple', $salt, 100000);

// Material that is already uniform is spread instead, and `$info` keeps two
// uses of one secret apart.
secret bytes $root = Core\Crypto::generateKey();
secret bytes $forCookies = Core\Crypto::expandKey($root, $salt, 'cookies');
secret bytes $forTokens = Core\Crypto::expandKey($root, $salt, 'tokens');
if ($forCookies != $forTokens) {
    echo "one secret, two keys\n";
}

// Either answer is a key like any other, and is a `secret bytes` like any
// other: neither derivation is a way out of the qualifier.
bytes $message = 'attack at dawn' as bytes;
bytes $sealed = Core\Crypto::seal($message, $fromPassword, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305);
if (Core\Crypto::open($sealed, $fromPassword, Core\Crypto::Cipher::XChaCha20Poly1305) == $message) {
    echo "a derived key seals like a drawn one\n";
}

// The count is bounded on both sides. Under the floor the answer is cheap to
// attack; over the ceiling one call is a denial of service against the process
// that made it, which is what stops a token naming its own.
try {
    secret bytes $cheap = Core\Crypto::deriveKey('correct horse battery staple', $salt, 1000);
    echo "1000 rounds accepted\n";
} catch (LogicError $outside) {
    echo "1000 rounds refused\n";
}
one secret, two keys
a derived key seals like a drawn one
1000 rounds refused

## A pair, and which half each member wants

A Core\Crypto\KeyPair is both halves of one key, and Core\Crypto\PublicKey is the half that is sent. ::generateKeyPair draws a pair of the kind it is given — P256, X25519 or Ed25519 — and refuses both RSA kinds, which are read from whatever PKCS#8 the issuer wrote rather than drawn here. A pair crosses a restart through $pair->write(), its PKCS#8, and a peer's key crosses the wire through $publicKey->write($format) and Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read($encoded, $kind, $format) over Raw, Spki and Jwk — WebCrypto's own three export encodings. **A public key is validated at read**: a point that is not on the curve, a coordinate of the wrong width or an RSA modulus outside 2048 to 8192 bits never becomes a Core\Crypto\PublicKey at all, so no later member can be handed a key nobody looked at.

<!-- src: rule:security/algorithm-comes-from-the-key --> The key's kind is the algorithm, at every member. A P256 or X25519 pair agrees and signs nothing or agrees nothing respectively; ::sign writes ECDSA under P256, Ed25519 under Ed25519 and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 or RSASSA-PSS under the RSA kind the key was read as. Nothing takes an algorithm argument that could disagree with the key it was given, and a pair asked for the operation its kind does not do is a LogicError rather than a weaker answer. ::agree answers the shared secret as material for ::expandKey, never as a key: a raw ECDH output is biased and is spread before it seals anything.

<?nvs
// Each end draws a pair and sends the half that is public, in the encoding the
// other end reads. `Raw` is the 32 octets a browser exports for a curve.
Core\Crypto\KeyPair $mine = Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair(Core\Crypto\KeyKind::X25519);
Core\Crypto\KeyPair $theirs = Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair(Core\Crypto\KeyKind::X25519);
bytes $sent = $mine->publicKey()->write(Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Raw);

// What arrives is read back before anything uses it, under the kind and the
// encoding the protocol says it is in.
Core\Crypto\PublicKey $peer = Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read(
    $theirs->publicKey()->write(Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Raw),
    Core\Crypto\KeyKind::X25519,
    Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Raw,
);
Core\Crypto\PublicKey $me = Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read(
    $sent,
    Core\Crypto\KeyKind::X25519,
    Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format::Raw,
);

// Both ends agree the same secret from opposite halves and spread it into a
// key, which is a key like any other: it seals here and opens there.
bytes $salt = 'a salt both ends know' as bytes;
secret bytes $ours = Core\Crypto::expandKey(Core\Crypto::agree($mine, $peer), $salt, 'session');
secret bytes $yours = Core\Crypto::expandKey(Core\Crypto::agree($theirs, $me), $salt, 'session');
bytes $sealed = Core\Crypto::seal('ping' as bytes, $ours, Core\Crypto::Cipher::Aes256Gcm);
if (Core\Crypto::open($sealed, $yours, Core\Crypto::Cipher::Aes256Gcm) == ('ping' as bytes)) {
    echo "one secret, agreed from both ends\n";
}

// A signing pair is a different kind, and `::verify` answers nothing at all —
// there is no boolean here for a loose comparison to get wrong.
Core\Crypto\KeyPair $signing = Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair(Core\Crypto\KeyKind::Ed25519);
bytes $announcement = 'the service says this' as bytes;
bytes $signature = Core\Crypto::sign($announcement, $signing);
Core\Crypto::verify($announcement, $signature, $signing->publicKey());
echo 'signed and verified, ', Core\Bytes::length($signature), " octets\n";

// Another message under the same signature is a forgery, with the one sentence
// every refusal here gets.
try {
    Core\Crypto::verify('the service says something else' as bytes, $signature, $signing->publicKey());
    echo "another message took the signature\n";
} catch (RuntimeError $notThisMessage) {
    echo "another message is refused\n";
}

// And the X25519 pair signs nothing: that is a bug in the program, not a
// verdict on anyone, so it is a `LogicError`.
try {
    bytes $never = Core\Crypto::sign($announcement, $mine);
    echo "a curve for agreement signed\n";
} catch (LogicError $signsNothing) {
    echo "an agreement key signs nothing\n";
}
one secret, agreed from both ends
signed and verified, 64 octets
another message is refused
an agreement key signs nothing

classes.name: Core\Crypto\KeyPair
classes.summary: A private key together with its public key. You use it to sign data and to agree on a shared secret with another party's public key.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a stored private key, as DER PKCS#8 or as one PEM PRIVATE KEY block. A service-account file has this form. The key is parsed here, so later methods can use the pair without parsing it again.

params.name: pkcs8
params.descHtml: The bytes of the key, as write returned them, or as the issuer of the key wrote them.

params.name: kind
params.descHtml: The kind of the key. You must give it, for the same reason as in Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read. A PKCS#8 key says that it is RSA, but not whether it is for RS256 or PS256.

doc.returnHtml: The key pair, ready to sign or to agree. Its publicKey() method returns the public key, which you can send to others.

errors.descHtml: $pkcs8 is not a PKCS#8 private key of that kind. For example, it is a key of another kind, or a PKCS#1 key. It can be an encrypted PKCS#8, which needs a password, and this method has no password argument. It can be an RSA key outside 2048 to 8192 bits, or any malformed data. A private key belongs to your program, never to the other side. So this error always means that your program was given a wrong key.

doc.shortHtml: Returns this key pair as DER PKCS#8, as secret bytes. A server can store the key between requests and read it back with read. This is the only way to get the private key out of a pair.
doc.returnHtml: The PKCS#8 as DER. It is DER even when the pair was read from PEM.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the public key of this pair, which you can send to others. It is computed from the private key and is not stored next to it. So it is always the public key of this pair, and never a different key that came with it.
doc.returnHtml: The public key, of the same kind as the pair. It is the same value that Core\Crypto\PublicKey::read returns for the key that the other side receives.

classes.summaryHtml: A private key together with its public key. You use it to sign data and to agree on a shared secret with another party's public key.

classes.name: Core\Crypto\PublicKey
classes.summary: The public half of a key pair, such as a key that another server sent you. You use it to check a signature or to agree on a shared secret.

doc.shortHtml: The encoding that a public key is read from or written to. The three cases are the export formats of WebCrypto, with the same names. So you can give a browser a key in the format it asks for.

Reads a public key from $encoded and checks it. For P256, the point must be on the curve. For an RSA kind, the key size must be in the allowed range. For a JWK, its fields must match $kind. A key that fails the check throws an error here. So every method that takes a key gets a checked key.

params.name: encoded
params.descHtml: The bytes of the key, in $format.

params.name: kind
params.descHtml: The kind of the key. You must give it, because the bytes do not always say it. An RSA SubjectPublicKeyInfo says rsaEncryption for both RS256 and PS256 keys. Only your program knows which one the key is for.

params.name: format
params.descHtml: The WebCrypto export format that $encoded is in.

doc.returnHtml: The key, ready to verify a signature or to agree. Its kind() method returns the case it was read as.

errors.descHtml: The kind has no such format, for example Raw with an RSA kind. It is also thrown when the JWK has d, because that is a private key given as a public key.

$encoded is not a public key of that kind in that format. For example, the point is not on the curve, or a coordinate has the wrong size. Or the modulus is outside the allowed range, the DER does not parse, or the JWK names another key type. All these cases have the same message. The key came from the sender, and a reason would tell the sender what was wrong.

doc.shortHtml: Returns this key in $format. The formats are the ones that read accepts, so you can give a browser the key in the format it asks for. The output is made from the key, not from the bytes it was read from. So one key always gives the same bytes in each format.

params.name: format
params.descHtml: The format to write. Jwk gives the fields that RFC 7638 requires, sorted. A thumbprint is computed over this form.

doc.returnHtml: The bytes of the key. For a JWK, this is its UTF-8 JSON.

errors.descHtml: $format is Raw and the key has an RSA kind. An RSA key has no raw form, so there is nothing to return.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the Core\Crypto\KeyKind case of this key. This is the kind that read was given. It is not read again from the key.
doc.returnHtml: The case the key was read as. For an RSA key, it is RsaPkcs1 or RsaPss. This is the scheme of the key, and it is set when the key is read.

classes.summaryHtml: The public half of a key pair, such as a key that another server sent you. You use it to check a signature or to agree on a shared secret.

classes.name: Core\Csrf
classes.summary: Protects forms against cross-site request forgery, a request that another site sends in the user's name. `token` creates a token for the visitor's session, which the server checks on the next request. `issue` creates a token for a value you choose, and `verify` checks one.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a CSRF token for the visitor's session. Put it in a form field named _csrf, in the x-csrf-token header or in a _csrf query parameter. The server checks it on the next request. Call Core\Session::start() first. If the visitor has no session yet, this call creates one and sends its cookie.
doc.returnHtml: A different string on every call. Each one is valid for the whole session. It uses only A-Za-z0-9-_, so a form field, a header and a URL carry it unchanged.

errors.descHtml: The request has not called Core\Session::start(), or [http] csrf_key is not set.
The call runs inside a function passed to Core\Task::afterResponse, after the response was sent. The session cookie cannot be sent then.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a CSRF token for $session, made with $key. Send it in a form field named _csrf, in the x-csrf-token header or in a _csrf query parameter. A form that uploads files must use the header or the query parameter. With [http] csrf_key set, the server checks the token before the handler runs. verify checks it with the same session and key.

params.name: session
params.descHtml: The value the token belongs to. This is a session id, or any other value that does not change while the token should be valid. A token made for one value never passes verify for another value.

params.name: key
params.descHtml: A 32-byte key, such as the one Core\Crypto::generateKey() returns. The key is not part of the token, so you can use the same key for every session.

doc.returnHtml: A URL-safe base64 string without padding. It uses only A-Za-z0-9-_, so a hidden field, a header and a query string can contain it without escaping. Each call returns a different string for the same inputs. Two tokens for one session are never equal, so == cannot check a token.

errors.descHtml: $key is not 32 bytes long. Such a value is not a key.
The process does not have enough memory for the token.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $token was made by issue for $session with $key. This is the only way to check a token. No method returns the expected token, so you cannot compare tokens with ==.

params.name: token
params.descHtml: The token from the request. A tainted value is allowed here, because a token always comes from a request.

params.name: session
params.descHtml: The value you gave issue. A token made for a different session returns false.

params.name: key
params.descHtml: The key you gave issue. When you change the key, every token made with the old key returns false.

doc.returnHtml: true for a token made with this key for this session. false for any other text: a changed token, a token made with an old key, a token for another session, or text that is not base64. The comparison takes the same time in every case. All four cases return the same false, so an attacker cannot learn which check failed.

errors.descHtml: $key is not 32 bytes long. A forged token returns false and never throws. Only a bug in the program throws here.

classes.summaryHtml: Protects forms against cross-site request forgery, a request that another site sends in the user's name. token creates a token for the visitor's session, which the server checks on the next request. issue creates a token for a value you choose, and verify checks one.

classes.name: Core\Csv
classes.summary: Reads CSV text into rows of strings, and writes rows back as CSV. It can use a header row, and a different separator or quote character.

members.name: parse
members.signature: parse(string $text, { separator?: string, quote?: string, escape?: string, header?: bool }): array<array<string>>

doc.shortHtml: Parses the whole CSV document $text into records, with the grammar of RFC 4180. A field may be quoted. Inside a quoted field, two quotes are read as one quote. A record ends at LF or CRLF, and a blank line is not a record.

params.name: text
params.descHtml: The whole CSV document.

params.name: separator
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character between fields. The default is ,.

params.name: quote
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character that quotes a field. The default is ".

params.name: escape
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character that escapes a quote inside a quoted field. The default is the empty string, which means no escape character. Then two quotes are read as one quote, as RFC 4180 says.

params.name: header
params.descHtml: When true, the first record is read as column names, and every returned row uses them as keys. By default, each field has its column number as the key.

doc.returnHtml: One array per record, and every field is a string. The keys are the column numbers. With header, the keys are the names from the header. A field after the last header name keeps its column number. The header row is not in the result. The document never fails to parse, and an empty document gives an empty array.

errors.descHtml: An option for the CSV format is empty, longer than one ASCII character, or CR or LF. It is also thrown when two of separator, quote and escape are the same character.

members.name: format
members.signature: format(array<array<string>> $rows, { separator?: string, quote?: string, header?: array<string> }): string

doc.shortHtml: Writes $rows as a CSV document. A field is quoted only when it contains the separator, the quote, CR or LF. A quote inside a quoted field is doubled. Every record ends with LF, so parse(format($rows)) returns $rows.

params.name: rows
params.descHtml: The records to write. Each record is an array of string fields, written in order, and its keys are ignored. A field can be a tainted string, such as a value read from a database. Then the result is a tainted string too.

params.name: separator
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character written between fields. The default is ,.

params.name: quote
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character that quotes a field. The default is ".

params.name: header
params.descHtml: Column names, written as the first record. The default is null, which writes no header row.

doc.returnHtml: The CSV document. It is an empty string when there are no rows and no header.

errors.descHtml: An option for the CSV format is empty, longer than one ASCII character, or CR or LF. It is also thrown when separator and quote are the same character.

members.name: rows
members.signature: rows(Core\IO\File $file, { separator?: string, quote?: string, escape?: string, header?: bool }): Core\Csv\Rows

doc.shortHtml: Reads an open file one record at a time, in a foreach loop. It uses the same RFC 4180 rules and the same options as parse. Only one record is in memory at a time, so a file larger than memory works. It reads forward from the current position of the file, and you can loop over it only once.

params.name: file
params.descHtml: The open file to read from. Reading starts at its current position.

params.name: separator
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character between fields. The default is ,.

params.name: quote
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character that quotes a field. The default is ".

params.name: escape
params.descHtml: The one ASCII character that escapes a quote inside a quoted field. The default is the empty string, which means no escape character. Then two quotes are read as one quote, as RFC 4180 says.

params.name: header
params.descHtml: When true, the first record is read as column names, and every record uses them as keys. By default, each field has its column number as the key.

doc.returnHtml: The records, one at a time. Each record is an array of string fields with the same keys that parse gives. Nothing is read until the loop starts.

errors.descHtml: An option for the CSV format is empty, longer than one ASCII character, or CR or LF. It is also thrown when two of separator, quote and escape are the same character, or the file was closed before or during the loop.
The operating system could not read the file during the loop.
A field is not valid UTF-8. The message gives the line where the field ends, and the loop stops there.

classes.summaryHtml:
Reads CSV text into rows of strings, and writes rows back as CSV. It can use a header row, and a different separator or quote character.

Core\Csv::parse reads a whole document into array<array<string>> — every field is a string, quoted fields and embedded newlines included. With { header: true } the first record is consumed as column names and every row is keyed by them; without it a row's keys are "0", "1", …. format writes each row by its values in order (its keys are ignored), quotes a field only where a byte would change the parse, and { header: [...] } writes a first record. A field can be a tainted string, such as a value read from a database, and then the document is a tainted string too. The dialect options separator, quote and escape are single ASCII bytes.

<?nvs
string $doc = "name,qty,note\nfig,2,ripe\nplum,10,\"a, b\"\n";
var $rows = Core\Csv::parse($doc, { header: true });
echo Core\Arr::count($rows), " rows\n";
foreach ($rows as array<string> $row) {
    echo $row['name'], '=', $row['qty'], ' (', $row['note'], ")\n";
}

var $plain = Core\Csv::parse("a;b\n1;2\n", { separator: ';' });
echo $plain['1']['0'], '+', $plain['1']['1'], "\n";

array<array<string>> $out = [['fig', '2'], ['plum', 'a, b']];
echo Core\Csv::format($out, { header: ['item', 'note'] });
2 rows
fig=2 (ripe)
plum=10 (a, b)
1+2
item,note
fig,2
plum,"a, b"

classes.name: Core\Csv\Rows
classes.summary: The rows of a CSV file, read one at a time while a `foreach` loop runs. The whole file is never in memory at once.
classes.summaryHtml: The rows of a CSV file, read one at a time while a foreach loop runs. The whole file is never in memory at once.

classes.name: Core\Db
classes.summary: Opens a connection to a database. The name of a connection in the server's configuration is enough, or the program can give the settings itself.

doc.shortHtml: How much a TCP connection checks the server's identity before it sends credentials. Every connection uses VerifyFull, and it is the default when the settings name no mode. The three weaker modes throw an error. A connection that checks less than it promises is a security hole.

members.name: connect
members.signature: connect(string $name, { shared?: bool, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }): Core\Db\Connection

doc.shortHtml: Opens the database connection that a [db.<name>] block of nvs.toml describes. Later calls in the same request return the same connection. The password is in the configuration file, not in the program. It needs the db.connect capability for that name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The block to open. It must match exactly: "main" is [db.main]. Two blocks for the same server give two connections, because whoever wrote two blocks wanted two.

params.name: shared
params.descHtml: Whether this call may return the connection that an earlier call opened. false opens a separate connection. You need one for a write that must stay after a rollback, for a session lock, or for a second statement during a stream.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long opening the connection may take, including the DNS lookup and TLS. Without it, only the server and the network limit the time.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Connection. The same call twice in one request returns the same object, unless shared is false. The connection is closed when the request ends.

errors.descHtml: db.connect does not grant $name, or there is no [db.<name>] block of that name. It is also thrown when the block does not describe a valid connection. Examples are a missing driver, a setting of another driver, or a time_zone that is not an offset.

The host name does not resolve, or the connection, the TLS handshake or the login failed. It is also thrown when this CPU core already uses [db.<name>.pool] max connections with that name and none is free within acquire. When the server sends its own error message, the error includes it.

members.name: open
members.signature: open({ driver: Core\Db\Driver::MySql|Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb|Core\Db\Driver::Postgres|Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer, host: string, port?: uint, database: tainted string, user: tainted string, password: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Db::Tls, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, statementCache?: uint }|{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite, path: string, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration } $settings, { shared?: bool }): Core\Db\Connection

params.name: settings
params.type: { driver: Core\Db\Driver::MySql|Core\Db\Driver::MariaDb|Core\Db\Driver::Postgres|Core\Db\Driver::SqlServer, host: string, port?: uint, database: tainted string, user: tainted string, password: secret tainted string, tls?: Core\Db::Tls, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration, statementCache?: uint }|{ driver: Core\Db\Driver::Sqlite, path: string, timeZone?: Core\Time\Zone, timeout?: Core\Time\Duration }

doc.shortHtml: Opens a connection to a server that the program names itself. Use it when a [db.<name>] block does not work. Examples are a customer whose database is stored as a row in another database, or an admin tool where a person types a host. It needs the db.open capability for that host. The address is fully checked against the blocked address ranges. This check is stricter than for connect.

params.name: settings
params.descHtml: All settings of the connection. The object has one of two shapes, and driver selects the shape. Four of the five databases need a host, and SQLite needs a file path.

shape.descHtml: Which database this is. It selects which of the two shapes the rest of the object must have.
The server to connect to. Its certificate is checked against this name. It cannot be tainted, and no check can remove that, because no check on a string proves that a host is safe for a password.
The port to connect to. Without it, the driver's default is used: 5432 for PostgreSQL, and 3306 for MySQL and MariaDB.
The database or schema to use. It may be tainted, because it is sent as a separate value and never read as SQL.
The role to log in as. It may be tainted for the same reason.
The role's password. It is secret, so it cannot reach a log line, a message or a trace.
How much of the certificate is checked. Only VerifyFull works, and it is the default. The three weaker modes throw an error.
The time zone for reading a column that has no time zone. The server is also told to use it. The default is UTC.
How long opening the connection may take, including the DNS lookup and TLS.
How many prepared statements this connection may keep on the server. 0 turns the cache off.
The SQLite file, used in place of a host. It cannot be tainted, and it also needs the fs.read and fs.write capabilities.

params.name: shared
params.descHtml: Whether this call may return the connection that an earlier call opened with the same settings. false opens a separate connection.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Connection. It is closed when the request ends. Two calls with the same value in every setting return the same object, unless shared is false.

errors.descHtml: db.open does not grant the host, or the host's address is in a private range that net.internal does not allow. It is also thrown when this build cannot open a connection with these settings, or when tls names a mode weaker than VerifyFull.

The host name does not resolve, or the connection, the TLS handshake or the login failed. It is also thrown when this CPU core already uses its max connections with these settings and none became free in time.

doc.shortHtml: Binds $values as a list of values. The placeholder it is bound to becomes a list in parentheses with one placeholder per value, such as IN (?, ?, ?). Nothing else in a statement changes the SQL text.

params.name: values
params.descHtml: The values to bind, one placeholder each, in the order of the array. Keys are ignored: the values fill positions inside one placeholder and have no names.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\InList to bind to a single placeholder. It has no methods, and you can use it only as a bound parameter. Two lists of different lengths with the same SQL are two entries in the statement cache. The expanded statement has a different number of placeholders.

errors.descHtml: $values is empty. An empty list means "match nothing" inside IN and "match everything" inside NOT IN. Check for an empty list in your code instead.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $name is a plain SQL identifier: a letter or _, then letters, digits or _. It returns the name unchanged and no longer tainted, so you can write it into the text of a statement. Use it for a table or column name. It checks the syntax only. A visitor can still name any table or column, such as users. If a visitor chooses the name, check it against a list of allowed names first.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The identifier to check. It is returned exactly as given. Nothing is escaped, shortened or lower-cased, because a name that passes the check needs none of it.

doc.returnHtml: The same text, without the tainted qualifier. It has no quotes around it. This method has no connection, so it has no SQL dialect. The five databases use different quote characters.

errors.descHtml: $name is empty, starts with a digit, or contains a character that is not a letter, a digit or _. This includes a name that is valid only inside quotes. It is also thrown when the database reads $name as a value without quotes, such as current_user, user or current_timestamp, in upper or lower case.

classes.summaryHtml: Opens a connection to a database. The name of a connection in the server's configuration is enough, or the program can give the settings itself.

classes.name: Core\Db\Column
classes.summary: Describes one column of a query result: its name, its type, and whether it can contain `null`.

doc.shortHtml: The type a result column was declared with. It describes the column, not the value you get when you read it. For example, a JSON column and a TEXT column both read as tainted string. This type tells them apart, if the database has a separate type for each.
Returns the column's label as the server described it. If the select list gives the column an alias, the label is the alias.
doc.returnHtml: The label. It is not a unique key: select a, a gives two columns with one label. So read a column by its position in the array that columns() returns.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the type the column was declared with, as a Core\Db\Column::Type case. Each database has its own type names, but the cases are the same for every database.
doc.returnHtml: The case. It describes the column, not the value you get when you read it. For example, a JSON column and a TEXT column both read as tainted string, and this case tells them apart. A type with no matching Novis type is Other. This includes every array and, on PostgreSQL, every ENUM.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether the column can contain NULL. On PostgreSQL this is always true. The server does not send a NOT NULL flag with the result. Only an extra catalog query for each statement could find it, and this driver does not run one.
doc.returnHtml: true for every column this driver describes, so treat every column as nullable. The typed methods of Core\Db\Row already do this, and each returns ?T. A database that sends the flag gives its value here.

classes.summaryHtml: Describes one column of a query result: its name, its type, and whether it can contain null.

classes.name: Core\Db\Connection
classes.summary: An open connection to one database. It runs SQL queries and statements, and it starts transactions.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement with its values bound, and reads every row it returns into memory. Every statement is prepared, so there is no separate prepare step. The connection is free again as soon as this returns. stream keeps the connection while you read.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, with a ? or a :name for each value. Never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array. A Core\Db::inList element expands into several placeholders at its position. Nothing else expands.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Rows<Core\Db\Row> with every row the statement returned, in the server's order. A statement that returns no rows, such as an update or a create table, gives an empty result. It is not an error.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a :name has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an inList. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.

The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.
The connection failed while the statement was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement as query does and returns each row as an object of the class written at the call site. #[Db\Derive] generates the mapping from the class's declared properties.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, bound the same way as in query. Use a ? or a :name for each value, and never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind, with the same rule as query: one array, with list keys for ? and string keys for :name.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Rows<T> with one T per row, in the server's order. Each object is created when you read its row with all, first or a foreach. If you only count the rows, no object is created.

errors.descHtml: The type argument is an array<...>. A result is already a list of arrays, one per row. It is also thrown when T has no #[Db\Derive], so there is no column mapping to create it from. Both errors come from the call itself, but they are found when the program runs.

A row did not match T. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not ?T, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of the row is reported at once in issues, and each path is the column's name.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement that changes data, such as an insert, an update, a delete or a create table. It returns how many rows changed and the new key, if there is one. The values are bound the same way query binds them.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, with a ? or a :name for each value. Never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array. This is the same rule as in query.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Write with the number of affected rows as the server reported it, and the id that a RETURNING clause returned. Any rows the statement returned are read and discarded, so the connection is free again. Use query to keep rows.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a :name has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an inList. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.
The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message.
The connection failed while the statement was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement once for each set of values and returns how many rows the whole batch wrote. The statement is prepared once, and all sets go to the server in one round trip.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, written once and bound once for each set. A tainted string does not compile here, as in execute. All sets use this one text.

params.name: sets
params.descHtml: One $params array for each run, each with keys as execute needs them. All sets must bind the same number of values. A set whose inList has a different length is a different statement.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: The sum of the counts each run reported. A command that reports no count adds nothing. An empty $sets writes nothing and returns 0. Rows from a RETURNING clause are discarded. There is no lastId, because no single run owns it.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. A set uses both list keys and string keys, two sets bind different numbers of values, or an element cannot be bound. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.

The server rejected one run, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. Each run is its own transaction, so the writes before the failed run stay. Use transaction to save all or nothing.
The connection failed while the batch was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement and gives its rows one at a time to a foreach loop. The connection stays open until the loop ends. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are. Use it instead of query for a large result.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, bound the same way as in query. Use a ? or a :name for each value, and never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind, with the same rule as query. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long reading all the rows may take. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError, and the connection cannot be used again. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: The statement's rows for a foreach loop, each one a Core\Db\Row, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy until the loop reaches the last row, and no other statement can run on it. A loop that writes for each row needs a second connection ({ shared: false }), or query instead.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a :name has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it.
The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.
The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or timeout passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a result one row at a time as stream does, and builds each row into an object of the class written at the call site, as queryAs does. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, bound the same way as in query. Use a ? or a :name for each value, and never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind, with the same rule as query. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long reading all the rows may take, with the same rule as stream. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: The statement's rows for a foreach loop, each one created as a T, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy, as with stream. Only one T exists at a time. That is the only difference from queryAs.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, a :name has no element, or an element cannot be bound. It is also thrown when the connection is closed, or when a statement is already streaming on it. A T without #[Db\Derive] also throws it here, although the compiler already reports that.

A row did not match T. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not ?T, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of that row is reported at once in issues, and each path is the column's name. The loop stops there, because the rest of the result is not read.
The server rejected the statement, at the start or while the rows were read. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.
The connection failed while the statement or one of its rows was being sent, or timeout passed before the loop ended. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

members.name: transaction
members.signature: transaction(callable(Core\Db\Transaction): T $fn, { isolation?: Core\Db\Isolation, readOnly?: bool, retries?: uint }): T

doc.shortHtml: Runs $fn inside a transaction and returns what $fn returns. If $fn returns, the transaction is committed. If $fn throws, the transaction is rolled back and the error is thrown again. An early return cannot leave the transaction open.

params.name: fn
params.descHtml: The work to run. It gets a Core\Db\Transaction, which has the same query methods as the connection. The function may declare that parameter or no parameter.

params.name: isolation
params.descHtml: How much this transaction can see of other transactions running at the same time. Without it, the transaction uses the level set on the server. A nested call cannot set it. The level is for the whole transaction, not for a savepoint inside it.

params.name: readOnly
params.descHtml: Writes are not allowed during the transaction, so the server can plan for reads only. The default is false. A nested call cannot set it, for the same reason as isolation.

params.name: retries
params.descHtml: How many times $fn runs again when the commit reports a deadlock or a serialization failure. This applies to the outermost transaction only. The default is 0, because a function with side effects should run again only when you ask for it. Nothing else is retried, and there is no wait between attempts. A conflict from a statement inside $fn is thrown and not retried.

doc.returnHtml: What $fn returned, after the commit. A nested call on the same connection is a savepoint. So you can call a function that wraps its own writes in a transaction from inside another transaction.

errors.descHtml: $fn called rollBack. This call throws it even if code inside $fn caught it, because the rollback is recorded on the transaction itself.

A statement inside $fn was not allowed because of the way it was written. It is also thrown when the transaction is used after its transaction() call returned, or when a nested call sets its own isolation or readOnly.
The server rejected the BEGIN, or rejected the COMMIT after $fn returned, for example for a serialization failure or a deferred constraint. In both cases nothing is committed.
The connection failed while the transaction was open. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the connection to the pool before the request that opened it ends. After that, every other method of this connection throws an error. isOpen returns false, and a second close does nothing.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The only effect is that the connection goes back to the pool, and a program cannot use the pool directly.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the database this connection uses. This is the Core\Db\Driver case that the [db.<name>] block or the open settings named.
doc.returnHtml: The connection's own Core\Db\Driver case.

errors.descHtml: The connection has been closed.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the version the database server reported, exactly as it reported it. This is PostgreSQL's server_version, the greeting banner of MySQL and MariaDB, major.minor.build from the SQL Server login reply, or SQLite's library version. The server sent it when the connection opened, so reading it runs no statement. You can call it while a stream is using the connection.
doc.returnHtml: The version. It is never empty and never changed. A suffix that a distribution adds is part of it.

errors.descHtml: The connection has been closed.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether this connection can still be used. It returns true until close is called, and false after that. It is the only method that works on a closed connection.
doc.returnHtml: true if statements can still run on the connection. false if close has returned it to the pool.

classes.summaryHtml: An open connection to one database. It runs SQL queries and statements, and it starts transactions.

classes.name: Core\Db\InList
classes.summary: A list of values for a SQL `IN (...)` condition. You can use it only as a bound parameter of a query.
classes.summaryHtml: A list of values for a SQL IN (...) condition. You can use it only as a bound parameter of a query.

classes.name: Core\Db\Plan
classes.summary: Every difference between a schema and a database, as a list of steps. A program can read the steps before any of them runs.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every step of the plan in the order they must run, including reports.
doc.returnHtml: The steps. An empty array means the database already matches the schema. No apply runs a step whose isRefused() is true.

classes.summaryHtml: Every difference between a schema and a database, as a list of steps. A program can read the steps before any of them runs.

classes.name: Core\Db\Plan\Step
classes.summary: One difference in a plan: how risky the change is, the reason for that grade, and the SQL that makes the change.

doc.shortHtml: The worst risk of one step of a schema plan. A deployment can use it to run only the steps it is willing to run without a person watching.
Returns the worst risk of this step.
doc.returnHtml: Safe, Locking or Destructive. The grade is the worst case, not the likely case. When there is no rule for a change, it gets the higher grade. Too high a grade costs one confirmation, and too low a grade can cost an outage.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one sentence for a person that says why the step has its grade.
doc.returnHtml: The sentence. It is written for the same database as the SQL. So it gives the reason for that database, such as a table rewrite that this server does and another does not.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the complete SQL of this step, with terminators, in the right dialect for the database. It is never shortened, also for a step that no apply runs. Some applications cannot run DDL and give the plan to a database administrator. A summary does not help there.
doc.returnHtml: The statements, one per line. Most steps are one statement, and you can pass it directly to Core\Db::execute. SQLite's table rebuild is four statements. A person pastes those, and a program does not run them.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether this step is a report. A report is a table, column or key that the database has and the schema does not name.
doc.returnHtml: true for a step that no apply ever runs. Something missing from the schema is never deleted. A database is often shared with a queue, a reporting view or tables an administrator added. A program that wants the drop runs this step's sql().

classes.summaryHtml: One difference in a plan: how risky the change is, the reason for that grade, and the SQL that makes the change.

classes.name: Core\Db\Row
classes.summary: One row of a query result. Its methods read a column by name and return it as a given type.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether the row has a column with this name. Call it first when a method would throw an error for an unknown column.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it. It may be tainted, because this method returns a result and does not throw.

doc.returnHtml: true if the row has the column, whatever its value. A NULL column is present. false otherwise.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column's value, as whatever Novis type the SQL type maps to. It reads any column. Use as to narrow the value when no typed method fits.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The value, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole row as an array with string keys, in the server's column order.
doc.returnHtml: An array<mixed> with the column labels as keys. A NULL column is a null entry, and the key is present.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as string. It reads text columns only: CHAR, VARCHAR, TEXT, ENUM and JSON. Each gives a tainted string.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The text, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not text. A BYTEA is bytes, so read it with ->bytes. A number is not converted to text here.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as bytes. It reads BINARY, BLOB and BYTEA columns. These have no text form, and bytes is a separate type from string.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The bytes as tainted bytes, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is text. Text and bytes are separate types, and this method reads only bytes.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as int. It reads SMALLINT, INT and BIGINT, and an unsigned column whose value fits.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The integer, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, the column is not an integer, or it is an unsigned value larger than the largest int.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as uint. It reads an UNSIGNED integer on MySQL and MariaDB, and a signed column that is not negative.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The integer, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, the column is not an integer, or its value is negative. A negative value cannot be converted to uint.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as float. It reads only FLOAT, REAL and DOUBLE.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The number, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not a floating-point column. A DECIMAL is exact, so read it with ->decimal. Binary floating point gives wrong sums for money.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as bool. It reads BOOLEAN, BIT(1), and an integer column that contains 0 or 1. Use it to read a TINYINT(1) on MySQL and MariaDB. That column is an int, and this method converts it.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The truth value, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is neither boolean nor an integer. It is also thrown for an integer other than 0 or 1. A stored 7 throws this error.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as an exact decimal. It reads DECIMAL, NUMERIC and MONEY columns.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The exact number, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not an exact numeric one.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as a Core\Time\Instant. It reads TIMESTAMPTZ and datetimeoffset, the two types that store their own time zone.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The instant, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not a timestamp with a time zone. A timestamp without a time zone is a Core\Time\DateTime in the time zone set for the connection.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as a Core\Time\Date. It reads a DATE, which is a calendar day with no time.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The day, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not a DATE.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as a Core\Time\TimeOfDay. It reads a TIME, which is a time of day with no date.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The time of day, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not a TIME.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one column as a Core\Uuid. It reads PostgreSQL's UUID, SQL Server's uniqueidentifier and the UUID of MariaDB 10.7 and later. MySQL stores a UUID as BINARY(16), and that column is bytes.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The column label, as the server described it.

doc.returnHtml: The identifier, or null for a NULL column.

errors.descHtml: The row has no column with that name, or the column is not a UUID type. A BINARY(16) is bytes, and a UUID stored as text is a string.

classes.summaryHtml: One row of a query result. Its methods read a column by name and return it as a given type.

classes.name: Core\Db\Rows
classes.summary: The whole result of a query, read into memory at once. A `foreach` loop gives its rows one by one.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every row of the result, in the order the server sent them.
doc.returnHtml: An array<T>. It is empty for a statement that returned no rows. T is a Core\Db\Row for query, and the class you named for queryAs<T>. The rows are already read, so this creates one object for each row and decodes nothing again.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the first row, or null if there is none. A second call returns the same row.
doc.returnHtml: A T, as all describes it, or null for an empty result. Everywhere in Core, ?T means that a value can be missing. A query that matched nothing is not an error.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the first column of the first row. Use it to read the result of a select count(*).
doc.returnHtml: That column's value, or null if the result has no rows. A NULL column also gives null, because the declared type is mixed. To tell the two apart, call count() first.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the value of one column from every row, in the order the server sent them.

params.name: key
params.descHtml: The column. An int is its position in the server's column list, counted from zero. A string is its label.

doc.returnHtml: An array<mixed> with one entry per row, empty for a result with no rows.

errors.descHtml: No column has that name, or the position is negative or past the last column. An empty result returns an empty array and does not throw.

doc.shortHtml: Returns how many rows the statement returned. For the number of rows a write changed, use Core\Db\Write::affected.
doc.returnHtml: The number of rows in the result. It is exact, because query reads all rows before it returns.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a description of each column of the result, as one Core\Db\Column per column. The columns are in the order the server sent them.
doc.returnHtml: The columns. An empty result has them too. A select that matched nothing still describes the columns it would return, so you can read them before any row.

classes.summaryHtml: The whole result of a query, read into memory at once. A foreach loop gives its rows one by one.

classes.name: Core\Db\Schema
classes.summary: Describes the tables a database should have. You can compare it with a real database and apply the changes that make them match.

doc.shortHtml: Creates a schema from its standard array form. This is the form that toArray returns, that a schema file contains and that nvs schema dump prints. Every rule is checked here, so any schema value works with all five databases.

params.name: array
params.descHtml: The schema, as ["tables" => [...]]. A table has name, columns, and optionally primary_key, unique and indexes. A column has name and type, and optionally null, identity and a one-key default. A missing key means the empty list or false.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Schema in normalized form: tables in name order, columns in declaration order, and every optional key filled in. So toArray returns the same array for every way to write one schema. This is what makes two schemas comparable.

errors.descHtml: A key is missing or has the wrong type of value, a type name is not supported, or an identifier is not a plain identifier. It is also thrown when the schema is not consistent. Examples are a table with no columns, a second identity column, an identity column outside the primary key, or an index on a missing column.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the schema in its standard array form. You can save it to a file, pass it to Core\Json::encode, or compare it with another schema.
doc.returnHtml: The array that fromArray reads back as the same schema. Tables are in name order. Columns are in the order they were declared, because create table keeps that order. Constraints and indexes are in name order, because the order they were added in has no effect.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the database of this connection and returns every difference between it and this schema. The differences are in the order they must be fixed. Making a plan changes nothing. An empty plan means the database already matches the schema.

params.name: connection
params.descHtml: The database to compare with. Planning only reads, so it needs only the db.connect capability this connection was opened with.

doc.returnHtml: The plan. Each of its steps() has a grade, Safe, Locking or Destructive, and the complete SQL for the change. A table or column that the database has and this schema does not is a report. It is in the plan with the SQL that would remove it, but no apply ever runs it.

errors.descHtml: The database has a type, a default or an identifier that a schema cannot describe, so a plan could not cover every difference.

doc.shortHtml: Makes a plan for this connection and runs it, but only if every step it would run is graded Safe. It needs the db.schema capability for the connection's block. Running DDL needs this extra permission, beyond access to the database.

params.name: connection
params.descHtml: The database to change. db.schema is granted for the name of its [db.<name>] block. So you cannot use a connection from Core\Db::open here.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Afterwards the database matches the schema. Only what the schema does not declare is different: it is reported and not changed.

errors.descHtml: The plan has a step that is not Safe, and the message names it. It is also thrown when the connection has no block to grant db.schema for, and for every error that planAgainst throws.
The db.schema capability is not granted for this connection's block.

doc.shortHtml: Works like applySafe, without the grade check. It runs every step of the plan. This includes steps that can hold a long lock, rewrite a table or fail on rows that already exist. The long name shows a reviewer the risk at the call.

params.name: connection
params.descHtml: The database to change. It works as in applySafe, and needs the same db.schema capability.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. A reported drop still does not run, because a risky change is not the same as data loss. The step has the SQL for the drop if a program wants to run it.

errors.descHtml: The connection has no block to grant db.schema for. It is also thrown for every error that planAgainst throws.
The db.schema capability is not granted for this connection's block.

classes.summaryHtml: Describes the tables a database should have. You can compare it with a real database and apply the changes that make them match.

classes.name: Core\Db\Stream
classes.summary: The rows of a query, read from the database one at a time while a `foreach` loop runs. Use it for a result too big to keep in memory.
classes.summaryHtml: The rows of a query, read from the database one at a time while a foreach loop runs. Use it for a result too big to keep in memory.

classes.name: Core\Db\Transaction
classes.summary: Runs SQL statements inside one transaction. Either all of their changes are saved, or none of them are.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement with its values bound, and reads every row it returns into memory. Every statement is prepared, so there is no separate prepare step. The connection is free again as soon as this returns. stream keeps the connection while you read.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, with a ? or a :name for each value. Never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array. A Core\Db::inList element expands into several placeholders at its position. Nothing else expands.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Rows<Core\Db\Row> with every row the statement returned, in the server's order. A statement that returns no rows, such as an update or a create table, gives an empty result. It is not an error.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a :name has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an inList. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.

The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message. It is also thrown for a column type this driver cannot read yet.
The connection failed while the statement was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement as query does and returns each row as an object of the class written at the call site. #[Db\Derive] generates the mapping from the class's declared properties.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, bound the same way as in query. Use a ? or a :name for each value, and never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind, with the same rule as query: one array, with list keys for ? and string keys for :name.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Rows<T> with one T per row, in the server's order. Each object is created when you read its row with all, first or a foreach. If you only count the rows, no object is created.

errors.descHtml: The type argument is an array<...>. A result is already a list of arrays, one per row. It is also thrown when T has no #[Db\Derive], so there is no column mapping to create it from. Both errors come from the call itself, but they are found when the program runs.

A row did not match T. A column is missing, or has a different type than the property. A SQL NULL is in a property that is not ?T, or a property's type has no column mapping. Every bad column of the row is reported at once in issues, and each path is the column's name.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement that changes data, such as an insert, an update, a delete or a create table. It returns how many rows changed and the new key, if there is one. The values are bound the same way query binds them.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, with a ? or a :name for each value. Never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here, and no escape function can make one allowed.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array. This is the same rule as in query.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Db\Write with the number of affected rows as the server reported it, and the id that a RETURNING clause returned. Any rows the statement returned are read and discarded, so the connection is free again. Use query to keep rows.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. The placeholders and the array use different styles or different counts, or a :name has no element. It is also thrown for an element that cannot be bound, such as an array or an object that is not an inList. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.
The server rejected the statement, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. The error has the server's SQLSTATE and message.
The connection failed while the statement was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement once for each set of values and returns how many rows the whole batch wrote. The statement is prepared once, and all sets go to the server in one round trip.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, written once and bound once for each set. A tainted string does not compile here, as in execute. All sets use this one text.

params.name: sets
params.descHtml: One $params array for each run, each with keys as execute needs them. All sets must bind the same number of values. A set whose inList has a different length is a different statement.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long this statement may take. The limit covers the whole statement: the prepare, the execution and every row of the result. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError. The connection cannot be used again, because it stopped in the middle of a message. Without it, the statement waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: The sum of the counts each run reported. A command that reports no count adds nothing. An empty $sets writes nothing and returns 0. Rows from a RETURNING clause are discarded. There is no lastId, because no single run owns it.

errors.descHtml: The call is wrong, not the database. A set uses both list keys and string keys, two sets bind different numbers of values, or an element cannot be bound. A statement already streaming on this connection throws it too.

The server rejected one run, for example for a syntax error, a constraint or a permission. Each run is its own transaction, so the writes before the failed run stay. Use transaction to save all or nothing.
The connection failed while the batch was running, or timeout passed before it finished. The connection cannot be used for the rest of the request.

doc.shortHtml: Runs one statement and gives its rows one at a time to a foreach loop. The connection stays open until the loop ends. The memory used stays the same however many rows there are. Use it instead of query for a large result.

params.name: sql
params.descHtml: The statement, bound the same way as in query. Use a ? or a :name for each value, and never write a value into the text. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The values to bind, with the same rule as query. Use list keys for ? and string keys for :name, and never both in one array.

params.name: timeout
params.descHtml: How long reading all the rows may take. The limit applies while the rows are being read, so it covers every row and not only the first call. When the time passes, the statement stops with an IOError, and the connection cannot be used again. Without it, the loop waits as long as the server takes.

doc.returnHtml: The statement's rows for a foreach loop, each one a Core\Db\Row, in the server's order. No row has been read yet when this returns. The connection is busy until the loop reaches the last row, and no other statement can run on it. A loop that writes for each row needs a second connection ({ shared: false }), or query instead.
