doc.shortHtml: Returns the type the property is declared with, written the way the class writes it.
doc.returnHtml: The type as a string, such as int, ?int, array<string> or Customer. The properties of a built-in error class, such as message on LogicError, have no written type, so the result is null. To find the type of a value, use Core\Reflect::typeOf.

classes.summaryHtml: One property of a class, as Core\Reflect\ClassInfo::properties returns it. name and isPublic describe the declaration. type returns the type the property is declared with.

classes.name: Core\Regex
classes.summary: Finds, extracts, replaces and splits text with regular expressions. Every method takes a pattern as a `string` or as a `Core\Regex\Pattern` that `compile` returns.

members.name: compile
members.signature: compile(string $pattern, { caseInsensitive?: bool, multiline?: bool, dotAll?: bool, ungreedy?: bool }): Core\Regex\Pattern

doc.shortHtml: Compiles a regular expression once, with options, and returns a Core\Regex\Pattern. You can pass the Pattern to every Core\Regex method that takes a pattern.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: The regular expression, with no delimiters. A tainted string does not compile here. Use Core\Regex::quote to match a user's text literally.

params.name: caseInsensitive
params.descHtml: true makes letters match in upper and lower case. The default is false.

params.name: multiline
params.descHtml: true makes ^ and $ match at the start and end of every line. The default is false.

params.name: dotAll
params.descHtml: true makes . match a newline too. The default is false.

params.name: ungreedy
params.descHtml: true makes * and + match as little as possible, and *? as much as possible. The default is false.

doc.returnHtml: The compiled Core\Regex\Pattern. The pattern is checked here, so a mistake in it throws at this line and not at its first use.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression. The message contains the pattern.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $pattern matches anywhere in $subject. The match can be at any position. Write ^ and $ in the pattern to match the whole text.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to search.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

doc.returnHtml: true if the text contains at least one match, and false if it does not.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, or matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows.

doc.shortHtml: Finds the first match of $pattern in $subject and returns it as a Core\Regex\Match. The Match has the matched text, each group and the position of the match.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to search.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: from
params.descHtml: The character position where the search starts. The default is 0. A negative position counts from the end of $subject.

doc.returnHtml: The first Core\Regex\Match at or after from, or null if there is no match.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, or matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows.

doc.shortHtml: Finds every match of $pattern in $subject and returns them as an array of Core\Regex\Match. The matches do not overlap, and they are in the order they appear in the text.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to search.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

doc.returnHtml: One Core\Regex\Match for each match, from left to right. The array is empty if there is no match.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, or matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows.

members.name: replace
members.signature: replace(string $subject, Core\Regex\Pattern|string $pattern, string $replacement, { limit?: uint }): string

doc.shortHtml: Replaces every match of $pattern in $subject with $replacement, and returns the new text. In $replacement, $1 is the text of group 1 and $0 is the whole match.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to search.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: replacement
params.descHtml: The text that replaces each match. $1 to $99 insert a numbered group, and ${name} inserts a named group. Write ${1}0 when a digit follows the group. $$ is one $. A group the pattern does not have inserts nothing. \1 is not a group. A tainted string does not compile here. To insert text from outside, return it from the function of replaceWith.

params.name: limit
params.descHtml: How many matches to replace, counted from the start of the text. The default is every match. 0 replaces nothing.

doc.returnHtml: The text with the matches replaced. It is the same text if there is no match.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, or matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows.

members.name: replaceWith
members.signature: replaceWith(string $subject, Core\Regex\Pattern|string $pattern, callable(Core\Regex\Match): string $fn, { limit?: uint }): string

doc.shortHtml: Replaces every match of $pattern in $subject with the text your function returns for that match, and returns the new text. The function gets one Core\Regex\Match.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to search.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: fn
params.descHtml: A function that gets one Core\Regex\Match and returns a string. It is called once for each match, from left to right. The text it returns is inserted as it is, so $1 in it is two characters.

params.name: limit
params.descHtml: How many matches to replace, counted from the start of the text. The default is every match. 0 replaces nothing. The function is not called for a match after the limit.

doc.returnHtml: The text with the matches replaced. It is the same text if there is no match.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows, or the new text is larger than the memory limit.

members.name: split
members.signature: split(string $subject, Core\Regex\Pattern|string $pattern, { limit?: int, keepEmpty?: bool }): array<string>

doc.shortHtml: Splits $subject at every match of $pattern, and returns the pieces as an array. The matches are not part of any piece.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The text to split.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: A Core\Regex\Pattern from Core\Regex::compile, or a pattern string with no options. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: limit
params.descHtml: The largest number of pieces. The last piece contains the rest of the text. A negative number removes that many pieces from the end. 0 returns the whole text as one piece. The default is no limit.

params.name: keepEmpty
params.descHtml: Whether empty pieces are kept. The default is true. With false, empty pieces are removed after limit is applied.

doc.returnHtml: The pieces, from left to right. If there is no match, the array has one piece: the whole text.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid regular expression, or matching it against $subject needs more steps than the limit allows.

doc.shortHtml: Puts a \ before every character that has a special meaning in a pattern. The result is a pattern that matches $text exactly. A tainted text is allowed here, and the result can be used as a pattern.

params.name: text
params.descHtml: The text to match exactly.

doc.returnHtml: The escaped pattern. A text with no special characters is returned unchanged. & and ~ are escaped, and !, :, <, =, > and / are not.

classes.summaryHtml:
Finds, extracts, replaces and splits text with regular expressions. Every method takes a pattern as a string or as a Core\Regex\Pattern that compile returns.

A Core\Regex pattern is a plain string — no /…/ delimiters and no trailing modifiers; the flags are options to Core\Regex::compile, which answers a Core\Regex\Pattern every other member also takes in place of the string. A single-quoted string is the cheap spelling — '\d+' has no escapes to double, where "\\d+" does. A pattern runs on a linear-time engine; one that needs a lookaround or a backreference runs on a backtracking engine under a step budget, and exhausting that budget throws rather than answering false. A pattern neither engine can compile throws too. match answers ?Core\Regex\Match — null when nothing matched — and matchAll a list of them; in replace's template $1 and ${name} are group references and $$ a plain $, while the value replaceWith's callback returns is inserted as it is. Fixed text built into a pattern goes through quote.

<?nvs
string $log = '2026-08-30 GET /a 200; 2026-08-31 POST /b 404';
echo Core\Regex::matches($log, "\\b\\d{3}\\b") ? 'has status' : 'none', "\n";
var $m = Core\Regex::match($log, "(?<y>\\d{4})-(?<mo>\\d{2})-(?<d>\\d{2})");
echo $m?->text() ?? 'none', ' at ', $m?->offset() ?? -1, ' day=', $m?->group('d') ?? '?', "\n";
foreach (Core\Regex::matchAll($log, "(GET|POST) (\\S+)") as Core\Regex\Match $hit) {
    echo $hit->group(1) ?? '?', ' ', $hit->group(2) ?? '?', "\n";
}
echo Core\Regex::replace('2026-08-30', "(\\d+)-(\\d+)-(\\d+)", '$3/$2/$1'), "\n";
echo Core\Regex::replaceWith('a1b22', "\\d+", fn(Core\Regex\Match $x): string => '<' . $x->text() . '>'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::join(Core\Regex::split('a, b,c', ",\\s*"), '|'), "\n";
Core\Regex\Pattern $word = Core\Regex::compile('^[a-z]+$', { caseInsensitive: true });
echo Core\Regex::matches('Hello', $word) ? 'word' : 'not a word', "\n";
echo Core\Regex::quote('a.b*c?'), "\n";
has status
2026-08-30 at 0 day=30
GET /a
POST /b
30/08/2026
a<1>b<22>
a|b|c
word
a\.b\*c\?

classes.name: Core\Regex\Match
classes.summary: One match of a regular expression in a text. It has the matched text, the position where the match starts and the text of each group. `Core\Regex::match` and `Core\Regex::matchAll` return it.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the text of one group, by its number or by its name.

params.name: group
params.descHtml: The number of the group, or its name. Group 0 is the whole match.

doc.returnHtml: The text of the group. The result is null if the pattern has the group but this match did not use it.

errors.descHtml: The pattern has no group with this number or name.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the text of every group in one array. A named group is in the array twice: under its name and under its number.
doc.returnHtml: An array with group 0 first. A group that this match did not use is in the array, and its value is null.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the position in the text where the whole match starts. The position counts characters, not bytes.
doc.returnHtml: The position of the first character of the match. A match at the start of the text is at 0.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole text that the pattern matched. This is the same text as group(0).
doc.returnHtml: The matched text. It is never null, but it can be an empty string.

classes.summaryHtml:
One match of a regular expression in a text. It has the matched text, the position where the match starts and the text of each group. Core\Regex::match and Core\Regex::matchAll return it.

Core\Regex::match returns a Core\Regex\Match, or null when nothing matched. Core\Regex::matchAll returns a list of them, and Core\Regex::replaceWith gives one to its callback. You never create one yourself. text() returns the whole match. group() returns one group by number or by name. It returns null for a group the pattern declares but this match did not use. groups() returns every group in pattern order: a named group appears under its name, then under its number. offset() returns where the match starts, counted in graphemes.

<?nvs
var $m = Core\Regex::match('café au lait', '(?<drink>lait)');
if ($m != null) {
    echo $m->text(), ' ', $m->offset(), ' ', $m->group('drink') ?? '?', ' ', $m->group(1) ?? '?', "\n";
    foreach ($m->groups() as string $k => ?string $v) {
        echo $k, '=', $v ?? 'null', ';';
    }
    echo "\n";
}
var $opt = Core\Regex::match('ac', '(a)(b)?(c)');
echo $opt?->group(2) ?? 'no b', ' ', $opt?->group(3) ?? 'no c', "\n";
lait 8 lait lait
0=lait;drink=lait;1=lait;
no b c

classes.name: Core\Regex\Pattern
classes.summary: A regular expression and its options, which `Core\Regex::compile` returns. You can pass it to every `Core\Regex` method that takes a pattern string.
classes.summaryHtml:
A regular expression and its options, which Core\Regex::compile returns. You can pass it to every Core\Regex method that takes a pattern string.

A Core\Regex\Pattern is a compiled pattern with its four flags — caseInsensitive, multiline, dotAll, ungreedy — answered by Core\Regex::compile and accepted wherever a Core\Regex member takes a pattern. It has no members of its own: compile once where a pattern is reused or where a flag is needed, and pass the handle. A pattern neither engine can compile throws from compile itself.

<?nvs
Core\Regex\Pattern $tag = Core\Regex::compile('<.+>', { ungreedy: true });
echo Core\Regex::match('<a><b>', $tag)?->text() ?? 'none', "\n";
Core\Regex\Pattern $vowel = Core\Regex::compile('[aeiou]', { caseInsensitive: true });
echo Core\Regex::replace('Banana', $vowel, '.'), ' ', Core\Arr::count(Core\Regex::matchAll('Banana', $vowel)), "\n";
string $bad = '(unclosed';
try {
    Core\Regex\Pattern $never = Core\Regex::compile($bad);
    echo "compiled\n";
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    echo "refused\n";
}
<a>
B.n.n. 3
refused

classes.name: Core\Request
classes.summary: The request your program is handling: its method, path, query, headers, cookies and body. Text the client sent, such as a header or the body, is `tainted`. A program that answers no request, such as a command-line program, gets a `LogicError` from every method.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the method of the request, such as GET or POST, as a case of Core\Http\Method. A HEAD request returns Get. Use isHead to tell the two apart.
doc.returnHtml: The Core\Http\Method case of the request. It is never Head.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request, such as a command-line program or a test. It is also thrown when the method is not one of the cases of Core\Http\Method. The server answers such a request with 501 before your program runs.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether the request is a HEAD request. method returns Get for a HEAD request, so this is the only way to tell the two apart.
doc.returnHtml: true when the request method is HEAD, and false for every other method. The server sends no body in the response to a HEAD request, so a program can skip the work of building one.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the request path without the prefix of the mount that matched. An application reads the same paths wherever it is mounted.
doc.returnHtml: The rest of the path after the mount prefix, percent-encoded as it arrived. It is tainted. mount() returns the prefix that was removed.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one query-string parameter by its name, as text. The query is read the same way Core\Uri::parseQuery reads it.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The parameter's name, decoded. Upper and lower case are different.

doc.returnHtml: The parameter's value as a tainted string, or null when the query has no parameter with this name. A name with square brackets, such as tag[]=a, also gives null. Read those values with queryArray. Use as to convert the text, for example as ?int.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request.
The query string has a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every value of one query-string parameter that has square brackets, such as tag[]=a&tag[]=b.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The parameter's name without the brackets. For tag[]=a, the name is tag.

doc.returnHtml: An array<tainted string>. tag[]=a&tag[]=b gives ["a", "b"], and filter[color]=red gives ["color" => "red"]. A name without brackets gives an array with its one value. A name that is not in the query gives an empty array.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request.
The query string has a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.
A value under this name has a second pair of brackets, such as tag[a][b]=c. Read nested values with queryAs.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the query string as the type T that you write at the call. It works like Core\Arr::shapeAs on what query reads, and converts each field with as. Without name, it reads all parameters. With name, it reads the nested value under that name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The parameter whose nested value is read, written without brackets. Brackets work the same way as in query. If you leave it out, the whole query string is read.

doc.returnHtml: A new T with every field of its declared type, or one T for each entry for an array<T>. Nothing is kept. Every call reads the query string again, so two callers never get the same object.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. Or the query string has percent escapes that decode to bytes that are not UTF-8. Or T is a class without #[Json\Derive].

A field that T needs is missing, or as cannot convert its value to the declared type. It is also thrown when the value under name is not a set of fields. The error has one issue for each wrong field, at its own dotted path, so a form can show the whole list.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the value of one request header by its name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the header. Upper and lower case do not matter, so Content-Type and content-type are the same header.

doc.returnHtml: The value as a tainted string, exactly as it arrived. The result is null when the request has no header of that name. When the header arrived on more than one line, the values are joined with , in the order they arrived. headers() returns each line on its own.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request.
The value of this header is not valid UTF-8.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every header of the request, grouped by name.
doc.returnHtml: An array<array<tainted string>>. Each key is a header name in lower case. Its value is a list with one entry for each line of that header, in the order the lines arrived. The array is empty when the request has no headers.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request.
The value of a header is not valid UTF-8.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the value of one cookie by its name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the cookie, exactly as it was set. Upper and lower case are different, and a.b and a_b are two different cookies.

doc.returnHtml: The value as a tainted string, exactly as it arrived. Nothing is decoded. The result is null when the request has no cookie of that name. When the name starts with __Host- and the cookie arrived twice, the result is null too.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request.
The value of this cookie is not valid UTF-8.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole request body as one string.
doc.returnHtml: Every byte the client sent, in order and unchanged. The string is tainted. It is empty when the request has no body, and every call returns the same string.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or bodyStream or files already read the body, and those two do not keep it.
The body is larger than [limits] request_body. The bytes past that limit are never stored.
The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its Content-Length said.
The body is not valid UTF-8, so it cannot be a string. bytes returns the same body as bytes.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole request body as bytes. Use it for a body that is not text, such as an uploaded file.
doc.returnHtml: Every byte the client sent, in order and unchanged. The value is tainted. It is empty when the request has no body. A body that is not valid UTF-8 is returned too, where body throws an error.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or bodyStream or files already read the body, and those two do not keep it.
The body is larger than [limits] request_body. The bytes past that limit are never stored.
The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its Content-Length said.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the request body as one JSON document and returns the decoded value.

params.name: maxDepth
params.descHtml: How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded value, the same as Core\Json::decode returns for the body. A JSON object becomes an array with string keys. Every string in it is tainted. Every call returns the same value.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or bodyStream or files already read the body, and those two do not keep it. Or maxDepth is not from 1 to 1024.
The body is not one whole JSON document, or it nests deeper than maxDepth. An empty body throws this error too. The Content-Type header is not checked.
The body is larger than [limits] request_body. The bytes past that limit are never stored.
The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its Content-Length said.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the request body as one JSON object and returns a new instance of the class T. The class needs #[Core\Json\Derive]. Write array<T> to read a JSON array with one object for each element.

params.name: maxDepth
params.descHtml: How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1.

doc.returnHtml: A new T with its properties read from the body, or one T for each element for an array<T>. Every call creates new objects, so two callers never get the same object.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or bodyStream or files already read the body, and those two do not keep it. Or T has no #[Core\Json\Derive] attribute. Or maxDepth is not from 1 to 1024.

The body is not one whole JSON object, or it nests deeper than maxDepth. An empty body throws this error too. It is also thrown when a field is missing or has the wrong type. The issues list has one entry for each wrong field. The Content-Type header is not checked.

The call stack is full when a constructor runs. This happens when the call starts with the stack almost full, or when a constructor recurses deeply. A deep body within maxDepth does not throw this error.
The body is larger than [limits] request_body. The bytes past that limit are never stored.
The connection failed while the body arrived, or the client sent fewer bytes than its Content-Length said.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the request body in pieces, in the order they arrive. Use it for a large body that you do not want in memory all at once.
doc.returnHtml: A value that a foreach loop reads once. Each piece is a tainted bytes value. How the body is split has no meaning. The loop runs zero times when the request has no body.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or body, bytes, json, files or bodyStream already read the body. After this call, those methods throw this error too.
The connection failed while the loop read the body. The pieces before the failure are still given to the loop.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the files that a form uploaded, one at a time in a foreach loop.
doc.returnHtml: An Iterable<Core\Request\Part>. Each loop step gives the next file as it arrives. The text fields are not in the loop, and post reads them after it. The loop runs zero times when the request has no multipart/form-data body.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. Or body, bodyStream or post already read the body. After this call, body, bytes, bodyStream and json throw this error too. post still works after the loop.

The request says it has a multipart/form-data body, but its boundary is missing, given twice or not valid. Or the body does not have the form that the request declared. Or the name, file name or Content-Type of a part is not valid UTF-8.
The connection failed while the loop read the body, or the body ended before its last boundary.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one submitted form field by its name, as text. The fields are read the same way query reads them. The body can be multipart/form-data, where the parts that are not files are read, or urlencoded.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The field's name, as the form declared it. Upper and lower case are different.

doc.returnHtml: The field's value as a tainted string, or null when the form has no field with this name. A name with square brackets, such as item[]=pen, also gives null. Read those values with postArray. This method reads the body to its end. On a multipart/form-data request, call it after files(), because it skips the uploads on its way to the last field.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request, or body or bodyStream already read the body of this request. Calling post after files() is allowed.
The body is not the form it says it is, or a multipart/form-data body has no boundary.
The name or value of a field is not valid UTF-8. In an urlencoded form, this includes a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.
The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every value of one form field that has square brackets, such as item[]=pen&item[]=book.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The field's name without the brackets. For item[]=pen, the name is item.

doc.returnHtml: An array<tainted string>. item[]=pen&item[]=book gives ["pen", "book"], and size[shirt]=M gives ["shirt" => "M"]. A name without brackets gives an array with its one value. A name that is not in the form gives an empty array. Like post, this method reads the body to its end, so call it after files().

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request, or body or bodyStream already read the body of this request.
The body is not the form it says it is, or a value under this name has a second pair of brackets, such as item[a][b]=c. Read nested values with postAs.
The name or value of a field is not valid UTF-8. In an urlencoded form, this includes a percent escape that decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8.
The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the submitted form as the type T that you write at the call. It works like Core\Arr::shapeAs on what post reads, and converts each field with as. Without name, it reads the whole form. With name, it reads the nested value under that name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The field whose nested value is read, written without brackets. Brackets work the same way as in post. If you leave it out, the whole form is read.

doc.returnHtml: A new T with every field of its declared type, or one T for each entry for an array<T>. Like post, this method reads the body to its end. On a multipart/form-data request, call it after the files() loop. Nothing is kept. Every call reads the form again, so two callers never get the same object.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. Or body or bodyStream already read the body of this request. Or T is a class without #[Json\Derive].

The body is not the form it says it is, for the same reasons as in post. Or a field that T needs is missing, or as cannot convert its value to the declared type. Or the value under name is not a set of fields. The error has one issue for each wrong field, at its own dotted path.
The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the length it declared.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the network address of the client that sent this request. Behind a proxy that is listed in [server] trusted_proxies, the address comes from X-Forwarded-For.
doc.returnHtml: The address as a tainted string, such as 203.0.113.7 or 2001:db8::1. An IPv6 address is always in its short form. The result is null when the request has no address, for example over a Unix socket.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a job or a test.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the scheme the request arrived over. A connection without TLS gives https only when a trusted proxy sends X-Forwarded-Proto.
doc.returnHtml: "http" or "https", as a tainted string. The result is never null, because every request arrived over one of them. A server that trusts no proxy always returns the scheme of the connection itself.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the host name the request was sent to, read from its Host header.
doc.returnHtml: The host name as a tainted string in lower case. A port and one dot at the end are removed, so Shop.Example.com.:8443 returns shop.example.com. An IPv6 address keeps its brackets. The result is null when the request has no Host header. header("host") returns the header exactly as it arrived, with the port. Headers such as X-Forwarded-Host are never read.

errors.descHtml: The program is not handling a request.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the route this request matched. The server matches the route once, before your program runs. The CSRF check and the route metric label use the same match, so a handler never needs to match its own path again.
doc.returnHtml: A Core\Router\Match with the declared name and the captures of the path. The result is null when no route matches this method and path. Such a request is still served like any other, because a match does not decide which code runs. A program with no #[Route] has no route table, so the result is also null.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test. The method throws this error and does not return null, because "no request arrived" and "no route matched" are different things.
A capture percent-decodes to bytes that are not UTF-8, so it cannot be a tainted string. The error names the capture and the position of the first byte that is not valid in a string.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the mount that is serving this request. It gives the prefix the server removed from the path before path() returns it. It also gives the glob captures of that mount. A program served for many customers uses them to learn which customer this request is for.
doc.returnHtml: A Core\Request\Mount. The result is never null, because every request reaches the program through a mount. A mount with no prefix and no glob gives the prefix "" and an empty array of captures.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. For example, it is a command-line program, a scheduled script, a job worker or a test. None of these is mounted.

classes.summaryHtml:
The request your program is handling: its method, path, query, headers, cookies and body. Text the client sent, such as a header or the body, is tainted. A program that answers no request, such as a command-line program, gets a LogicError from every method.

Core\Request is the whole of what arrived: method, isHead, path, query, header, headers, cookie and the body readers, plus route and mount for where the router put it. The host never fills a variable for the program. No lookup merges the query, the form fields and the cookies into one. Every member throws LogicError in a program that is not answering a request, so a CLI run, a scheduled script and a job worker say "no request arrived" rather than answering empty.

The body is read once, and every reader is one of two kinds. body(), post(), postAs<T>(), json() and jsonAs<T>() buffer: the first of them fills the request's hold, bounded by [limits] request_body, and any of the five may follow any other in any order and answer the same octets. bodyStream() and files() stream: they hand the octets over as they arrive, keep none, and so consume the body — a reader after one of those is refused, naming the member that consumed it. That refusal is a defect in the program, never something a peer can provoke.

json() decodes the body as one JSON document and answers mixed; jsonAs<T>() hydrates it straight into a class carrying #[Core\Json\Derive], exactly as Core\Json::decodeAs does, so a handler names the shape it expects instead of walking an array. Neither consults the Content-Type the peer declared — a header is what a peer wrote, not what a body is — and both throw ParseError on a document that is malformed, too deep, or absent altogether. json() keeps what it decoded and jsonAs<T>() hydrates per call, so writing to what a second call answered leaves the first alone.

queryAs<T>() and postAs<T>() are that idea over the parameters rather than the body: each reads what query() and post() parse as the type written at the call site — an inline shape, { page: uint }, or a class carrying #[Core\Json\Derive] — converting every named field with as and leaving the keys the type does not name behind. Called with nothing, the whole parameter set is the subject, and that is the only way a program reaches it: there is no query(): array<mixed>. Called with { name: "filter" }, the subject is the one bracket-named subtree under that name. A field that is absent, or that holds a value as refuses for its declared type, is a ParseError listing every field that failed at its own path — so a form reports the whole list rather than the first item of it.

Everything a peer chose is tainted, including the path, every header and the body, so it reaches a sink only through a launderer named for that sink — echo escapes for HTML on its own. A class hydrated from a body declares that on the fields receiving it: an unqualified string property is a compile error at the jsonAs<T>() call rather than a silent laundering.

<?nvs
#[Core\Json\Derive]
class Author
{
    public tainted string $name;
    public int $tags;

    public function constructor(tainted string $name, int $tags)
    {
        $this->name = $name;
        $this->tags = $tags;
    }
}

if (Core\Request::method() == Core\Http\Method::Post) {
    Author $author = Core\Request::jsonAs<Author>();
    echo 'hello ', $author->name, "\n";
}

That one needs a request in front of it; examples/json-body.nvs is the same program as a fixture, run with nvs run --request <file>, which answers the request a file describes without standing a listener up. Without one, this is what every member does:

<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::method();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
no request here

classes.name: Core\Request\BodyStream
classes.summary: The request body, read in pieces as it arrives. `Core\Request::bodyStream` returns it. Use it in a `foreach` loop to get each piece as `tainted` bytes, so the whole body is never in memory at once.
classes.summaryHtml:
The request body, read in pieces as it arrives. Core\Request::bodyStream returns it. Use it in a foreach loop to get each piece as tainted bytes, so the whole body is never in memory at once.

Core\Request\BodyStream is what Core\Request::bodyStream() answers with: an Iterable<tainted bytes> that a foreach walks once. It has no members — the walk is everything it does — and it holds nothing but the chunk the loop body is looking at, so a body far larger than the machine's memory passes through a program that never has more than one chunk of it resident. That is the whole difference from body(), which fills the request's hold under [limits] request_body and can be read back any number of times. This walk is under no such cap, because what a program keeps out of it is the program's own decision and its own bill.

A chunk boundary is the wire's, and carries no meaning. It is where the octets happened to arrive, so a program that needs lines, records or frames finds them itself, across chunks; nothing here aligns a chunk to anything the sender wrote. Each chunk is copied out as the loop body receives it and stays valid after the next pull, so keeping one keeps bytes the wire cannot revoke. The walk is empty where the request carried no body at all.

Naming the walk is the reading. bodyStream() claims the body when the walk is built, long before a single byte moves, so body(), post(), json(), jsonAs<T>() or files() after it is refused with LogicError whether or not the loop ever ran — and refused the same way in the other direction. That refusal is a defect in the program, never something a peer can provoke; the split between the readers that share the body and the ones that consume it is rule:http-server/buffering-readers-share-the-body-and-streaming-readers-consume-it, and Core\Request is where all five readers are named together.

Every chunk is tainted bytes, like everything else a peer chose, so it reaches a sink only through a launderer named for that sink. The common destination is disk, and Core\IO::writeStream takes this walk directly — it is where every stream reaches a file, under a byte bound of its own, and it removes the partial file if a write fails, so there is no half-written upload to clean up after.

<?nvs
int $total = 0;
foreach (Core\Request::bodyStream() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
    $total = $total + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
}
echo 'read ', $total, " bytes\n";

Or spent on a file instead, where the bytes never become a value the program holds. One request carries one body, so this is the other program, not the next few lines of that one:

<?nvs
Core\IO::writeStream('incoming.bin', Core\Request::bodyStream(), { max: 64 * 1024 * 1024 });

Both of those need a request in front of them. Without one, naming the walk is what every other member of Core\Request does:

<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::bodyStream();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
no request here

classes.name: Core\Request\Files
classes.summary: The files uploaded with a multipart request, which `Core\Request::files` returns. Use it in a `foreach` loop to get each file as a `Core\Request\Part`.
classes.summaryHtml:
The files uploaded with a multipart request, which Core\Request::files returns. Use it in a foreach loop to get each file as a Core\Request\Part.

Core\Request\Files is what Core\Request::files() answers with: an Iterable<Core\Request\Part> that a foreach walks once, yielding each uploaded part as it comes off the wire. It has no members — the walk is everything it does — and it is the only way a program receives an upload. There is no temporary file and no directory the host chose: nothing lands on disk until the program names a path it holds the fs.write capability for, so an upload nobody saves has cost the machine nothing but the bytes that crossed the socket.

The parse runs as the loop does. The next part does not exist when the walk is named, so files() holds one part at a time and nothing accumulates. A part is valid only while it is the walk's current one: keeping one past the iteration that opened the next is holding a name for bytes the parse has already drained, and it is refused rather than answered with the wrong part's content. Advancing past a part the loop body never read simply drains it — skipping an upload the application does not recognise costs a walk over bytes the door already charged for, and no memory at all.

**A part is a file part iff its Content-Disposition carries a filename**, which is RFC 7578's own distinction and not a second one invented here. Every other part is an ordinary form field: the walk buffers those as it passes them, and Core\Request::post() reads them back afterwards. That is why post() on a multipart/form-data request is called after this walk and never before — the fields are behind the uploads on the wire, and reading them first would mean draining the uploads to reach them.

The walk is empty where the request declared no multipart/form-data body, which is what a request carrying no upload is. It throws LogicError where the program is not answering a request, or where body(), bodyStream() or post() already read this body; ParseError where the request declared a multipart body and then did not say how to read one — no boundary, two of them, or one outside the grammar — since an ambiguous body is refused rather than guessed at; and IOError where the connection failed under the body or the peer stopped short of the length it declared.

What bounds it is the server, not this walk. [limits] request_body bounds what is parsed into memory and has nothing to say about a streamed body; the server carries at most 256M of one request body, declared or chunked, refusing an oversize before the program runs and stopping a chunked one at the part being read. That number is a constant today — the directive that makes it settable per deployment is not on disk yet.

<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    string $path = Core\IO::within('uploads', $part->filename());
    $part->saveTo($path);
    echo $part->name(), " saved\n";
}

filename() is tainted, so Core\IO::within above is not decoration: it is the one way a name the client chose reaches a path. Without a request in front of it, naming the walk does what every member of Core\Request does:

<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::files();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
no request here

classes.name: Core\Request\Mount
classes.summary: The mount that is serving this request, as `Core\Request::mount()` returns it. `prefix()` returns the part of the path that the server removed, such as `/shop`. `captures()` returns the parts of that prefix that a pattern matched, such as a customer name. The captures are `tainted`, because the client chose the address.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the part the server removed from the start of the path before Core\Request::path() returns it. A program mounted at /acme sees /orders in path(), and /acme here.
doc.returnHtml: The prefix, with a slash at the start and none at the end. The result is "" when the mount removes nothing. It is not tainted, because the server configuration sets every mount when the server starts. The prefix is the operator's text, and the client did not choose it.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the glob captures of the mount serving this request, in order. {1} is captures[0]. One program that runs at many prefixes uses them to learn which customer the request is for.
doc.returnHtml: The captures as tainted string values. The array is empty for a mount whose prefix has no glob. They are tainted because the client chose which mount serves the request. Before you use one in a query or a path, check it as you check any other value from a request.

classes.summaryHtml:
The mount that is serving this request, as Core\Request::mount() returns it. prefix() returns the part of the path that the server removed, such as /shop. captures() returns the parts of that prefix that a pattern matched, such as a customer name. The captures are tainted, because the client chose the address.

Core\Request\Mount is what Core\Request::mount() answers with, and it holds two facts about the door this request arrived at: prefix() is what the server took off the front of the path before Core\Request::path() answered it, and captures() are the glob captures of the mount row that took the request, in order — {1} is captures[0]. One member answers the pair because a request holding one mount's prefix and another mount's captures is a bug the shape rules out.

**It is never null**, where Core\Request::route() is. Every request that reached a program reached it through a mount, so a door that strips nothing and holds no glob answers "" and an empty array rather than an absence — there is no case to write for "served without a mount". With no request in front of it at all, naming it refuses the way every reader of Core\Request does.

A mount says where a request arrives and which file answers it, and nothing else. Its key set is closed — prefix, host, scan, entry, origin — and carries no mode, no limits and no capabilities; what the code answering the request may do is the [[app]] block's, keyed on the entry file path. The two usually cover the same tree, and reading one for the other is the mistake this split exists to prevent: what you learn here is routing, never policy.

The table expands at boot, not per request. A scan glob is resolved against the disk once at startup — and again at each configuration reload, in development also under hot reload's revalidation — into ordinary mounts whose paths were each checked to lie inside [server] root. So a prefix reaching a program is a row an operator wrote, and no path is ever derived from a URL at request time.

That is why the prefix is plain text and **the captures are tainted**: which row answers is the peer's choice, and a capture is exactly what a multi-tenant program keys its data by. A capture reaching a query or a path launders the way anything else off a request does. Nothing here is cached — both facts live on the inbound request and this class is a reading of them — so a read costs one instance and one array of the mount's own captures, a handful of values against a glob's one or two.

<?nvs
// Served by a mount that scans `*/public/index.nvs` under `[server] root` and
// mounts each match at `/{1}`, so `/acme/orders` arrives here as `/orders`.
Core\Request\Mount $mount = Core\Request::mount();
tainted string $tenant = $mount->captures()[0];

echo 'serving ', $tenant, ' under ', $mount->prefix(), "\n";

A program therefore never derives its own base path from the request target, and Core\Router::url prepends the prefix on the way back out, so the same compiled route table serves at /ModuleA, at /{1} or at / with no recompile. Without a request, the class is unreachable in the ordinary way:

<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::mount();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "nothing was mounted here\n";
}
nothing was mounted here

classes.name: Core\Request\Part
classes.summary: One uploaded file, as the `Core\Request::files()` loop gives it. `name()`, `filename()` and `contentType()` return what the client sent about the file, and all three are `tainted`. `readAll()` returns the content as one value, `content()` returns it in pieces, and `saveTo()` writes it to a file. Read the content before the loop moves to the next file.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the name of the form field this file was sent under. This is the name attribute of the <input>, as the client sent it.
doc.returnHtml: The field name. It is tainted because the client chose it. A client can send a name the form never declared, so the name is untrusted input like every other byte of the part.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the file name the client sent. It names a file on the client's computer. It is never a path on this server.
doc.returnHtml: The name the client sent, tainted. It cannot be used as a file path until Core\IO::within checks it. This stops a client from choosing where its upload is saved.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the media type this part declared. This is what the client said the bytes are. The bytes may be something else.
doc.returnHtml: The declared type, tainted. The result is text/plain when the part declared no type, which is the default that RFC 7578 sets. To know what the bytes really are, read the bytes.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the bytes of this part, one piece at a time. Use it for an upload that must never be in memory all at once. saveTo and readAll both read the part this way.
doc.returnHtml: An Iterable<tainted bytes> over the pieces of the part as they arrive. Each piece is a value of its own. The loop runs zero times for a part with no bytes. It works only while the files() loop is still on this part.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. Or the files() loop has moved to a later part, and the bytes of this part are gone.
The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the closing boundary.
The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the whole content of this part into one value. Use it for an upload small enough to keep in memory.

params.name: max
params.descHtml: The most bytes this call reads into memory. If you leave it out, the limit is [limits] request_body. If you give it, the limit is this number. A number larger than the request's own [limits] memory throws an error. It is not lowered to fit.

doc.returnHtml: Every byte of this part, in order and not decoded. The value is tainted. It is empty for a part with no bytes. That part was still sent by the client.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. Or the files() loop has moved to a later part. Or max is larger than this request may use at all.
The part is larger than the limit. The bytes over the limit are never stored, because the error is thrown at the piece that would pass it. Use content() for a part that does not fit.
The connection failed while the body was read, or the body ended before the closing boundary.
The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

members.name: saveTo
members.signature: saveTo(string $path, { max?: uint, overwrite?: bool }): void

doc.shortHtml: Writes this part directly to $path, one chunk at a time. Use it to save an upload. It needs the fs.write capability for the path. The part's own filename() is tainted, so Core\IO::within must check it before it is used here.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The file to write the part to. It must not already exist, unless overwrite is true.

params.name: max
params.descHtml: The most bytes to accept from this part. If you leave it out, there is no limit, because no other limit applies to a file on disk. readAll keeps what it reads in memory, so [limits] request_body limits it.

params.name: overwrite
params.descHtml: Whether an existing file may be replaced. The default is false, because the path is usually built from a name the client sent.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If the write fails partway, the partial file is deleted before the error is thrown. No later reader finds a cut-off upload that the program thinks is complete.

errors.descHtml: This program is not handling a request. Or the files() loop has moved to a later part, and the bytes of this part are gone.
The configuration does not grant fs.write for this path, or the part is larger than max bytes.
A file is already at the path and overwrite is false. Or the operating system did not allow the file to be created or written. Or the connection failed while the body was read.
The body is not the multipart body the request declared.

classes.summaryHtml:
One uploaded file, as the Core\Request::files() loop gives it. name(), filename() and contentType() return what the client sent about the file, and all three are tainted. readAll() returns the content as one value, content() returns it in pieces, and saveTo() writes it to a file. Read the content before the loop moves to the next file.

A Core\Request\Part is one file part of a multipart/form-data body, handed to the loop body by the Core\Request::files() walk. Three members say what it declared about itself — name(), the form field it arrived under; filename(), the name the client claimed; and contentType(), which answers text/plain where the part declared none, RFC 7578's own default rather than a repair of a missing value. All three are tainted string: they are what a peer wrote back, and a client is free to send a field name the form never declared.

**filename() is a claim about a file on someone else's machine, and never a path on this one.** As a tainted string it reaches a path only through Core\IO::within, which is the same refusal every other untrusted string meets — and it is the refusal that matters most here, since the one place an upload could choose where it lands is the one place the qualifier stands in the way.

**There is no size.** Nothing honest can be said about a part's length before it has been consumed, and inventing a number is the kind of repair this language refuses everywhere. A program that needs the count gets it from the bytes it read.

Three ways to spend a part, and each of them spends it. readAll({max?}) pulls the whole part into one tainted bytes — the reading for an upload small enough to hold — bounded by [limits] request_body (8M) when max is omitted, by that number when it is named, and refusing outright a max larger than the request's own [limits] memory rather than quietly clamping it. content() walks the part a chunk at a time, holding none of it, for an upload that must never be resident whole. saveTo($path, {max?, overwrite?}) writes it straight to disk one chunk at a time — the path almost every upload takes — under the fs.write capability for that path; it is Core\IO::writeStream underneath, so the path must not already exist unless overwrite says so, and a write that fails leaves no partial file behind.

All of them are valid only while this part is the walk's current one. A part kept past the iteration that opened the next names bytes the parse has already drained, so it is refused rather than answered with the current part's content.

<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    int $bytes = 0;
    foreach ($part->content() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
        $bytes = $bytes + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
    }
    echo $part->name(), ' (', $part->filename(), ', ', $part->contentType(), '): ', $bytes, "\n";
}

The same part, held whole or sent to disk instead — one part is spent once, so these are two programs and not two halves of one:

<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    tainted bytes $whole = $part->readAll({ max: 1 * 1024 * 1024 });
    echo Core\Bytes::length($whole), "\n";
}
<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    $part->saveTo(Core\IO::within('uploads', $part->filename()), { overwrite: true });
}

Every one of those needs a request in front of it; Core\Request\Files is where the walk that produces a part is described, and what it does in a program answering no request.

classes.name: Core\Request\PartContent
classes.summary: The content of one uploaded file, read in pieces as it arrives. `Core\Request\Part::content` returns it. Read it in a `foreach` loop before the `files()` loop moves to the next file.
classes.summaryHtml:
The content of one uploaded file, read in pieces as it arrives. Core\Request\Part::content returns it. Read it in a foreach loop before the files() loop moves to the next file.

Core\Request\PartContent is what Core\Request\Part::content() answers with: an Iterable<tainted bytes> that a foreach walks once over one uploaded part. It has no members — the walk is everything it does — and it holds nothing but the chunk the loop body is looking at, so a part far larger than the machine's memory passes through a program that never has more than one chunk of it resident. It is the reading for an upload that must never be whole in memory, and readAll and saveTo are both written over it: those two are the bounded and the on-disk answers to the same question, and this is the one where the program decides what to keep.

A part is a position in a body, and this walk is only valid while it is the current one. The files() parse moves whether or not this walk is what moved it, so the part the walk was named on is remembered and checked on every pull: once the loop over files() has advanced, a pull here refuses with LogicError rather than handing back a later part's bytes. That is a defect in the program — a name kept past the iteration that opened the next part — and never something a peer can provoke.

A chunk boundary is the wire's, and carries no meaning. It is where the octets happened to arrive, so a program that needs lines, records or frames finds them across chunks; nothing here aligns a chunk to anything the sender wrote. The walk is empty for a part that carried no bytes, which is an ordinary thing for a form to send.

Every chunk is tainted bytes, like everything else a peer chose, so it reaches a sink only through a launderer named for that sink — and the filename the part carries is tainted too, which is why a path is built rather than concatenated. Where the destination is simply disk, saveTo is the shorter spelling of this loop and bounds itself; reach for content() when the bytes are being counted, hashed, decoded or forwarded rather than stored.

<?nvs
foreach (Core\Request::files() as Core\Request\Part $part) {
    int $seen = 0;
    foreach ($part->content() as tainted bytes $chunk) {
        $seen = $seen + Core\Bytes::length($chunk);
    }
    echo $part->name(), ': ', $seen, " bytes\n";
}

Beyond the LogicError above, the walk carries the failures the body itself has: IOError where the connection failed underneath it or the peer stopped short of the closing boundary, and ParseError where what arrived is not the multipart body the request declared. Reaching the walk at all needs a request in front of it, and without one the entry to it refuses the way every member of Core\Request does:

<?nvs
try {
    Core\Request::files();
    echo "not reached\n";
} catch (LogicError $none) {
    echo "no request here\n";
}
no request here

classes.name: Core\Response
classes.summary: The response your program sends back to a request. `html()`, `text()`, `json()`, `bytes()`, `sendFile()` and `stream()` write the body, and each one sets the matching `Content-Type`. `setStatus()`, `setHeader()`, `redirect()` and `addCookie()` change the status line and the headers.

doc.shortHtml: The kind of redirect a response sends. Every browser handles these three statuses in the same way, so the browser does exactly what your program says.

Which requests from other sites send a cookie. The three cases are the values of the cookie's SameSite attribute. The default is Lax. A cookie that is sent with requests from other sites makes a CSRF attack possible.
Sends the HTML page $body and adds the header Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The page to send. It is a Core\Html\Markup, which is HTML that is already safe: an html template, `html… , escaped the values in its {...}, or Core\Html::escape made it. It is sent as it is and nothing is escaped again. A string` does not compile.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Using this and echo in one response does not compile.

doc.shortHtml: Converts $value to JSON, sends it, and adds the header Content-Type: application/json. It uses the same encoder as Core\Json::encode, and the JSON is on one line.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The value to send, of any type Core\Json::encode accepts. A tainted value is allowed anywhere inside it. Each string is written as a JSON string, so its quotes are escaped and it cannot change the JSON around it.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Using this and echo in one response does not compile.

errors.descHtml: $value contains something JSON cannot write: a float that is NaN or infinite, a value of a type JSON has no form for, an object of a class without #[Core\Json\Derive], an object that points to itself, or nesting deeper than 1024 levels. Nothing is sent.

doc.shortHtml: Sends $body as plain text and adds the header Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The text to send. It is sent exactly as it is. A tainted value is allowed: the server also sends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so a browser never reads the text as HTML.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Using this and echo in one response does not compile.

doc.shortHtml: Sends $body exactly as it is, with $contentType as the Content-Type header. Use it for an image, a CSV file or any other body that is not HTML, text or JSON.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The bytes to send. Nothing is escaped or changed.

params.name: contentType
params.descHtml: The content type, such as image/png or text/csv; charset=utf-8. A tainted value does not compile, because the browser obeys this header.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Using this and echo in one response does not compile.

errors.descHtml: $contentType is empty, or has a character that is not printable ASCII: a line break, a control character or a letter like é. Nothing is sent.

doc.shortHtml: Sends the file at $path as the whole response. The server reads the file in small pieces, and chooses the content type from the end of the file name.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The file to send. fs.read in nvs.toml must allow it. A tainted value does not compile, because the path decides which file is read. To give a download its own name, set Content-Disposition with Core\Response::setHeader.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The server also responds to a browser that requests only part of the file, so a browser can jump to any point in a video and resume a download that stopped. If the file changed since the download started, the browser gets the whole new file. Using this and echo in one response does not compile.

errors.descHtml: fs.read does not allow $path. This error comes whether or not the file exists, the same as for Core\IO::read.
There is no file at $path, or the operating system does not allow this program to read it.
$path is a folder, or something else that is not a regular file. Nothing is sent.

doc.shortHtml: Starts a response body that your program sends in parts, and sets the header Content-Type to $contentType. The status and the headers are sent when this is called. The body ends when the program ends, or when your program calls end() on the stream.

params.name: contentType
params.descHtml: The content type of the body, for example text/csv. It becomes a header, so a tainted value does not compile. It must be printable ASCII and not empty.

params.name: length
params.descHtml: The size of the whole body in bytes, or null if you do not know it. With a size, the response has a Content-Length header and a browser can ask for one part of the body, for example to seek in a video. The request header Range says which part. Then offset() and length() of the stream say which bytes to write. Without a size, the whole body is sent and Range is ignored.

params.name: etag
params.descHtml: A version name for the body, or null. It is sent as the ETag header. Give a new name when the bytes change. A browser that resumes a download sends the name back, and gets the whole body if the name is old. It becomes a header, so a tainted value does not compile.

params.name: mustEnd
params.descHtml: A name for the body, such as the name of a download, or null. With a name, the body is complete only after your program calls end() on the stream. If the program stops before that, the body is cut off. The browser then shows a failed download, and the error log names the body.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Response\Stream. Call its write() method to send each part. Set the status and the headers before you call this method. Using this and echo in one response does not compile. A browser that reads this body with EventSource connects again when the body ends. For events that a page receives while it is open, use Core\Sse::upgrade.

errors.descHtml: $contentType is empty, or it contains a character a header cannot contain: a control character, a line break, or a character that is not ASCII. It is also thrown when $length is negative, when $etag contains such a character or a ", and when this request already started a body stream, because a response has one body.

doc.shortHtml: Sets the HTTP status of the response to $code, such as 404 or 201. It does not write a body, so you can use it together with echo or a body method.

params.name: code
params.descHtml: The status code, from 100 to 599.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If you call it more than once, the last call sets the status. If the request fails with an error, the status is 500.

errors.descHtml: $code is less than 100 or greater than 599. The status does not change.

doc.shortHtml: Sends the page as soon as the main script ends. Each Core\Html::later part follows when it is ready. A route with slotted: true does the same for every request.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Calling it twice is the same as calling it once.

errors.descHtml: The main script has already ended. This is the case in a Core\Html::later function and in Core\Task::afterResponse work.

doc.shortHtml: Sets the response header $name to $value. If the server already sets this header, your value replaces the server's value.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The header name, such as Cache-Control. It contains letters, digits and a few marks such as - and _. Spaces and : are not allowed. It cannot be Content-Type, because the body method you use sets that header. It cannot be Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Connection or Upgrade. The server sets these from the body it sends. A tainted value is not allowed.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The header value. It contains only printable ASCII characters, so it cannot contain a newline. It can be empty. A tainted value is not allowed.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If you set the same name twice, the header has the last value. The comparison of names ignores upper and lower case. If the request fails with an error, the response has none of these headers.

errors.descHtml: $name is empty, contains a character that is not allowed, or is one of the headers the server sets, such as Content-Type or Content-Length. Or $value contains a character that is not printable ASCII.

doc.shortHtml: Sends the browser to another address. It sets the redirect status and the Location header together. It does not write a body.

params.name: url
params.descHtml: The address to send the browser to. It can be a full URL or a path such as /orders/42. It is not empty and contains only printable ASCII characters. A tainted value is not allowed, because a visitor must not choose where the browser goes.

params.name: status
params.descHtml: The kind of redirect: SeeOther (303), Temporary (307) or Permanent (308). The default is SeeOther, which you use after a form is sent.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If you call it more than once, the last call wins. If the request fails with an error, the status is 500 and there is no Location header.

errors.descHtml: $url is empty, or contains a character that is not printable ASCII, such as a newline. Or it starts with two slashes or backslashes, such as //example.com, which a browser reads as another host. Nothing is set.

members.name: addCookie
members.signature: addCookie(string $name, string $value, { secure?: bool, httpOnly?: bool, sameSite?: Core\Response::SameSite, path?: string, domain?: string, maxAge?: Core\Time\Duration }): void

doc.shortHtml: Adds one Set-Cookie header to this response. Each option you leave out comes from [http.cookies]. With the default settings, a cookie without options is Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The cookie name. When the cookie comes back, the name is compared byte for byte, and nothing in it is changed. A __Host- prefix needs Secure and Path=/, and does not allow Domain. A __Secure- prefix needs Secure. A cookie that breaks these rules throws an error.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The cookie value. It can contain printable ASCII characters, as RFC 6265 says. A space, a comma, a semicolon, a backslash and a quote are not allowed. Each of them would end the value and start text your program did not write.

params.name: secure
params.descHtml: Whether the browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS. The default is [http.cookies] secure, which is true if you do not set it.

params.name: httpOnly
params.descHtml: Whether the cookie is hidden from scripts in the page. The default is [http.cookies] http_only, which is true if you do not set it. Set it to false here for a cookie that a script must read.

params.name: sameSite
params.descHtml: Which requests from other sites send the cookie. The default is [http.cookies] same_site, which is Lax if you do not set it. None without Secure throws an error, because every browser ignores that cookie. The same pair in the configuration stops the server from starting.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The path prefix under which the browser sends the cookie. The default is [http.cookies] path, which is / if you do not set it.

params.name: domain
params.descHtml: The domain the browser sends the cookie to. By default the cookie has no domain, so the browser sends it only to this host and not to its subdomains. [http.cookies] has no setting for it.

params.name: maxAge
params.descHtml: How long the cookie lives. By default it has no age, so it is a session cookie. 0s deletes the cookie. A negative duration throws an error.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Each call adds one cookie, so two calls send two Set-Cookie lines. If you add the same name twice, the response sends it twice.

errors.descHtml: $name is not a valid cookie name, or it breaks the rules of its __Host- or __Secure- prefix. It is also thrown when $value, path or domain contains a character that would end the attribute and start another one. It is also thrown when sameSite is None without secure, and when maxAge is negative.

classes.summaryHtml: The response your program sends back to a request. html(), text(), json(), bytes(), sendFile() and stream() write the body, and each one sets the matching Content-Type. setStatus(), setHeader(), redirect() and addCookie() change the status line and the headers.

classes.name: Core\Response\Stream
classes.summary: A response body that your program sends in parts. `Core\Response::stream()` returns it, and its `write()` method sends each part. The body ends when the program ends, or when your program calls `end()`.

doc.shortHtml: Sends one part of the body. If the client has not finished reading the last part, this method waits until it has. So only one part waits in memory at a time.

params.name: chunk
params.descHtml: The part to send, as a string or as bytes. It is sent exactly as it is. An empty part sends nothing and is not an error. A tainted value does not compile, because the browser may read the part as HTML.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. When this method returns, the part has been given to the connection. If the client has gone, this method returns at once and the part is thrown away. The client has gone when it closed the connection, or when it did not read a part before the server's send timeout. Your request still runs to its end.

errors.descHtml: The part is larger than the server allows for one part. Nothing is sent, and you can still send smaller parts.
The stream was started with a $length, and this part goes past the end of length(). Nothing is sent. It is also thrown when end() was already called on the stream.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the position of the first byte your program writes, counted from the start of the whole body. It is 0 unless the browser asked for a part of the body.
doc.returnHtml: An int. Start writing the body at this byte.

errors.descHtml: The stream was started without a $length.

doc.shortHtml: Returns how many bytes your program writes. This is the whole body, or the part the browser asked for.
doc.returnHtml: An int. It is 0 when nothing is sent: the browser already has this version, or it asked for a part the body does not have. Your writes must add up to exactly this number. If the program ends before that, the connection is closed, so the browser knows the body is not complete.

errors.descHtml: The stream was started without a $length.

doc.shortHtml: Ends the body. The client receives the end of the body at once, and your program can go on running. Calling end() a second time does nothing.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. A stream started with $mustEnd needs this call, or the body is cut off when the program stops. A write() after end() throws an error.

classes.summaryHtml: A response body that your program sends in parts. Core\Response::stream() returns it, and its write() method sends each part. The body ends when the program ends, or when your program calls end().

classes.name: Core\Router
classes.summary: The routes of your program. `url()`, `urlAbsolute()` and `urlSigned()` build a link to the route of a method. `match()` and `methodsFor()` check a path against the routes, and `signedRoute()` checks the signature of a signed link. `dispatch()` calls the method of the route that the request matched.

doc.shortHtml: Builds the link to the route of the method $route. Each value in $params fills the capture with the same name, and the other values become the query string. Every value is percent-encoded, so it stays inside its own part of the link.

params.name: route
params.descHtml: The method that has the #[Route], written as a method reference such as Shop::show. The link does not call the method. So the method may be an instance method or a private method. A method reference written directly in the call is checked when the program compiles. A method without a #[Route] is a compile error.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The path's captures by name, plus any query parameters. A key written directly in the code must be a capture or a declared #[Query] parameter. Any other key is a compile error. url and urlAbsolute use [] when you leave it out.

doc.returnHtml: The path, for example /users/42?page=2. An optional {name?} capture is left out when $params has no value for it. The / characters in a {name...} capture stay as they are.

errors.descHtml: When $route is a variable and not a method reference written in the call. When $params has no value for a capture that the path needs. When a value cannot be written as text. When a value is . or .., or a {name...} value has one of them between its / characters, because a browser would move that link to another path.

doc.shortHtml: Builds the same link as url, with the origin of your site in front. The origin is the origin setting of the [[app]] block in nvs.toml. It never comes from the Host or X-Forwarded-Host header of a request.

params.name: route
params.descHtml: The method that has the #[Route], written as a method reference such as Shop::show. The link does not call the method. So the method may be an instance method or a private method. A method reference written directly in the call is checked when the program compiles. A method without a #[Route] is a compile error.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The path's captures by name, plus any query parameters. A key written directly in the code must be a capture or a declared #[Query] parameter. Any other key is a compile error. url and urlAbsolute use [] when you leave it out.

doc.returnHtml: The full URL, for example https://example.test/users/42?page=2. There is exactly one / between the origin and the path.

errors.descHtml: For every case where url throws an error. When no origin is set for the program in nvs.toml.

members.name: urlSigned
members.signature: urlSigned(callable $route, array<mixed> $params, { keys: array<secret bytes>, until: ?Core\Time\Instant } $settings): string

doc.shortHtml: Builds the same link as url, with a signature in the _sig query parameter at the end. The signature is made from the route's path in its #[Route] and from $params. So the link still works when the program is mounted at another path, or when the method gets a new name. Core\Router::signedRoute checks the signature.

params.name: route
params.descHtml: The method that has the #[Route], written as a method reference such as Shop::show. The link does not call the method. So the method may be an instance method or a private method. A method reference written directly in the call is checked when the program compiles. A method without a #[Route] is a compile error.

params.name: params
params.descHtml: The path's captures by name, plus any query parameters. A key written directly in the code must be a capture or a declared #[Query] parameter. Any other key is a compile error. url and urlAbsolute use [] when you leave it out.

params.name: settings
params.descHtml: The keys and the time when the link stops working. Both are required.

shape.descHtml: The keys, newest first. $keys[0] signs the link. The older keys are there so that signedRoute still accepts links made before you changed the key. A signature made by Core\Signature or $uri->sign is not accepted here, even with the same keys.

When the link stops working. It is part of the signature, so nobody can change it. null means the link never stops working. You must write null yourself, because anybody who has such a link can use it forever.

doc.returnHtml: The link from url with _sig=… at the end, for example /users/42?page=2&_sig=…. The same route, values, keys and end time always give the same link. The signature adds about 4/3 × (path + params + 40) characters.

errors.descHtml: For every case where url throws an error. When $params has a _sig key, because this method writes that key itself.
When $settings.keys is empty. When its first key is not 32 bytes long.

doc.shortHtml: Checks the _sig signature of the request that this program is handling. The signature must be one that Core\Router::urlSigned made with $keys for the route that the request matched. The check covers the route's path in its #[Route] and the values. It does not cover the path the program is mounted at.

params.name: keys
params.descHtml: The keys, newest first. Give the same keys that you give urlSigned. A signature made with any key in the list is accepted. So you can add a new key and keep the old one until the old links stop working.

doc.returnHtml: The route that the request matched, as a Core\Router\Match. It is the same value that Core\Request::route() returns. When the check fails, this method throws an error and returns nothing.

errors.descHtml: When the signature is not valid: there is no _sig parameter or there are two, the signature was changed, a key that is not in $keys made it, a value was added, removed or changed, or the request matched no route with a name. All of these have the same message. When the link is too old, with a message of its own. When an escape in the query gives bytes that are not UTF-8.
When the program is not handling a request, for example a command-line program, a job or a test. When $keys is empty. When its first key is not 32 bytes long.

doc.shortHtml: Finds the route that $method and $path belong to. It checks every #[Route] in the program and does not run the route's handler.

params.name: method
params.descHtml: The HTTP method. A route declared for Get does not match a Post.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The path, with no query string. A mount prefix is not removed from it.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Router\Match with the route's name and its captures. Each capture is decoded and has the type of its handler parameter. The result is null when no route has this method and this path, or when the program has no routes.
