A position or a cut that does not exist is null — indexOf, lastIndexOf, before, after — never false.

<?nvs
string $s = Core\Str::trim('  Grüße aus Köln  ');
echo Core\Str::length($s), ' ', Core\Str::upper($s), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice($s, 0, 5), '|', Core\Str::at($s, 2), '|', Core\Str::reverse('café'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::indexOf($s, 'aus') ?? 'none', ' ', Core\Str::indexOf($s, 'Bonn') ?? 'none', "\n";
echo Core\Str::contains($s, 'Köln') ? 'yes' : 'no', ' ', Core\Str::countOf($s, 'ü'), "\n";
array<string> $words = Core\Str::split($s, ' ');
echo Core\Arr::count($words), ' ', Core\Str::join(Core\Arr::reverse($words), '-'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::replace($s, 'Köln', 'Bonn'), '|', Core\Str::before($s, ' ') ?? 'none', "\n";
echo Core\Str::padStart('7', 3, '0'), ' ', Core\Str::repeat('ab', 3), ' ', Core\Str::upperFirst('ßig'), "\n";
echo Core\Str::format('%-6s|%05.1f|%x', 'id', 3.14159, 255), "\n";
echo Core\Str::compare('img10', 'img9'), ' ', Core\Str::compare('img10', 'img9', { natural: true }), "\n";
14 GRÜSSE AUS KÖLN
Grüße|ü|éfac
6 none
yes 1
3 Köln-aus-Grüße
Grüße aus Bonn|Grüße
007 ababab SSig
id    |003.1|ff
-1 1

classes.name: Core\Taint
classes.summary: A `tainted` value came from outside the program, such as a visitor's request. `assertTrusted()` returns it as a plain `string` after your own check, and `assertTrustedBytes()` returns plain `bytes`. Each call needs a reason, which says what was checked.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a tainted string as a plain string. Use it only after your own check, when no function made for that one place fits, such as Core\Html::escape.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The value your program has checked. A plain string is also allowed, and the result is the same text.

params.name: reason
params.descHtml: What was checked, and why the value can be trusted. It is written for the people who read the code. The program never reads it.

doc.returnHtml: The same text as a plain string. Nothing is escaped or removed. A secret value does not compile here, so call Core\Secret::reveal on it first. For tainted bytes, use assertTrustedBytes().

doc.shortHtml: Returns tainted bytes as plain bytes. Use it after your own check, for example when Core\Serialize::decode reads bytes that your program wrote itself.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The bytes your program has checked. Plain bytes are also allowed, and the result is the same bytes.

params.name: reason
params.descHtml: What was checked, and why the bytes can be trusted. It is written for the people who read the code. The program never reads it.

doc.returnHtml: The same bytes as plain bytes. Nothing is changed. A secret value does not compile here, so call Core\Secret::revealBytes on it first.

classes.summaryHtml:
A tainted value came from outside the program, such as a visitor's request. assertTrusted() returns it as a plain string after your own check, and assertTrustedBytes() returns plain bytes. Each call needs a reason, which says what was checked.

Core\Taint::assertTrusted answers its operand with the tainted qualifier dropped, on your own written authority. Every other way out of tainted is sink-named: Core\Html::escape for HTML text, Core\Regex::quote for a pattern, Core\Uri::encodeComponent for a URI component. That is deliberate — a value safe for HTML text is not safe for a shell argument, and a generic sanitize() would invite exactly the false confidence taint tracking exists to prevent. This member is the one case that rule cannot cover: you validated the value yourself, and you need to say so.

It is modeled on the unsafe keyword's job in Rust rather than on a cast. It is forbidden by default, it is rare, it is greppable by its own name, and it carries in the source the reason the value can be trusted. Nothing reads that reason at run time; it is written for the next person to read the line.

The place it is not a fallback but the only route is a database host. Core\Db\Settings.host refuses a tainted value and has no launderer of its own, because no string check can establish that a hostname is safe to send credentials to — a malicious server can answer any query with a LOCAL INFILE request and read files off the application host. An Adminer-style tool where a human genuinely types the host is the case that call site exists for, and this is its honest spelling.

Asserting a value that was never tainted is the identity and is legal: refusing it would cost a diagnostic and prevent no injection.

The two qualifiers are independent bits, and this member answers on one of them. A secret operand is refused outright — Core\Secret::reveal is the escape hatch on that axis. A value carrying both reveals first, whose answer is still tainted, and asserts second; the other order does not compile.

classes.name: Core\Task
classes.summary: Runs work as tasks. `all()` and `map()` run several tasks at the same time and return when every one has finished. `afterResponse()` runs one function after the response is sent.

members.name: all
members.signature: all({ name: callable(): T, ... } $tasks, { limit?: uint, deadline?: Core\Time\Duration }): S

doc.shortHtml: Runs every function in the $tasks object at the same time, and waits until all of them have finished. The result is an object with the same field names, and each field has the type its function returns.

params.name: tasks
params.descHtml: An object whose fields are anonymous functions with no parameters, such as { a: fn (): int => 1 }. Write them directly in the call. A variable of type callable in a field does not compile.

params.name: limit
params.descHtml: The most tasks that run at the same time. The other tasks wait until one finishes. Without it, every task starts at once.

params.name: deadline
params.descHtml: The time limit for the whole call, not for each task. Without it, the request's [limits] wall_time setting is the limit.

doc.returnHtml: An object with the value each function returned. No task is still running when the call returns. If a task throws an error, the other tasks are stopped, and the call throws that same error.

errors.descHtml: When limit is 0. No task could start, so the call could never finish.
When deadline runs out before every task has finished. Every task is stopped first, and the call waits until they have stopped.

members.name: map
members.signature: map(array<T> $items, callable(T, string): U $fn, { limit?: uint, deadline?: Core\Time\Duration }): array<U>

doc.shortHtml: Calls $fn once for each element of $items, and runs the calls at the same time. The result has the same keys in the same order as $items, whichever call finishes first.

params.name: items
params.descHtml: The array. Each element is given to $fn in a task of its own.

params.name: fn
params.descHtml: The function to call. It gets ($value, $key), and it may declare only $value. The key is always a string. Its return type is the type of each element of the result.

params.name: limit
params.descHtml: The most tasks that run at the same time. The other tasks wait until one finishes. Without it, every task starts at once.

params.name: deadline
params.descHtml: The time limit for the whole call, not for each task. Without it, the request's [limits] wall_time setting is the limit.

doc.returnHtml: An array with what $fn returned for each element, under the element's own key. An empty $items gives an empty array. No task is still running when the call returns. If a task throws an error, the other tasks are stopped, and the call throws that same error.

errors.descHtml: When limit is 0. No task could start, so the call could never finish.
When deadline runs out before every task has finished. Every task is stopped first, and the call waits until they have stopped.

doc.shortHtml: Runs $fn after the response is sent, so the client does not wait for it. Use it for receipts, webhooks and audit logs. The work is not saved anywhere: if the process stops, the work is lost and nothing tries it again.

params.name: fn
params.descHtml: The function to run. It takes no arguments, and its return value is ignored. An error it throws is written to the log, and no catch in the request sees it.

params.name: deadline
params.descHtml: The longest time $fn may run. Without it, the [deferred] deadline setting is the limit. The request's [limits] wall_time does not apply here, but its other [limits] settings do.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The functions run one at a time, in the order you added them. They do not run if the request ends with an uncaught error, an exit or a fatal error.

errors.descHtml: When the call is made inside a task that Core\Task::all, Core\Task::map or afterResponse started. Only the request itself may call it, so return the work to the request and call afterResponse there.

classes.summaryHtml:
Runs work as tasks. all() and map() run several tasks at the same time and return when every one has finished. afterResponse() runs one function after the response is sent.

Core\Task runs callables as concurrent child tasks and never returns while one is still running. all takes a shape whose every field is a zero-argument callable and answers a shape with the same names, each field typed by that field's declared return — a field whose callable declares no return type answers mixed, and only that field. map calls one callable per element and answers the results under the subject's own keys, in the subject's order, whatever order the children finished in. Both take the same options: limit caps how many children run at once (the rest wait, nothing is refused) and deadline bounds the whole call — when it expires every child is cancelled and the call throws TimeoutError. The first child to throw cancels its siblings and its throw propagates once they are gone; a cancelled child runs no more of its own code, not even a catch.

<?nvs
var $page = Core\Task::all({
    rows: fn(): array<int> => [1, 2, 3],
    label: fn(): string => 'all',
});
echo $page->label, '=', Core\Arr::count($page->rows), "\n";

var $lengths = Core\Task::map(['fig' => 'fig', 'pear' => 'pear'], fn(string $word): uint => Core\Str::length($word), { limit: 1 });
foreach ($lengths as string $key => uint $length) {
    echo $key, ':', $length, "\n";
}

try {
    Core\Task::map([1, 2], fn(int $n): int => {
        Core\Time::sleep(200ms);
        return $n;
    }, { deadline: 20ms });
    echo 'finished in time', "\n";
} catch (TimeoutError $late) {
    echo 'deadline hit', "\n";
}
all=3
fig:3
pear:4
deadline hit

classes.name: Core\Task\Channel
classes.summary: A queue with a fixed size that sends values from one task to another. `send` waits while the queue is full, and a `foreach` loop over the channel receives the values.

doc.shortHtml: Adds $value to the queue for the task that receives it. While the channel is full, the calling task waits.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The value to send.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. send returns when the value is in the queue. A send on a closed channel is a fatal error, and a catch block cannot catch it.

doc.shortHtml: Closes the channel. A foreach loop over the channel ends after it has received the values that are still in the queue.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Values sent before close are still received. Calling close twice does nothing.

classes.summaryHtml:
A queue with a fixed size that sends values from one task to another. send waits while the queue is full, and a foreach loop over the channel receives the values.

Core\Task\Channel<T> carries values from one task to another. It is built with new Core\Task\Channel<T>($capacity) — the capacity is at least 1 — and holds that many values: a send into a full channel suspends the sending task until the consumer has taken one, which is the whole of the backpressure. The channel is its own consumer loop: a foreach over it takes each value out, waits while the channel is empty and still open, and ends once the channel is empty and closed. close is what ends that loop, and every value sent before it is still delivered; a send after close is a fatal error that no catch sees. Both ends are normally children of one Core\Task::all, so the call returns only when the producer and the consumer are both done.

<?nvs
class Log
{
    public static string $seen = '';
}

var $line = new Core\Task\Channel<int>(2);

Core\Task::all({
    produce: fn(): int => {
        foreach (Core\Arr::range(1, 6) as int $n) {
            $line->send($n * $n);
        }
        $line->close();
        return 6;
    },
    consume: fn(): int => {
        foreach ($line as int $square) {
            Log::$seen = Log::$seen . $square . ' ';
        }
        return 0;
    },
});

echo Log::$seen, "\n";
1 4 9 16 25 36

classes.name: Core\Test
classes.summary: The methods you call inside a `#[Test]` method. They check a result, move the fixed clock and give fake replies to the web requests your code sends. `nvs test` runs the test and reports each check that fails.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that $actual is identical to $expected. Two objects are identical only when they are the same object.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The value under test.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The value $actual must be identical to. T is the type of $actual, so $expected must have the same type. Otherwise the call does not compile.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: The two values are not identical. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that $actual equals $expected. Two objects are compared with Comparable::compareTo, and every other value must be identical.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The value under test.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The value $actual must equal. T is the type of $actual, so $expected must have the same type. Otherwise the call does not compile.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: The two values are not equal. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.
Both are objects and $actual's class declares no compareTo.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $actual and $expected have the same structure and values. Arrays are compared entry by entry, and objects property by property. Other values are compared by identity. A failure shows where the two values first differ.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The value under test.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The value $actual must match everywhere. T is the type of $actual, so $expected must have the same type. Otherwise the call does not compile.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: The two values differ. The message gives the path to the first difference, written the way code indexes into $actual. The failure is recorded before it is thrown.
The values are nested more than 64 levels deep.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $actual is true. The value must be a bool, so a call with a number or a string does not compile.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The bool to check.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: $actual is false. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that $actual is null. $actual is mixed, so it can be a value of any type.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The value under test.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: $actual is not null. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that the array $actual has exactly $expected entries. To check the length of a string, assert on Core\Str::length.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The array under test.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The number of entries the array must have.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: The array has a different number of entries. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that some entry of $actual is identical to $expected, as Core\Arr::contains checks. To check for a substring, assert on Core\Str::contains.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The array under test.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The entry the array must contain. It is compared by identity. int, uint, float and decimal values compare as numbers, so 1 finds 1.0.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: No entry of the array is identical to $expected. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Asserts that $actual, rendered as Core\Debug::render renders it, is exactly $expected. This is an inline snapshot: the expected text is a string written in the test itself, not a file beside it.

params.name: actual
params.descHtml: The value to render. A secret property inside it is shown redacted, so a snapshot never puts a secret into your source code.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The text you expect the rendering to be, written in the test. nvs test --update writes it here for you. It changes only this string in the file.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed.

errors.descHtml: The rendering is different from $expected. The failure message shows both. The failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

members.name: assertThrows
members.signature: assertThrows(callable(): mixed $body, string $expected, { message?: string }): void

doc.shortHtml: Runs $body and asserts that it throws $expected or a subclass of it. The error it throws is caught here, so only a failed assertion reaches the caller.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The function to run. A value it returns is ignored.

params.name: expected
params.descHtml: The full class name, as ParseError::class gives it. The thrown class matches if it is this class or extends it.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed. A FATAL error or an exit inside $body is not caught, and it is not changed. A check that fails inside $body still counts as a failure of its own.

errors.descHtml: $body returned without throwing, or it threw a class that is not $expected. The message names the class it threw and the message of that error. The failure is recorded before it is thrown.

doc.shortHtml: Runs $body and checks that it returns without throwing an error. A test with no check fails, and this call counts as a check. An error from $body is caught, so only the failure of this check reaches the caller.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The function to run. A value it returns is ignored.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message. The default is no text.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The check is recorded as passed. A FATAL error or an exit inside $body is not caught, and it is not changed.

errors.descHtml: $body threw an error. A check that failed inside $body counts too, and it still counts as a failure of its own. The failure message includes the error's message. The failure is recorded before it is thrown.

doc.shortHtml: Runs $body and checks that a check inside it failed. Those failures then no longer count against the test. Use it to test a check you wrote yourself.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The function to run. A failed check counts even when $body catches the Core\Test\Failure itself.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The failed checks inside $body are removed from the test's result, and the Core\Test\Failure it threw is caught. The checks that passed still count.

errors.descHtml: No check inside $body failed. This failure is recorded before it is thrown, so a catch does not remove it from the test's result.

doc.shortHtml: Moves the clock that #[Test(at: ...)] fixed forward by $by. A test of something that expires can then check the time after it expires, without waiting.

params.name: by
params.descHtml: How far to move the clock. A negative duration moves it back.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The next Core\Time::now() returns the moved time.

errors.descHtml: The running test has no at:, so there is no fixed clock to move. The real clock of the computer is never moved.
The moved time is outside the range a clock can show, about the years -9999 to 9999. The clock does not move.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the address of the test server that a #[Test(server: true)] test starts. The server runs on this computer, on a free port. Use it when a test needs a real network connection.
doc.returnHtml: An address such as http://127.0.0.1:52341, with no / at the end, so you can add a path directly. The result is null everywhere else, which includes a test without server: true and a program started with nvs run.

doc.shortHtml: Gives the answers for the next Core\Cli prompts, so you can test a program that asks questions. Each prompt takes the first answer that is still waiting. It does not read the terminal.

params.name: answers
params.descHtml: One answer per prompt, in the order the program asks. Write what a person would type, without the line ending. A select reads the number of a choice, and a confirm reads y or n.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. A second call adds its answers after the ones still waiting. When no answer is left, a prompt returns its default or throws Core\Cli\NotInteractive.

members.name: request
members.signature: request(Core\Http\Method $method, string $path, { headers?: array<string>, body?: string|bytes, mount?: string, captures?: array<string> }): Core\Test\Response

doc.shortHtml: Sends one request to your own program and returns the answer. It opens no network connection. The request goes through the same route table and the same code as a real request.

params.name: method
params.descHtml: The HTTP method of the request, such as Core\Http\Method::Get.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The path of the request, such as /orders/7. A ? and the text after it are the query string.

params.name: headers
params.descHtml: The headers of the request, with the header name as the key. If you give no content-type or content-length, the length is set from body.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The body of the request, as a string or as bytes. If you give no body, the request has no body. An empty string is a body of length 0.

params.name: mount
params.descHtml: The prefix the program is served under, such as /shop. Core\Request::mount() returns it, and Core\Router::url adds it in front of each link. The default is "", which means the root.

params.name: captures
params.descHtml: The parts of the prefix that the mount's pattern matched, in order. For the pattern /shops/{1} and mount: "/shops/acme", this is ["acme"]. Core\Request::mount()->captures() returns this list. The default is an empty list. You need mount to give captures.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Test\Response. status() returns the status the program set, or 200 if it set none. body() returns the text the program wrote, and json() and jsonAs() decode it. header(), headers() and cookies() return the headers and cookies the program set. A path that no route matches still gets an answer, because your program decides what to do with it. A body that is not text, such as a PDF file, also gets an answer. Then body(), json() and jsonAs() throw an error.

errors.descHtml: captures is not empty and mount is "". The root has no pattern, so it has no captures. captures is also an error when it is not a list.
There is no program to answer, because the call is not in nvs test or nvs run. The call is also an error inside a request that request sent, because a request cannot send another request.

members.name: answerHttp
members.signature: answerHttp(string $url, uint $status, { json?: mixed, body?: string|bytes, headers?: array<string|array<string>>, tls?: Core\Http\TlsInfo }): void

doc.shortHtml: Gives a fake reply for one outbound URL. After the first call to answerHttp, every Core\Http\Client call in this test gets a fake reply. No call connects to the network.

params.name: url
params.descHtml: The URL this reply is for: the whole URL, or a prefix that ends in *. Nothing is resolved and no host is looked up. The URL of each call is compared with this text.

params.name: status
params.descHtml: The status code of the reply. It has three digits, from 100 to 999.

params.name: json
params.descHtml: A value that the reply sends as a JSON document. It is written exactly as Core\Json::encode writes it. The reply has the content type application/json, unless headers sets a content type.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The body of a reply that is not JSON. It can be text, or the bytes of a reply that is not text. Core\Http\Response::bytes reads such a body, and ::text throws an error for it. Give body or json, not both.

params.name: headers
params.descHtml: The headers of the reply, with the name as the key. This is the shape Core\Http\Options uses for the headers of a request, with one addition. An array of strings under a name means the reply has that header on that many lines. Core\Http\Response::headers returns it that way. Upper and lower case do not matter in a name, as for any header name.

params.name: tls
params.descHtml: The TLS session the reply reports, from Core\Test::tlsSession. Core\Http\Response::tls returns it for every call this answer serves. Without it, tls() returns null.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Each call adds one more reply, so a test can give a reply for each call it makes. An exact URL wins over a prefix, and the longest prefix wins among prefixes.

errors.descHtml: The call gives both json and body, which are two ways to write one body. Or the status is not from 100 to 999. Or the call gives a tls session for an http:// URL, which has no TLS.

members.name: tlsSession
members.signature: tlsSession({ version?: string, cipher?: string, verified?: bool, subject?: string, issuer?: string, expiry?: Core\Time\Instant }): Core\Http\TlsInfo

doc.shortHtml: Builds a TLS session for a test, with a real certificate chain, so a test can read a Core\Http\TlsInfo without a network.

params.name: version
params.descHtml: TLSv1.3 or TLSv1.2. The default is TLSv1.3.

params.name: cipher
params.descHtml: A cipher suite this build supports for that version, under its IANA name. The default is TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 for TLS 1.3 and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 for TLS 1.2.

params.name: verified
params.descHtml: What verified() returns. The default is true.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: The leaf certificate's subject, written as subject() returns it: KEY=value pairs such as CN=api.example.com, O=Shop, with the keys CN, O, OU, C, ST and L. The default is CN=example.com.

params.name: issuer
params.descHtml: The subject of the CA certificate that signs the leaf, which is what issuer() returns. Written like subject. The default is CN=Novis Test CA.

params.name: expiry
params.descHtml: When the leaf certificate expires, in whole seconds. The default is 90 days after Core\Time::now(), so a test with a fixed clock gets the same value every run.

doc.returnHtml: A Core\Http\TlsInfo. Its peerChain() has two certificates: the leaf, then the CA that signed it. Pass it to Core\Test::answerHttp as tls to make a faked reply report it.

errors.descHtml: The version is not TLSv1.3 or TLSv1.2. Or the cipher is not one this build supports for that version. Or a subject or issuer is not written as KEY=value pairs with the keys above. Or the expiry is before 1950 or after 9999.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every HTTP request the program sent after the first Core\Test::answerHttp call. The oldest request comes first.
doc.returnHtml: One Core\Test\SentRequest for each request, in the order the program sent them. The list is empty when the program sent nothing. Nothing in a request is tainted, because the program wrote all of it.

doc.shortHtml: Gives a fake peer for one outbound WebSocket URL, and this test does not use the network. A socket opened to a matching URL completes its handshake without connecting. It receives these frames in order, and then a close.

params.name: url
params.descHtml: The URL this peer is for: the whole URL, or a prefix that ends in *. Nothing is resolved and no host is looked up. The URL given to Core\Http\Client::openSocket is compared with this text. Its scheme is still checked, so a https URL given here is not allowed when openSocket runs.

params.name: frames
params.descHtml: What the peer sends, in order. A string is a text message and bytes is a binary message, the same as send and sendBytes write. After the last frame, receive returns null, which means the peer closed the socket.

params.name: protocol
params.descHtml: The subprotocol the peer chooses in its 101 reply. It must be one that the call offered in protocols. If the peer chooses a name that was never offered, openSocket throws an error, as it does with a real peer. If you leave it out, the handshake chooses no subprotocol.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Each call adds one more peer, so a test can give a peer for each socket it opens. An exact URL wins over a prefix, and the longest prefix wins among prefixes. Two sockets opened to one URL read that peer's frames separately. Each socket keeps its own place in the list.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every frame the program sent over a fake socket, oldest first. These are the frames the program sent, not the frames it received.
doc.returnHtml: One Core\Socket\Message for each frame, in the order the program sent them. text is set for a send, and bytes for a sendBytes. When two sockets are open at once, their frames are mixed in the order they were written. To check them apart, a test uses one peer at a time.

doc.shortHtml: Creates a test double: a fake T built from an object of functions, one for each method. The double is a T, so you can pass it anywhere a T is needed.

params.name: answers
params.descHtml: One field per method of T, with the same name as the method. Each field has the function that runs when that method is called. A field for a method that T does not declare does not compile. A method of T that has no field does not compile either.

doc.returnHtml: The double, typed as T. It records every call made to it, and Core\Test::assertCalled reads that record later. A backtrace shows no class that you did not write.

errors.descHtml: T declares more methods than one double supports. This limit is fixed, and it is far above the size of the interfaces a test usually replaces.

doc.shortHtml: Creates a test double for T that runs the functions in $answers for the methods they name. Every call to another method goes to $real.

params.name: real
params.descHtml: The object that gets the calls to the methods $answers does not replace. Each call reaches $real with the same arguments.

params.name: answers
params.descHtml: One field for each method you replace, with the same name as the method. A field for a method that T does not declare does not compile. A method you leave out is allowed, because $real handles it. This is not allowed in double.

doc.returnHtml: The partial double, typed as T. Every call is recorded, both the calls a function in $answers handles and the calls $real handles.

errors.descHtml: T declares more methods than one double supports. The limit and the error message are the same as for double.

members.name: assertCalled
members.signature: assertCalled(object $double, method $method, { times?: uint, with?: array<mixed>, message?: string }): void

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $method was called on $double. The check runs after your code, on the record of calls that the double kept. You do not declare the expected calls in advance.

params.name: double
params.descHtml: The double or partial double to check.

params.name: method
params.descHtml: The method, written as Mailer::send. The compiler checks this reference, so renaming the method updates or breaks the test.

params.name: times
params.descHtml: The exact number of calls you expect. If you leave it out, any number above zero passes.

params.name: with
params.descHtml: The arguments that one of the recorded calls must have. They are compared the way Core\Test::assertEquals compares. If you leave it out, the arguments are not checked.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message, as on every other check.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The call throws an error if the method was not called, or was called a different number of times or with different arguments.

errors.descHtml: The record does not contain the call that the options describe. The message names the method, what you expected, and every call in the record.
$double is an ordinary object. Core\Test::double or Core\Test::partial did not create it, so it has no record of calls.

doc.shortHtml: Checks that $method was never called on $double. It is the opposite of assertCalled, and it reads the same record of calls.

params.name: double
params.descHtml: The double or partial double to check.

params.name: method
params.descHtml: The method, written as Mailer::purge. It is checked the same way as in assertCalled.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message, as on every other check.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. One recorded call is enough to throw an error.

errors.descHtml: The method was called. The message shows the first recorded call and the total number of calls.
$double is not a double. This is the same error as in assertCalled.

members.name: assertCompletes
members.signature: assertCompletes(callable(): mixed $body, { within: Core\Time\Duration } $settings, { message?: string }): void

doc.shortHtml: Moves the test's clock forward by $settings.within, runs $body, and checks that no task it started is still running. The real time is never read. A budget of many seconds takes microseconds, and every run gives the same result.

params.name: body
params.descHtml: The work to run. It is called once, on the test's own task. Its return value is ignored.

params.name: settings
params.descHtml: The time budget. You must always give it, because no default duration fits every caller.

shape.descHtml: How far the test's clock moves before $body runs. A retry, a backoff or a timeout inside $body then does not wait. Core\Test::advance moves the same clock. The move stays: after this call, the test reads the moved clock.

params.name: message
params.descHtml: Your own text, added at the start of the failure message, as on every other check.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If $body returns while a task it started is still running, the call throws an error that names the budget. The check runs when $body returns.

errors.descHtml: $body returned while a task it started was still running. The message gives the number of tasks and the within value they had.
The test has no at:, so there is no fixed clock to move. Core\Test::advance throws the same error for the same reason.
The moved clock is outside the range an Instant can have. Core\Test::advance throws the same error.

classes.summaryHtml:
The methods you call inside a #[Test] method. They check a result, move the fixed clock and give fake replies to the web requests your code sends. nvs test runs the test and reports each check that fails.

Core\Test is the assertion surface: every member is static, takes the subject first (assertEquals($actual, $expected)), and is generic, so comparing an int with a string is a compile error rather than a failed test. A failed assertion throws Core\Test\Failure, an ordinary Throwable a catch may take — but the runner keeps its own ledger of what held and what failed, and a catch does not erase an entry; expectFailure is the one member that discharges one. A test is a public, non-static method returning void and marked #[Core\Test] (or #[Test] after use Core\Test;), run by nvs test; a test that asserts nothing fails. Marking, fixtures, data rows and the runner's report belong to testing.

<?nvs
final class Cart
{
    private array<int> $prices = [];

    public function add(int $price): void
    {
        if ($price < 0) {
            throw new LogicError('a price is never negative');
        }
        $this->prices = Core\Arr::append($this->prices, $price);
    }

    public function total(): int
    {
        return Core\Arr::sum($this->prices) as int;
    }

    public function lines(): array<int>
    {
        return $this->prices;
    }
}

final class CartTest
{
    #[Core\Test]
    public function sumsWhatWasAdded(): void
    {
        var $cart = new Cart();
        $cart->add(3);
        $cart->add(4);
        Core\Test::assertSame($cart->total(), 7);
        Core\Test::assertCount($cart->lines(), 2, { message: 'two lines were added' });
    }

    #[Core\Test]
    public function refusesANegativePrice(): void
    {
        var $cart = new Cart();
        Core\Test::assertThrows(fn(): void => { $cart->add(-1); }, LogicError::class);
        Core\Test::assertTrue($cart->total() == 0);
    }
}
  CartTest
    ✓ sumsWhatWasAdded
    ✓ refusesANegativePrice
  0 failed, 2 passed

classes.name: Core\Test\Outcome
classes.summary: How one run of one test ended. A method with `#[AfterEachTest]` can take one as its parameter. The test runner creates it. You cannot create one yourself.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the name of the test class.
doc.returnHtml: The class name, with its namespace.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the name of the test method that ran.
doc.returnHtml: The method name. A test with #[TestWith] rows has #0, #1 and so on after the name, as the report prints it.

doc.shortHtml: Returns which run of the test this was.
doc.returnHtml: 1 for the first run. Each retry from retries: adds one.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether this run of the test passed.
doc.returnHtml: true when the run passed, and false when it failed.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the failure messages of this run.
doc.returnHtml: One message per failure, as the report prints it. The list is empty when the run passed.

classes.summaryHtml: How one run of one test ended. A method with #[AfterEachTest] can take one as its parameter. The test runner creates it. You cannot create one yourself.

classes.name: Core\Test\Response
classes.summary: The answer to one request that `Core\Test::request` sent to your own program. `status()` returns the status code, `header()` and `headers()` return the headers, `cookies()` returns the cookies the program set, and `body()`, `bytes()`, `json()` and `jsonAs()` return the body. You cannot create one yourself.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the HTTP status code of the answer to this request.
doc.returnHtml: The code the program set with Core\Response::setStatus. If the program set no code, the result is 200. If the program threw an error it did not catch, the result is 500, the same code the server sends.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the text the program wrote while it answered this request.
doc.returnHtml: Everything the program wrote with echo, in order. If the program wrote nothing, the result is an empty string. If the program threw an error it did not catch, the result is also an empty string, because the server sends no body for a failed request.

errors.descHtml: The body is not valid UTF-8, so it is not a string. Core\Response::bytes and Core\Response::sendFile can write such a body. Read it with bytes().

doc.shortHtml: Returns the body the program wrote while it answered this request, as bytes.
doc.returnHtml: Every byte of the body, in order. The bytes do not have to be valid UTF-8, so this works for a PDF, an image or a file sent with Core\Response::sendFile. If the program wrote nothing, or threw an error it did not catch, the result is empty bytes.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the value of one header of the answer, by its name.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the header. Upper and lower case do not matter, so Content-Type and content-type are the same header.

doc.returnHtml: The value, exactly as the program set it. The result is null when the answer has no header of that name. When the answer has the header on more than one line, the values are joined with , in order. The answer always has a Content-Type header. If the program set none, its value is text/html; charset=utf-8, the same as the server sends. A request that failed has no headers.

errors.descHtml: The name is Set-Cookie. Two cookies joined into one string are not a cookie, so cookies() and headers() read that header.

doc.shortHtml: Returns every header of the answer, grouped by name.
doc.returnHtml: An array<array<string>>. Each key is a header name in lower case. Its value is a list with one entry for each line of that header, in order. Set-Cookie has one line for each cookie. A request that failed returns an empty array.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the cookies the program set in this answer, by name.
doc.returnHtml: An array<string>. Each key is a cookie name and each value is the cookie value, exactly as the program set it. Nothing is decoded. Attributes such as Path and HttpOnly are not in the result, and headers()["set-cookie"] returns the whole lines. When the program set one name twice, the result has the last value. A cookie that the program deleted is in the result with an empty value. The array is empty when the program set no cookie.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the body of the answer as one JSON document and returns the decoded value.

params.name: maxDepth
params.descHtml: How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded value, the same as Core\Json::decode returns for the body. A JSON object becomes an array with string keys. Every call decodes the body again and returns the same value.

errors.descHtml: maxDepth is not from 1 to 1024.
The body is not one whole JSON document, or it nests deeper than maxDepth. An empty body throws this error too. The Content-Type header is not checked.
The body is not valid UTF-8, so it is not text.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the body of the answer as one JSON object and returns a new instance of the class T. The class needs #[Core\Json\Derive]. Write array<T> to read a JSON array with one object for each element.

params.name: maxDepth
params.descHtml: How deep the document may nest. The default is 512, and the value must be from 1 to 1024. A document with no array or object in it has depth 1.

doc.returnHtml: A new T with its properties read from the body, or one T for each element for an array<T>. Every call creates new objects.

errors.descHtml: T has no #[Core\Json\Derive] attribute. Or maxDepth is not from 1 to 1024.

The body is not one whole JSON object, or it nests deeper than maxDepth. An empty body throws this error too. It is also thrown when a field is missing or has the wrong type. The issues list has one entry for each wrong field. The Content-Type header is not checked.
The body is not valid UTF-8, so it is not text.

The call stack is full when a constructor runs. This happens when the call starts with the stack almost full, or when a constructor recurses deeply. A deep body within maxDepth does not throw this error.

classes.summaryHtml:
The answer to one request that Core\Test::request sent to your own program. status() returns the status code, header() and headers() return the headers, cookies() returns the cookies the program set, and body(), bytes(), json() and jsonAs() return the body. You cannot create one yourself.

Core\Test\Response is the value Core\Test::request(...) answers: what the program under test wrote while answering one synthetic request. status() is the status, header() and headers() the headers, cookies() the cookies it set, and body(), json() and jsonAs<T>() the body. It has no constructor — the only way to obtain one is to make a request.

The readers are Core\Request's, read from the answer's side: header matches any case and joins repeated lines with , , headers keys lower-cased names to lists of lines, and json and jsonAs take the same {maxDepth?} option and throw the same errors. The headers are the ones a visitor is sent by the program — its Content-Type, which is HTML for a page that only echoed, a redirect's Location, the Set-Cookie of each addCookie, and every setHeader — and not the ones the server adds for itself. header("Set-Cookie") throws a LogicError, because two cookies joined are not a cookie; cookies() reads them by name.

The request runs in this process. There is no socket and no port: the program's own entry is run as an isolate with the compiled route table's match already on it, so Core\Request::route() inside the program reads the same match a served request would, and the handler chain that answers is the real one rather than a mock of it. What comes back is the status the program declared — 200 where it declared none — and every byte it echoed. A program that throws an error it does not catch answers 500, an empty body and no headers of its own, which is what the server sends for a failed request.

#[Test]
public function itReturnsTheUser(): void {
    var $rs = Core\Test::request(Core\Http\Method::Get, "/users/1");

    Core\Test::assertEquals($rs->status(), 200);
    Core\Test::assertEquals($rs->body(), "ada");
}

A request may not be made from inside one. The program answering an in-process request is the same program that asked for it, so a second one would answer its own request forever; the call throws RuntimeError instead, naming why. The same throw is what a call outside nvs test or nvs run gets, there being no program under test to answer it.

classes.summaryHtml:
Reads the clock and builds dates and times. now returns the current Instant. at builds a DateTime from a year, a month, a day and a zone, and fromIso reads a timestamp such as 2024-03-01T12:00:00Z. sleep waits for a Duration.

Core\Time is where a time value starts: now() reads the clock as an Instant, fromIso and fromEpoch build one from a timestamp, and at and parse build a DateTime from civil fields or text. Every value it answers is immutable, and there is no ambient time zone — a DateTime is always built in a Zone the call names, and an Instant becomes a calendar reading only through ->in($zone). The two arithmetics are told apart by type: an Instant moves by an exact Duration (->plus(24h)), a DateTime moves by a calendar step (->plus(1, Core\Unit::Day)), and across a DST boundary the two land an hour apart. There is no free-form date text: each phrase such as "next Monday" is a typed call, and a run-time offset such as "30d" is Core\Time\Duration::parse.

<?nvs
var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $meeting = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 9, minute: 30 });
echo $meeting->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";

var $parsed = Core\Time::parse('5 March 2024', 'd MMMM yyyy', $utc);
echo $parsed->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), "\n";

var $stamp = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-03-01T10:30:00+01:00');
echo $stamp->toIso(), "\n";
echo $stamp->compareTo($meeting->toInstant()) == 0 ? 'same instant' : 'different', "\n";

echo Core\Time::fromEpoch(0)->in($utc)->format('EEEE, d MMMM yyyy'), "\n";

var $berlin = Core\Time\Zone::of('Europe/Berlin');
echo $meeting->toInstant()->in($berlin)->format('HH:mm VV'), "\n";

var $eve = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 30, $berlin, { hour: 12 });
echo $eve->plus(1, Core\Unit::Day)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $eve->toInstant()->plus(24h)->in($berlin)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time::at(2024, 2, 30, $utc);
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "30 February does not exist\n";
}
2024-03-01 09:30
2024-03-05 00:00:00
2024-03-01T09:30:00Z
same instant
Thursday, 1 January 1970
10:30 Europe/Berlin
2024-03-31 12:00
2024-03-31 13:00
30 February does not exist

classes.summaryHtml:
A date with no time of day and no zone, such as a birthday or a due date. Core\Time\Date::at builds one from a year, a month and a day. plus and minus move it by days, months or years, and format turns it into text.

A Date is the year, month and day alone — no time of day and no zone — built by Date::at or read off a DateTime with ->date(). There is no Date::parse: text is read with Core\Time::parse (a pattern and a zone), and the DateTime it answers gives up its date. A date that does not exist throws where it is built. It steps by Core\Unit::Day and larger, with the same month-end clamping as DateTime::plus; a smaller unit is refused. format takes the date letters of the CLDR grammar DateTime::format uses, and a time or zone letter in the pattern is refused because a Date has none to render. Two dates are ordered with compareTo; the < operators do not compile on a Date.

<?nvs
var $d = Core\Time\Date::at(2024, 1, 31);
echo $d->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->format('EEEE, d MMMM'), "\n";

echo $d->plus(1, Core\Unit::Month)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->minus(1, Core\Unit::Day)->format('EEE d MMM'), "\n";
echo $d->with({ month: 3 })->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->compareTo(Core\Time\Date::at(2024, 2, 1)), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time\Date::at(2023, 2, 29);
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "2023-02-29 does not exist\n";
}

var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
echo Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 23 })->date()->format('d/M/yyyy'), "\n";

Wednesday, 31 January
2024-02-29
Tue 30 Jan
2024-03-31
-1
2023-02-29 does not exist
1/3/2024

classes.summaryHtml:
A date and a time of day in one time zone, such as the start of a meeting in Berlin. Core\Time::at builds one from its parts, and in on an Instant gives one for a moment. date and timeOfDay return its two halves, and format turns it into text.

A DateTime is a civil reading — year, month, day, hour, minute, second, nanosecond — in one Zone, built by Core\Time::at or Core\Time::parse or read off an Instant with ->in($zone). It is immutable: every member answers a new value. Its arithmetic is calendar arithmetic: plus(1, Core\Unit::Month) keeps the day-of-month clamped to the new month's length, plus(1, Core\Unit::Day) across a DST boundary is a 23- or 25-hour day, and difference counts whole units in the receiver's zone. format takes a CLDR pattern. Core\Time::parse reads the same patterns, and Date::format and TimeOfDay::format use them for their own fields. A pattern written directly in the code is checked when the program compiles, so a letter outside the table below is a compile error; a pattern computed at run time throws a LogicError instead. Month and weekday names are always in English.

LetterFieldCounts
yyearyy two digits; any other count zero-pads to it
MmonthM/MM numeric, MMM Mar, MMMM March, MMMMM M
dday of monthnumeric, zero-padded to the count
Dday of yearnumeric
EweekdayE–EEE Tue, EEEE Tuesday, EEEEE T, EEEEEE Tu
aAM/PMany count
h / H / K / khour 1–12 / 0–23 / 0–11 / 1–24numeric
mminutenumeric
ssecondnumeric
Sfractional secondone digit per count, truncated
Xoffset, Z at zeroX +01, XX +0100, XXX +01:00
xoffset, never Zthe same three counts
VVthe zone's IANA identifierVV only

Text between '…' is printed as it is, and '' is one apostrophe. G, Q, w, W, L, c, F and u are refused.

<?nvs
var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $d = Core\Time::at(2024, 1, 31, $utc, { hour: 9, minute: 30 });
echo $d->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $d->format("EEEE, d MMMM yyyy 'at' h:mm a"), "\n";

echo $d->plus(1, Core\Unit::Month)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->minus(1, Core\Unit::Week)->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->next(Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Monday)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $d->with({ month: 3, day: 1 })->format('yyyy-MM-dd'), "\n";
echo $d->startOf(Core\Unit::Day)->format('HH:mm'), ' ',
    $d->endOf(Core\Unit::Month)->format('dd HH:mm:ss.SSS'), "\n";

echo $d->difference(Core\Time::at(2026, 8, 30, $utc), Core\Unit::Year), "\n";
echo $d->weekday() == Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday::Wednesday ? 'midweek' : 'other', "\n";
echo $d->dayOfYear(), ' ', $d->isLeapYear() ? 'leap' : 'common', "\n";
echo $d->toInstant()->toIso(), "\n";

Wednesday, 31 January 2024 at 9:30 AM
2024-02-29
2024-01-24
2024-02-05 09:30
2024-03-01
00:00 31 23:59:59.999
2
midweek
31 leap

doc.shortHtml: Reads a duration such as 30s, 1h30m or 7d from text at run time. It uses the same syntax as a duration written in the code. Use it for an exact offset that comes from a config value or a flag. It accepts nothing else, so the result is not tainted, even when the text is.

params.descHtml: The text to read, written the same way as a duration in the code.

doc.returnHtml: The Duration the text describes.

A $text written directly in the code is checked when the program compiles, and an error there is E0769. Only a computed $text can throw this error.

errors.descHtml: The sum is longer than a Duration can hold.

errors.descHtml: The product is longer than a Duration can hold.

doc.shortHtml: Orders two durations by length and sign, as Comparable requires, so a shorter duration compares below a longer one and a negative one below every positive one. Use it to compare two durations by value. == on two objects tests identity, so 90m == 1h30m is false. To test that two durations are equal, write $a->compareTo($b) == 0.

params.name: other
params.descHtml: The duration to compare against.

doc.returnHtml: -1 when the receiver is shorter than $other, 0 when they are equal, 1 when it is longer.

doc.shortHtml: Writes the receiver as text in the same syntax as a duration in the code, such as 1h30m or 250ms. Stringable requires this method, and Duration::parse reads the text back to the same value.
doc.returnHtml: The receiver written as a duration, such as 1h30m.

classes.summaryHtml:
A length of time, such as 30 seconds or an hour and a half. You write a fixed one directly in the code, like 30s or 1h30m, and build a computed one with seconds, minutes or another constructor. It is an exact count of nanoseconds and can be negative. plus, minus and compareTo work on two of them.

A Duration is a signed count of nanoseconds. You write one directly in the code as a number and a unit — 30s, 250ms, 1h30m, 7d — with the units ns, us, ms, s, m, h, d and w, and Duration::parse reads the same grammar from text at run time. It is exact: days(1) and 1d are twenty-four hours, never a calendar day, which is what Core\Time\DateTime::plus($n, Core\Unit::Day) is. echo renders a duration back in that same syntax, so its text round-trips through parse. An argument to parse written directly in the code is read when the program compiles, so a bad one is a compile error; text computed at run time throws a ParseError. Two durations are ordered with compareTo; the < operators do not compile on a Duration.

<?nvs
var $d = 1h30m;
echo $d, "\n";
echo $d->toSeconds(), "\n";

echo $d->plus(15m), "\n";
echo $d->minus(2h), "\n";
echo $d->multipliedBy(2), "\n";
echo $d->negated(), "\n";

echo Core\Time\Duration::parse('250ms')->toMilliseconds(), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Duration::minutes(90)->compareTo($d), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Duration::seconds(90061), "\n";
echo 1500ms->toString(), "\n";

string $flag = '--since=30 seconds';
try {
    Core\Time\Duration::parse(Core\Str::slice($flag, 8));
} catch (ParseError $bad) {
    echo "not a duration\n";
}
