5400
1h45m
-30m
3h
-1h30m
250
0
1d1h1m1s
1s500ms
not a duration

classes.name: Core\Time\Instant
classes.summary: One exact point in time, the same everywhere in the world. It has no time zone and no calendar. `Core\Time::now`, `Core\Time::fromEpoch` and `Core\Time::fromIso` return one. `plus`, `minus` and `since` do exact arithmetic with a `Duration`, and `in` shows the instant on a zone's calendar.

doc.shortHtml: Shows this instant on the calendar and clock of $zone. This is the only way to get a date or an hour from an instant, so you always name the zone.

params.name: zone
params.descHtml: The time zone to show the instant in. Its offset at this instant is used, including summer time.

doc.returnHtml: A DateTime at the same instant, in $zone. The instant does not change.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the Unix timestamp of this instant: the whole seconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC.
doc.returnHtml: An int, negative before 1970. The part of a second is cut off, toward zero.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole milliseconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC, as JavaScript counts time.
doc.returnHtml: An int, negative before 1970. The part of a millisecond is cut off, toward zero. Every instant fits.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the whole microseconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC.
doc.returnHtml: An int, negative before 1970. The part of a microsecond is cut off, toward zero. Every instant fits.

doc.shortHtml: Moves the instant forward by an exact Duration. An instant has no time zone, so a change to or from summer time does not change the result. To add calendar days, use $i->in($zone)->plus($n, Unit::Day).

params.name: d
params.descHtml: The duration to add. A negative duration moves the instant back.

doc.returnHtml: A new Instant. The original instant does not change.

errors.descHtml: The result is before the year -9999 or after the year 9999.

doc.shortHtml: Moves the instant back by an exact Duration.

params.name: d
params.descHtml: The exact duration to subtract; a negative one moves the instant forward.

doc.returnHtml: A new Instant; the receiver is unchanged.

errors.descHtml: The result lies outside the representable range, about ±9999 years.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the exact time from $earlier to this instant, as a Duration. $earlier->plus($later->since($earlier)) is $later again.

params.name: earlier
params.descHtml: The instant to measure from.

doc.returnHtml: A Duration. It is negative when $earlier is after this instant.

errors.descHtml: The two instants are more than about 292 years apart. That is the longest Duration there is.

doc.shortHtml: Checks which of two instants comes first, as Comparable requires. The operators <, >, <=, >= and <=> use this method too. == on two instants checks whether they are the same object, so test for the same moment with $a->compareTo($b) == 0.

params.name: other
params.descHtml: The instant to compare against.

doc.returnHtml: -1 when the receiver is earlier than $other, 0 when they are the same instant, 1 when it is later.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the instant as RFC 3339 text in UTC. This is the date format that JSON and HTTP APIs use most.
doc.returnHtml: A string such as 2024-03-01T12:00:00Z. It has a fraction of a second only when the fraction is not zero.

classes.summaryHtml:
One exact point in time, the same everywhere in the world. It has no time zone and no calendar. Core\Time::now, Core\Time::fromEpoch and Core\Time::fromIso return one. plus, minus and since do exact arithmetic with a Duration, and in shows the instant on a zone's calendar.

An Instant is a point on the timeline with no calendar attached: it has an epoch count and an RFC 3339 rendering in UTC, and nothing else until ->in($zone) places it on a calendar. It moves only by an exact Duration — plus(36h) is thirty-six hours whatever a zone's clocks did in between — and since measures the exact gap between two instants; a step in days or months is taken on the DateTime that ->in($zone) answers. Two instants are ordered with compareTo; the <, > and <=> operators do not compile on an Instant.

<?nvs
var $start = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-03-01T12:00:00Z');
echo $start->toIso(), "\n";
echo $start->toEpochSeconds(), "\n";
echo $start->toEpochMillis(), "\n";

var $end = $start->plus(36h);
echo $end->toIso(), "\n";
echo $end->since($start), "\n";
echo $start->minus(30m)->toIso(), "\n";
echo $start->compareTo($end), "\n";

echo $start->in(Core\Time\Zone::of('Asia/Tokyo'))->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo Core\Time::fromEpoch(1709294400, { nanos: 500000000 })->toIso(), "\n";
2024-03-01T12:00:00Z
1709294400
1709294400000
2024-03-03T00:00:00Z
1d12h
2024-03-01T11:30:00Z
-1
2024-03-01 21:00
2024-03-01T12:00:00.5Z

classes.name: Core\Time\TimeOfDay
classes.summary: A time on a clock, such as 10:30, with no date and no time zone. `TimeOfDay::at` makes one, and `DateTime::timeOfDay` returns the time of a `DateTime`. `plus` and `minus` move it and wrap around at midnight. `with` changes single fields, and `format` returns it as text.

members.name: at
members.signature: at(uint $hour, uint $minute, { second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\TimeOfDay

doc.shortHtml: Makes a time of day from an hour and a minute. The seconds and the nanoseconds are optional, and their default is 0.

params.name: hour
params.descHtml: The hour, 0 to 23.

params.name: minute
params.descHtml: The minute, 0 to 59.

params.name: second
params.descHtml: The second, 0 to 59. The default is 0.

params.name: nanos
params.descHtml: The nanoseconds inside that second, 0 to 999999999. The default is 0.

doc.returnHtml: The new TimeOfDay.

errors.descHtml: A field is outside its range, for example an hour of 24.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the time as text in the pattern you give, such as HH:mm:ss or h:mm a. The pattern uses the letters of DateTime::format, but only the letters for a time.

params.name: pattern
params.descHtml: The pattern, such as HH:mm. It may use letters for the hour, the minute, the second, parts of a second and AM or PM. A tainted pattern (text from outside the program) is not allowed.

doc.returnHtml: The time as text.

errors.descHtml: $pattern is not a valid pattern, or it uses a letter for a date or a time zone.

doc.shortHtml: Moves the time forward by $count steps of $unit. The result wraps around at midnight, so 23:30 plus one hour is 00:30. To move a time across days, use DateTime::plus.

params.name: count
params.descHtml: How many steps. A negative count moves the time back.

params.name: unit
params.descHtml: Unit::Hour or a smaller unit.

doc.returnHtml: A new TimeOfDay. The original does not change.

errors.descHtml: $unit is Unit::Day or larger. A time of day has no days to move.
$count is too large for $unit.

doc.shortHtml: Moves the time back by $count steps of $unit. The result wraps around at midnight, so 00:15 minus 30 minutes is 23:45.

params.name: count
params.descHtml: How many steps. A negative count moves the time forward.

params.name: unit
params.descHtml: Unit::Hour or a smaller unit.

doc.returnHtml: A new TimeOfDay. The original does not change.

errors.descHtml: $unit is Unit::Day or larger. A time of day has no days to move.
$count is too large for $unit.

members.name: with
members.signature: with({ hour?: uint, minute?: uint, second?: uint, nanos?: uint }): Core\Time\TimeOfDay

doc.shortHtml: Returns a copy of the time with the fields you give changed. The fields you leave out keep their value.

params.name: hour
params.descHtml: The new hour, 0 to 23. If you leave it out, the hour stays the same.

params.name: minute
params.descHtml: The new minute, 0 to 59. If you leave it out, the minute stays the same.

params.name: second
params.descHtml: The new second, 0 to 59. If you leave it out, the second stays the same.

params.name: nanos
params.descHtml: The new nanoseconds inside the second, 0 to 999999999. If you leave it out, they stay the same.

doc.returnHtml: A new TimeOfDay. The original does not change.

errors.descHtml: A field is outside its range, for example a minute of 60.

doc.shortHtml: Checks which of two times comes first in the day, as Comparable requires. The operators <, >, <=, >= and <=> use this method too. == on two times checks whether they are the same object, so test for the same time with $a->compareTo($b) == 0.

params.name: other
params.descHtml: The time to compare against.

doc.returnHtml: -1 when the receiver is earlier in the day than $other, 0 when both are the same time, 1 when it is later.

classes.summaryHtml:
A time on a clock, such as 10:30, with no date and no time zone. TimeOfDay::at makes one, and DateTime::timeOfDay returns the time of a DateTime. plus and minus move it and wrap around at midnight. with changes single fields, and format returns it as text.

A TimeOfDay is a clock reading — hour, minute, second, nanosecond — with no date and no zone, built by TimeOfDay::at or read off a DateTime with ->timeOfDay(). It steps by Core\Unit::Hour and smaller and wraps within the day, so 23:30 plus an hour is 00:30; Core\Unit::Day and larger are refused, because a carry has no date to go to. format takes the time letters of the CLDR grammar DateTime::format uses, and a date or zone letter is refused. DateTime::withTime puts a reading back onto a date. Two readings are ordered with compareTo; the < operators do not compile.

<?nvs
var $t = Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at(23, 30);
echo $t->format('HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $t->format('h:mm a'), "\n";

echo $t->plus(1, Core\Unit::Hour)->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $t->minus(45, Core\Unit::Minute)->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $t->with({ second: 45 })->format('HH:mm:ss'), "\n";
echo $t->compareTo(Core\Time\TimeOfDay::at(9, 0)), "\n";

var $utc = Core\Time\Zone::UTC;
var $d = Core\Time::at(2024, 3, 1, $utc, { hour: 9 });
echo $d->withTime($t)->format('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'), "\n";
echo $d->timeOfDay()->format('HH:mm'), "\n";
23:30:00
11:30 PM
00:30
22:45
23:30:45
1
2024-03-01 23:30
09:00

classes.name: Core\Time\Zone
classes.summary: A time zone, such as `Europe/Berlin` or a fixed offset like `+02:00`. Every conversion between an `Instant` and a `DateTime` needs one, and there is no default zone. `Zone::of` finds a zone by its name, `Zone::fixed` makes one from an offset, and `offsetAt` returns the offset at one instant.

constants.name: UTC
constants.descHtml: The UTC zone — the only zone that is ever a default, and only where a call site writes it explicitly.

doc.shortHtml: Finds a time zone by its name, such as Europe/Berlin or America/New_York. The names come from the IANA time-zone database. A name that is not in the database throws an error.

params.name: id
params.descHtml: The name of the zone, such as Asia/Tokyo. An offset such as +02:00 is not allowed here. Use Zone::fixed for an offset.

doc.returnHtml: The Zone with that name.

errors.descHtml: $id is not a zone name in the database, or starts with + or -.

doc.shortHtml: Makes a zone that is always the same distance from UTC, such as +05:30. Its offset never changes for summer time. Use it for a timestamp that has an offset and no zone name, such as 2024-03-05T10:00:00+05:30.

params.name: offset
params.descHtml: The distance from UTC as a whole number of seconds. It is negative for a zone west of UTC.

doc.returnHtml: A Zone whose name is the offset, written +HH:MM, or +HH:MM:SS when it has seconds.

errors.descHtml: $offset has a part smaller than a second, or is more than 25:59:59 away from UTC.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the time zone of the computer the program runs on. There is no default zone, so you pass this Zone to each call that needs one.
doc.returnHtml: The computer's Zone with its IANA name, such as Europe/Berlin. When the computer has no zone name, the result is a fixed zone at its current offset, such as +02:00.

doc.shortHtml: Returns how far the zone is from UTC at one instant. A zone with summer time has two offsets in a year. Europe/Berlin is +01:00 in January and +02:00 in July.

params.name: i
params.descHtml: The instant to read the offset at.

doc.returnHtml: The offset as a Duration of whole seconds. It is positive east of UTC, negative west of UTC, and zero for UTC.

classes.summaryHtml:
A time zone, such as Europe/Berlin or a fixed offset like +02:00. Every conversion between an Instant and a DateTime needs one, and there is no default zone. Zone::of finds a zone by its name, Zone::fixed makes one from an offset, and offsetAt returns the offset at one instant.

A Zone is what turns an Instant into a calendar reading and back: Zone::of looks up an IANA identifier such as Europe/Berlin in the bundled database and throws on one it does not have, Zone::fixed is a constant offset with no DST rules, and Zone::UTC is the one constant. There is no ambient zone: Zone::system() answers the host's zone as an ordinary value the program then passes on, and no call sets a default zone for the program. A zone with DST has no single offset, so offsetAt asks for the instant.

<?nvs
var $berlin = Core\Time\Zone::of('Europe/Berlin');
var $jan = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-01-15T12:00:00Z');
var $jul = Core\Time::fromIso('2024-07-15T12:00:00Z');
echo $berlin->offsetAt($jan), "\n";
echo $berlin->offsetAt($jul), "\n";
echo $jul->in($berlin)->format('HH:mm xxx VV'), "\n";

var $india = Core\Time\Zone::fixed(5h30m);
echo $jul->in($india)->format('HH:mm xxx'), "\n";
echo Core\Time\Zone::UTC->offsetAt($jul)->toSeconds(), "\n";

echo Core\Time::at(2024, 7, 15, $berlin, { hour: 14 })->toInstant()->toIso(), "\n";

try {
    Core\Time\Zone::of('Mars/Olympus');
} catch (RuntimeError $unknown) {
    echo "not in the database\n";
}
1h
2h
14:00 +02:00 Europe/Berlin
17:30 +05:30
0
2024-07-15T12:00:00Z
not in the database

classes.name: Core\Topic
classes.summary: Sends values between WebSocket connections and event streams. A connection joins a topic by name with `subscribe`. Any script can send a value to everyone who joined with `publish`, and the value arrives at their next `receive()`.

doc.shortHtml: Joins this connection to $topic. A value published to that topic then arrives at the next receive(), and the message's topic() returns the name.

params.name: topic
params.descHtml: The name of the topic. It may not be tainted (come from user input), so you build it from values your program checked. Otherwise the call does not compile. This stops one user from joining the topic of another user.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. If a connection subscribes twice to the same topic, a published value still arrives only once.

errors.descHtml: $topic is empty or longer than 256 bytes, or this script is not a WebSocket connection or an event stream. Only a script that Core\Socket::upgrade or Core\Sse::upgrade started can subscribe. One connection can join at most 1024 topics at the same time, so joining one more also throws this error.

doc.shortHtml: Sends a copy of $value to every connection that subscribed to $topic, and returns how many connections it was sent to.

params.name: topic
params.descHtml: The name of the topic. As with subscribe, it may not be tainted, so a name built from user input does not compile.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The value to send. Each subscriber gets its own copy, so a change one subscriber makes is not seen by any other. A tainted value is still tainted when it arrives. A value that contains a secret cannot be published.

doc.returnHtml: The number of subscribers the value was sent to. It is 0 for a topic nobody joined. Any script can publish, so an ordinary web request can tell the connections that something changed. A connection that publishes to a topic it joined also receives the value. A subscriber with too many unread messages is skipped and not counted. It is being closed, and publish never waits for it.

errors.descHtml: $topic is empty or longer than 256 bytes, or $value cannot be copied to another connection, such as an object with a secret property. The error is thrown even when nobody joined the topic.

doc.shortHtml: Removes this connection from $topic. A value published to that topic after this call does not reach this connection.

params.name: topic
params.descHtml: The name of the topic. As with subscribe, it may not be tainted.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Leaving a topic this connection never joined is not an error.

errors.descHtml: $topic is empty or longer than 256 bytes, or this script is not a WebSocket connection or an event stream. subscribe throws the same errors.

classes.summaryHtml: Sends values between WebSocket connections and event streams. A connection joins a topic by name with subscribe. Any script can send a value to everyone who joined with publish, and the value arrives at their next receive().

classes.name: Core\Totp
classes.summary: One-time codes for two-factor login (TOTP, RFC 6238). These are the six-digit codes that an authenticator app on a phone shows, and a new one starts every 30 seconds. `code` returns the current code for a secret, and `check` tests a code that a user typed.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the current six-digit code for $secret. An authenticator app with the same secret shows the same code now. Use check to test a code that a user typed.

params.name: secret
params.descHtml: The shared secret, at least 16 bytes long. Core\Random::bytes(20) makes one of the recommended length.

doc.returnHtml: Six digits as a string, with leading zeros, such as 042311. It is a string so that the leading zeros stay.

errors.descHtml: $secret is shorter than 16 bytes, or the clock is outside the range of dates a code can have.

doc.shortHtml: Tests a code that a user typed. It accepts the code of the current 30-second step and of the step before and after it. It returns the number of the step, or null. Store that number and pass it as $after next time. Then the same code cannot be used twice.

params.name: code
params.descHtml: The code the user typed. A string that is not six digits returns null and does not throw an error.

params.name: secret
params.descHtml: The same secret that code uses, at least 16 bytes long.

params.name: after
params.descHtml: The step number that the last accepted code returned. Codes of this step and earlier steps return null. The default is 0, which accepts every code of the current steps. Use it only for the first code of an account.

doc.returnHtml: The step number of the code, or null when the code is wrong, too old, too new or already used.

errors.descHtml: $secret is shorter than 16 bytes, or the clock is outside the range of dates a code can have.

classes.summaryHtml: One-time codes for two-factor login (TOTP, RFC 6238). These are the six-digit codes that an authenticator app on a phone shows, and a new one starts every 30 seconds. code returns the current code for a secret, and check tests a code that a user typed.

classes.name: Core\Uri
classes.summary: Reads, builds and encodes URIs and query strings. `parse` reads a URI into its parts, and `with` and `resolve` build a new one. The `encode` and `decode` methods escape and unescape text, and `parseQuery` and `buildQuery` convert between a query string and an array. `sign` and `verifySignature` sign a link and check it.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the text of an address, such as https://example.com/cart?id=4, and returns a Uri. Its methods return the parts: scheme, userInfo, host, port, path, query and fragment. Each part is returned as it was written. Escapes such as %20 stay, and upper-case letters stay upper case.

params.name: uri
params.descHtml: The text to read. A relative link, such as /a?b, is allowed. Its scheme is null.

doc.returnHtml: A Uri. Its methods return the parts of the address as they were written.

errors.descHtml: The text is not an address under RFC 3986 (the standard for addresses). A space, a control character, a non-ASCII character, a % without two hex digits and a host in brackets that is not an IPv6 address all cause this. A port larger than 65535 causes it too. The message does not repeat the text, because the text can contain a password.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the text of an address and returns a Uri, the same way Core\Uri::parse does. When the text is not an address, the result is null and no error is thrown. A space, a % without two hex digits and a port above 65535 all give null.

params.name: uri
params.descHtml: The text to read. A relative link, such as /a?b, is allowed.

doc.returnHtml: A Uri. The result is null for every text that Core\Uri::parse throws an error for. To check if an address is absolute, use tryParse($text)?->scheme() != null.

doc.shortHtml: Escapes $s so that it can be one part of a URI, such as a path segment, a fragment or one side of a query pair. A space becomes %20. Every byte that is not a letter, a digit or one of -_.~ becomes a % and two hex digits. This includes / ? # & =.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to encode.

doc.returnHtml: The escaped text, with upper-case hex digits. A tainted argument (text from outside the program, such as a request) gives a plain result. No byte of the result can change the structure of the URI.

doc.shortHtml: Decodes one escaped part of a URI, such as a path segment or a fragment. Each %XX escape becomes the byte it encodes, so %20 becomes a space. A + stays a +. Core\Uri::encodeComponent writes the escapes that this function reads.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to decode.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded bytes, as bytes, because an escape can give any byte. as string converts them to text and throws an error when they are not valid UTF-8. A % that is not followed by two hex digits is kept, so 100% returns 100%.

doc.shortHtml: Escapes $s so that it can be one value of a form, such as a value in a query string or in the body of a POST request. A space becomes +. Every byte that is not a letter, a digit or one of -_. becomes a % and two hex digits. This includes ~, +, & and =.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to encode.

doc.returnHtml: The escaped text, with upper-case hex digits. A tainted argument (text from outside the program, such as a request) gives a plain result. No byte of the result can start a new pair of the form.

doc.shortHtml: Decodes one value of a form, such as a value in a query string or in the body of a POST request. A + becomes a space. Each %XX escape becomes the byte it encodes, so %2B becomes a + and %20 becomes a space. Core\Uri::encodeFormValue writes the escapes that this function reads.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to decode.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded bytes, as bytes, because an escape can give any byte. as string converts them to text and throws an error when they are not valid UTF-8. A % that is not followed by two hex digits is kept, so 100% returns 100%.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a query string, such as q=red+shoes&page=2, into an array. The text is split into pairs at each &, and each pair is split at its first =. Names and values are decoded like decodeFormValue, so + becomes a space. Brackets in a name build nested arrays: a[]=1&a[]=2 gives a list, and a[b]=c gives an array with the key b.

params.name: query
params.descHtml: The query text, without the ? at its start.

doc.returnHtml: An array. Each value is bytes or another array. A value is bytes because an escape can give any byte, and as string converts it to text. A pair without = has an empty value. A pair with an empty name is left out. When a name appears twice without brackets, the last value is kept.

errors.descHtml: A name decodes to bytes that are not valid UTF-8. A name is a key of the array, and a key must be text. A value can contain any bytes.

doc.shortHtml: Writes the array $parameters as a query string, such as page=2&sort=name. Core\Uri::parseQuery reads it back to the same array.

params.name: parameters
params.descHtml: The names and values to write. A value is a scalar or another array. A nested value is written under its whole path, such as filter[size][0]=M, with the brackets escaped as %5B and %5D.

doc.returnHtml: The query string, without a leading ?. Names and values are escaped as Core\Uri::encodeFormValue escapes them, so a space is +. true is written as 1 and false as 0. A null value writes nothing, and neither does an empty array.

errors.descHtml: A value is an object or a function, so it has no text form.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the scheme of the address, which is the part before the first :. For https://example.com/ the result is https. The scheme is returned as it was written, so HTTPS stays upper case.
doc.returnHtml: The scheme, without the :. The result is null when the address has no scheme, such as /about or //example.com/.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the user part of the address, which is the text between // and @. For ftp://ann@files.example.com/ the result is ann. A password written as ann:secret is returned as one text. Escapes such as %40 stay in it.
doc.returnHtml: The user part, without the @. The result is null when the address has no @ before its host. It is "" when nothing is written before the @.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the host of the address, such as example.com. The host is returned as it was written, so upper-case letters stay upper case. An IPv6 address keeps its brackets, such as [::1].
doc.returnHtml: The host. The result is null when the address has no // part. It is "" when the // part is empty, as in file:///tmp.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the port of the address as a number. For http://example.com:8080/ the result is 8080.
doc.returnHtml: The port, from 0 to 65535. The result is null when the address has no port. It is also null when the : has no digits after it, as in http://example.com:/. A default port, such as 443 for https, is never filled in.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the path of the address. For https://example.com/docs/guide?page=2 the result is /docs/guide. The path is returned as it was written, so escapes such as %20 and parts such as /../ stay in it.
doc.returnHtml: The path. It is never null. An address with no path, such as https://example.com, returns "".

doc.shortHtml: Returns the query of the address, which is the text after the ?. For https://example.com/search?q=shoes#top the result is q=shoes. Escapes such as %20 stay in it, and Core\Uri::parseQuery reads it into an array.
doc.returnHtml: The query, without the ?. The result is null when the address has no ?. It is "" when nothing is written after the ?.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the fragment of the address, which is the text after the #. For https://example.com/guide#install the result is install. Escapes such as %20 stay in it, and Core\Uri::decodeComponent decodes them.
doc.returnHtml: The fragment, without the #. The result is null when the address has no #. It is "" when nothing is written after the #.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the address as text. For a Uri from Core\Uri::parse, this is exactly the text that was read. Upper-case letters and escapes such as %2f do not change. echo $uri prints the same text.
doc.returnHtml: The address as a string. For HTTP://Example.COM/a%2fb the result is HTTP://Example.COM/a%2fb.

members.name: with
members.signature: with({ scheme?: string, host?: string, port?: ?int, path?: string, query?: ?string, fragment?: ?string }): Core\Uri

doc.shortHtml: Returns a new Uri with some parts of the address changed. You name the parts in a block, for example with({ scheme: "https", port: null }). Each part you do not name stays the same. null removes the port, the query or the fragment. The user part (userInfo) is always kept.

params.name: scheme
params.descHtml: The new scheme, without the :.

params.name: host
params.descHtml: The new host. An IPv6 address is written in brackets, such as [::1].

params.name: port
params.descHtml: The new port, from 0 to 65535. null removes the port.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The new path, already encoded. When the address has a host, the path must start with /.

params.name: query
params.descHtml: The new query, already encoded and without the ?. null removes the query. "" gives an empty query, so the address ends with ?.

params.name: fragment
params.descHtml: The new fragment, already encoded and without the #. null removes the fragment.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri. The Uri you call it on does not change. An empty port, as in h:/, is removed from the result.

errors.descHtml: The port is outside 0 to 65535. It is also thrown when a part makes the address invalid, or when a part would move into another part. For example, a path without / next to a host would become part of the host. The message names the part that moved.

doc.shortHtml: Returns one value from the query of the address, by its name. For /search?q=red+shoes the result of queryParameter("q") is red shoes. The query is read the same way as by Core\Uri::parseQuery, and each call reads it again. To read many parameters, call Core\Uri::parseQuery once on the query and read the array it returns.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the parameter, without brackets. For a[b]=c, the name is "a".

doc.returnHtml: The decoded value as bytes. Brackets in the name give an array<mixed>. The result is null when the name is not in the query, and also when the address has no query. query() tells these two apart.

errors.descHtml: A name in the query has escapes that do not decode to valid UTF-8 text. Core\Uri::parseQuery throws the same error.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a new Uri with one query parameter set, replaced or removed. For /search?q=shoes&page=2, withQueryParameter("page", 3) returns /search?q=shoes&page=3. The other pairs are kept. The Uri you call it on does not change.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the parameter, without brackets. An array value writes the brackets.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The new value. It can be a scalar or an array. An array is written with brackets, the same way Core\Uri::buildQuery writes it. null removes the parameter.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri. When the last parameter is removed, the address has no ?. The whole query is written again, so the encoding of the other pairs can change: %20 becomes +.

errors.descHtml: A name in the query has escapes that do not decode to valid UTF-8 text. It is also thrown when value is not a scalar, an array or null, for example an object.

doc.shortHtml: Turns a link found on a page into a full address, the way a browser does. The address of the page is the base. For the base https://example.com/blog/post and the link ../about, the result is https://example.com/about. The . and .. parts are removed from the path.

params.name: reference
params.descHtml: The link to follow. It can be a full address, a path such as /about or photo.jpg, a query such as ?page=2, or a fragment such as #top.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri with a scheme. The fragment of the base is not used. The base itself does not change.

errors.descHtml: The base has no scheme, such as /blog/post. The link has a character that is not allowed in an address, such as a space. Or the base has no / after its scheme, such as mailto:ann@example.com, so there is no path to add the link to.

doc.shortHtml: Compares this address with $other, to sort addresses or to check if two are the same. Before it compares, it changes a copy of each one. The scheme and the host become lower case. An escape such as %7E becomes ~ when that character needs no escape. The . and .. parts are removed from a path that starts with /. Neither address itself changes.

params.name: other
params.descHtml: The Uri to compare with.

doc.returnHtml: 0 when both are the same address, -1 when this address comes first, and 1 when $other comes first. The parts are compared in this order: scheme, userInfo, host, port, path, query, fragment. A missing part comes before a part that is there. http://example.com:80/ and http://example.com/ are different, because the default port of a scheme is not known.

members.name: sign
members.signature: sign({ keys: array<secret bytes>, until: ?Core\Time\Instant } $settings): Core\Uri

doc.shortHtml: Returns a copy of the address with a signature in the _sig query parameter. The signature covers the scheme, user info, host, port, path and every query parameter. If a parameter is added, removed or changed, verifySignature throws an error. A different order of the parameters and a fragment do not change the result.

params.name: settings
params.descHtml: The keys and the end date. You must write both.

shape.descHtml: A list of 32-byte keys, newest first. $keys[0] signs. The older keys are there so that verifySignature still accepts links signed before you changed the key. Core\Signature takes the same list, but a token from one does not work in the other.

The moment the link stops working. It is inside the signature, so nobody can change it. null means the link never expires. A link that never expires works for anybody who finds it later, for example in a browser history.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri with _sig set. You can use with and toString on it. If the address already has _sig, it is replaced. The same address, keys and end date always give the same link. The signature makes the address about twice as long. A relative address, such as /download?file=a, has no host in its signature, so it is valid on any site.

errors.descHtml: keys is empty, or its first key is not 32 bytes long.

doc.shortHtml: Checks the signature in the _sig query parameter with the keys in $keys, and checks that the link has not expired. It returns nothing. If the check fails, it throws an error, so the next line runs only for a valid link.

params.name: keys
params.descHtml: The same list of keys that sign used, newest first. A link signed with any key in the list is accepted. A link signed with a key you removed from the list is not.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. When the method returns, the link is valid and has not expired.

errors.descHtml: $keys is empty, or one of its keys is not 32 bytes long.

The link was not signed with these keys. This is the case when a parameter was added, removed or changed, when the token was changed, when the key was removed from the list, when there is no _sig, and when there are two. All of these give the same message. An expired link gives a different message.

classes.summaryHtml:
Reads, builds and encodes URIs and query strings. parse reads a URI into its parts, and with and resolve build a new one. The encode and decode methods escape and unescape text, and parseQuery and buildQuery convert between a query string and an array. sign and verifySignature sign a link and check it.

Core\Uri::parse reads a URI reference and answers an instance whose readers report each component exactly as written — still percent-encoded, in its own case. Every reader but path is ?string (port is ?int) and answers null where the component was not written; tryParse is the same read with null in place of RuntimeError, and is the spelling of "is this text a URI". with and resolve answer a fresh Uri, and compareTo is the normalized content comparison — == on two Uri objects is identity. parseQuery and buildQuery read and write the bracket convention, and queryParameter/withQueryParameter are the same convention over one parameter by name — a name with cannot take as a bag key, because a bag's keys are declared and a parameter's name is chosen at run time. The name is top-level, so an array $value is what writes a[b]; a null $value removes the pair, and removing the last one leaves no query at all rather than a bare ?. encodeComponent writes a space as %20, and encodeFormValue writes it as +. The two **decoders answer bytes**, because percent-decoding is defined over octets and a client may send any of them: Core\Uri::decodeComponent("%FF") has an answer, and text is one as string away — which throws for octets no string can hold, exactly where a string-returning decoder would have. parseQuery answers those same octets for a value; a name is the array key, so it is a string.

<?nvs
var $u = Core\Uri::parse('https://example.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&y=2#top');
echo $u->scheme() ?? '-', ' ', $u->host() ?? '-', ' ', $u->port() ?? 0, "\n";
echo $u->path(), ' ', $u->query() ?? '-', ' ', $u->fragment() ?? '-', "\n";
echo $u->with({ path: '/c', fragment: 'end' })->toString(), "\n";
echo $u->resolve('../d?z=3')->toString(), "\n";

var $rel = Core\Uri::parse('/only/a/path');
echo $rel->scheme() == null ? 'relative' : 'absolute', "\n";
echo Core\Uri::tryParse('http://example.com/a b') == null ? 'not a uri' : 'a uri', "\n";

var $same = Core\Uri::parse('HTTPS://EXAMPLE.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&y=2#top');
echo $u->compareTo($same) == 0 ? 'same uri' : 'different', "\n";

var $q = Core\Uri::parseQuery('a=1&b[]=2&b[]=3');
echo Core\Str::join(Core\Arr::keys($q), ','), "\n";
array<mixed> $params = ['name' => 'a b', 'page' => 2];
echo Core\Uri::buildQuery($params), "\n";
echo $u->queryParameter('x') as bytes as string, "\n";
echo $u->withQueryParameter('y', null)->withQueryParameter('z', '3')->toString(), "\n";
echo Core\Uri::encodeComponent('a b&c'), ' ', Core\Uri::encodeFormValue('a b&c'), "\n";
https example.com 8443
/a/b%20c x=1&y=2 top
https://example.com:8443/c?x=1&y=2#end
https://example.com:8443/d?z=3
relative
not a uri
same uri
a,b
name=a+b&page=2
1
https://example.com:8443/a/b%20c?x=1&z=3#top
a%20b%26c a+b%26c

classes.name: Core\Uuid
classes.summary: A UUID, which is a 128-bit identifier. `v4` and `v7` create a new one. `parse` reads one from its text, such as `f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4`, and `fromBytes` reads one from its sixteen bytes. `toString` and `toBytes` give the text and the bytes back.

doc.shortHtml: Creates a new random UUID, such as f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4. 122 of its 128 bits come from a secure random number generator. The other six bits say that it is a version 4 UUID.
doc.returnHtml: A new Uuid. Nobody can guess it, and it contains no date or time, so it is safe to show to other people.

doc.shortHtml: Creates a new UUID that starts with the current time, such as 0190d1e6-8e3c-7c2a-9a4b-1f2e3d4c5b6a. The first 48 bits are the number of milliseconds since 1970. 74 of the other bits are random. Use it as a database key, because new keys sort after older ones.
doc.returnHtml: A new Uuid. It sorts after every UUID created in an earlier millisecond. Two UUIDs created in the same millisecond sort in a random order. Anybody who has the UUID can read the time it was created, so use Core\Uuid::v4 for an ID that other people see. If the computer's clock is before 1970, the time part is zero.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the text $s as a UUID. The text must be 32 hexadecimal digits in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens, such as f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4. Upper case and lower case letters are both allowed.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to read. It must be exactly 36 characters long.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid that the text gives. The version digit is not checked, so the nil UUID (all zeros) and the max UUID (all f) are both valid.

errors.descHtml: $s is not in that form. The 32 digits without hyphens, a UUID in {} braces and a UUID after urn:uuid: all throw this error too. The message quotes up to 48 characters of $s.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the text $s as a UUID, like Core\Uuid::parse. When the text is not a UUID, it returns null and does not throw an error. Use it to check whether a text is a UUID.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to read. It must be 32 hexadecimal digits in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens. Upper case and lower case letters are both allowed.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid that the text gives, or null when the text is in any other form. The 32 digits without hyphens, a UUID in {} braces and a UUID after urn:uuid: all give null.

doc.shortHtml: Reads sixteen bytes as a UUID. Many databases store a UUID in a binary column in this form, and binary protocols send it this way.

params.name: b
params.descHtml: The sixteen bytes, in the same order as the digits of the UUID's text. $uuid->toBytes() gives them in this order.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid that the bytes give. Any sixteen bytes are a valid UUID, so only the length is checked.

errors.descHtml: $b is not exactly sixteen bytes long. The message gives the length of $b.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the text of the UUID, such as f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4. The digits are in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12, joined by hyphens. echo $uuid writes the same text.
doc.returnHtml: A string of 36 characters. The letters are always lower case, even when parse read them in upper case.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the sixteen bytes of the UUID. Use it to store a UUID in a binary database column or to send it in a binary message. The text form of the same UUID is 36 bytes long.
doc.returnHtml: Sixteen bytes, in the same order as the digits of the UUID's text. Core\Uuid::fromBytes reads them back as the same UUID.

classes.summaryHtml:
A UUID, which is a 128-bit identifier. v4 and v7 create a new one. parse reads one from its text, such as f9168c5e-ceb2-4faa-b6bf-329bf39fa1e4, and fromBytes reads one from its sixteen bytes. toString and toBytes give the text and the bytes back.

A Uuid is an opaque 128-bit value, not a string: v4 draws a random one, v7 a time-ordered one whose leading bits are a millisecond timestamp — the right database key and the wrong public identifier, since it tells the reader when the row was made. parse reads only the canonical hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 form, in either letter case, and refuses the unhyphenated, braced and urn:uuid: spellings; asking whether text is a UUID is tryParse($s) != null. toString — and echo — is the only way text comes back out, always lower-case. Two Uuid objects compare by identity under ==, so two values are compared through their text.

<?nvs
var $id = Core\Uuid::v4();
echo Core\Str::length($id->toString()), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice($id->toString(), 14, 1), "\n";
echo Core\Str::slice(Core\Uuid::v7()->toString(), 14, 1), "\n";

var $known = Core\Uuid::parse('123E4567-E89B-12D3-A456-426614174000');
echo $known, "\n";
echo Core\Uuid::tryParse('not-a-uuid') == null ? 'invalid' : 'valid', "\n";
echo Core\Uuid::tryParse('123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000') != null ? 'valid' : 'invalid', "\n";

var $again = Core\Uuid::parse('123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000');
echo $known == $again ? 'same object' : 'different objects', "\n";
echo $known->toString() == $again->toString() ? 'same value' : 'different values', "\n";

try {
    Core\Uuid::parse('{123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000}');
} catch (RuntimeError $bad) {
    echo "braces refused\n";
}
36
4
7
123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000
invalid
valid
different objects
same value
braces refused

classes.name: Core\Validate
classes.summary: Checks whether a text has a certain format. `isEmail`, `isDomain`, `isIp` and `isMac` check for an email address, a domain name, an IP address and a MAC address. `isAscii` and `isPrintable` check which characters a text contains. Each method returns `true` or `false` and never changes the text.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $s is an email address, such as ada@example.com. The part before the @ has at most 64 characters: letters, digits, single dots and some symbols such as + and _. The part after the @ is a domain name with at least one dot. The whole address has at most 254 characters.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for an email address. false for anything else, for example a space, two dots in a row, quotes, an address such as a@[192.0.2.1], a domain without a dot such as a@localhost, or a character that is not ASCII. The method does not check whether the address exists.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $s is a domain name, such as example.com. A domain name has one or more parts joined by single dots. Each part has 1 to 63 letters, digits or -, and does not start or end with -. The whole name has at most 253 characters.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for a domain name. localhost and a name of digits such as 1.2.3.4 are true too. false for an empty part, a dot at the end, a part that starts or ends with -, or a character that is not ASCII. The method does not check whether the name exists.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $s is an IP address. An IPv4 address is four numbers from 0 to 255 joined by dots, such as 192.0.2.1. An IPv6 address is up to eight groups of hex digits joined by :, such as 2001:db8::1.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

params.name: version
params.descHtml: 4 accepts only IPv4 addresses, and 6 accepts only IPv6 addresses. Without it, both are accepted.

doc.returnHtml: true for an IP address of the chosen version. false for anything else. A number with a leading zero, such as 192.0.2.01, gives false. An IPv6 address with a zone at the end, such as fe80::1%eth0, also gives false.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $s is a MAC address, the hardware address of a network card. It is six pairs of hex digits joined by : or by -, such as 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e. It can also be three groups of four hex digits joined by ., such as 001a.2b3c.4d5e.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for one of the three ways to write it, in upper or lower case. false otherwise. A text that mixes two separators, such as 00:1a-2b:3c:4d:5e, gives false.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether every character of $s is an ASCII character. ASCII has 128 characters: the English letters, the digits, common punctuation and the control characters. Each of them is one byte, from 0x00 to 0x7F.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true when every character is ASCII, and true for the empty string. false when the text contains any other character, such as é or 日.

doc.shortHtml: Checks whether $s contains no control characters. A control character has no visible form, for example a tab, a new line or the null byte. Letters from any language, such as é or 日, are printable.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true when the text has no control character, and true for the empty string. false for a tab, a new line, a carriage return, DEL or any other control character. Some invisible characters are not control characters, such as the zero-width joiner. They give true, so this method does not find text that hides what it really says.

classes.summaryHtml:
Checks whether a text has a certain format. isEmail, isDomain, isIp and isMac check for an email address, a domain name, an IP address and a MAC address. isAscii and isPrintable check which characters a text contains. Each method returns true or false and never changes the text.

Every Core\Validate member is a predicate over a string naming a format: isEmail, isDomain, isIp (with { version: 4 } or { version: 6 } to accept one family only), isMac, isAscii and isPrintable. None launders — a tainted string is as tainted after isEmail answers true — and none touches the network. There is no isUrl, isInteger or isFloat: those are Core\Uri::tryParse($s)?->scheme() != null and ($s as ?int) != null.

<?nvs
array<string> $emails = ['ada@example.test', 'no-at-sign', 'ada@localhost'];
foreach ($emails as string $e) {
    echo $e, ' ', (Core\Validate::isEmail($e) ? 'email' : 'not'), "\n";
}
echo (Core\Validate::isDomain('a-b.example.test') ? 'domain' : 'not'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isIp('192.0.2.1') ? 'ip' : 'not'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isIp('2001:db8::1', { version: 4 }) ? 'v4' : 'not v4'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isIp('2001:db8::1', { version: 6 }) ? 'v6' : 'not v6'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isMac('00:11:22:33:44:55') ? 'mac' : 'not'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isAscii('café') ? 'ascii' : 'not ascii'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isPrintable('café') ? 'printable' : 'not'), "\n";
echo (Core\Validate::isPrintable("a\tb") ? 'printable' : 'not'), "\n";
echo (('12' as ?int) != null ? 'int' : 'not'), "\n";
ada@example.test email
no-at-sign not
ada@localhost not
domain
ip
not v4
v6
mac
not ascii
printable
not
int

classes.name: Core\WebPush
classes.summary: Sends push notifications to a browser (Web Push). The browser gives your page a subscription. Your server reads it with `subscription`. Each message is encrypted for that one browser, and only that browser can read it.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a push subscription from the JSON that PushSubscription.toJSON() returns in the browser. It checks the endpoint URL and both keys. A subscription that fails a check throws an error here.

params.name: json
params.descHtml: The JSON text the browser sent, such as {"endpoint": "https://…", "keys": {"p256dh": "…", "auth": "…"}}. Other fields, such as expirationTime, are ignored.

doc.returnHtml: The subscription, ready to send a message to.

errors.descHtml: The text is not JSON or is longer than 8 KiB. Or the endpoint is not an https: URL, p256dh is not a P-256 public key, or auth is not 16 bytes. The message says which.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the public half of your VAPID key, as base64url text. Give it to pushManager.subscribe() in the browser as applicationServerKey. The private half is not in it.

params.name: vapid
params.descHtml: Your application's VAPID key: a Core\Crypto\KeyPair of kind P256. Create it once with Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair, keep it secret, and use the same key for every message.

doc.returnHtml: The public key: 87 characters of base64url, such as BCVxsr7N_eNg….

errors.descHtml: $vapid is not a key pair of kind P256.

members.name: send
members.signature: send(Core\WebPush\Subscription $to, bytes $payload, Core\Crypto\KeyPair $vapid, string $subject, int $ttl = 86400): Core\WebPush\Sent

doc.shortHtml: Encrypts $payload for one browser and sends it to the browser's push service. The message is signed with your VAPID key. The program needs net.connect for the host of the endpoint.

params.name: to
params.descHtml: The subscription that Core\WebPush::subscription returned.

params.name: payload
params.descHtml: The message, at most 3993 bytes. The browser's service worker receives it in its push event.

params.name: vapid
params.descHtml: Your application's VAPID key: a Core\Crypto\KeyPair of kind P256. Create it once with Core\Crypto::generateKeyPair, keep it secret, and use the same key for every message.

params.name: subject
params.descHtml: A way for the push service to contact you: a mailto: or an https: URL, such as mailto:admin@example.com.

params.name: ttl
params.descHtml: How many seconds the push service keeps the message while the browser is offline. 0 means the message is sent only if the browser is online now.

doc.returnHtml: The push service's answer. Its status() is 201 when the service accepted the message.

errors.descHtml: $vapid is not a key pair of kind P256.
$subject does not start with mailto: or https:, or $ttl is negative.
The payload is longer than 3993 bytes, the program may not connect to the host, or the push service cannot be reached.

classes.summaryHtml: Sends push notifications to a browser (Web Push). The browser gives your page a subscription. Your server reads it with subscription. Each message is encrypted for that one browser, and only that browser can read it.

classes.name: Core\WebPush\Sent
classes.summary: The answer of the browser's push service to one message that `Core\WebPush::send` sent. Check `gone()` to know when to delete a subscription.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the HTTP status code of the push service's answer.
doc.returnHtml: The status code, such as 201 for a message the service accepted.

doc.shortHtml: Returns true when the push service no longer knows the subscription. The status is then 404 or 410. Delete the subscription, because every later message fails too.
doc.returnHtml: true for a subscription the service has deleted, and false otherwise.

classes.summaryHtml: The answer of the browser's push service to one message that Core\WebPush::send sent. Check gone() to know when to delete a subscription.

classes.name: Core\WebPush\Subscription
classes.summary: A browser's push subscription, after `Core\WebPush::subscription` checked it. It contains the URL of the browser's push service and the two keys that encrypt a message for this browser. Save the JSON text with the user, and read it again when you send.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the URL of the browser's push service for this subscription. Use it to find the subscription again, for example to delete it. The browser wrote this URL, so it is tainted.
doc.returnHtml: The endpoint URL, such as https://push.example.com/send/abc123.

classes.summaryHtml: A browser's push subscription, after Core\WebPush::subscription checked it. It contains the URL of the browser's push service and the two keys that encrypt a message for this browser. Save the JSON text with the user, and read it again when you send.

classes.name: Core\Xml
classes.summary: Reads and writes XML documents. `parse` reads a whole document into a tree of `Core\Xml\Node` objects. `reader` returns the nodes of a document one at a time and does not build a tree. `writer` builds a new document one node at a time, and escapes every text for you.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a whole XML document and returns its document node. A document that is not well-formed throws a ParseError. Nothing is repaired or guessed. Core\Html::parse returns the same kind of tree, and repairs broken HTML instead of throwing.

params.name: document
params.descHtml: The document text. The five predefined entities, such as &, and numeric character references, such as A, are expanded. Any other entity reference throws a ParseError. Nothing is loaded from a file or from the network.

doc.returnHtml: The document node. Its children are the root element and any comments or processing instructions next to it. Every string you read from the tree is tainted, which means it came from outside the program. This is true even when $document was not tainted.

errors.descHtml: The document is not well-formed. For example: a tag is never closed or is closed with a different name, there is more than one root element, an attribute is written twice, or an entity reference is not one of the predefined ones. A document type declaration also throws, and so do elements nested more than 1024 levels deep.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a reader that goes through $document one node at a time. Call read until it returns null. The reader does not build a tree. It keeps the current node and the names of the elements that are open. This call reads nothing yet. The first read reads the first node.

params.name: document
params.descHtml: The document text. The reader does not copy it. Entity references are handled the same way as in Core\Xml::parse.

doc.returnHtml: A reader. Its first read returns the first node of the document.

doc.shortHtml: Returns a writer that builds an XML document one node at a time. The writer remembers which elements are open, so endElement needs no name. Ending the document while an element is still open throws a LogicError. Every method that takes text escapes it, so you never escape text yourself.

params.name: indent
params.descHtml: The text for one level of indentation, such as two spaces. The default is "", which means no indentation. It may contain only whitespace. The writer never adds indentation next to text content, because that would change the text.

doc.returnHtml: A new writer with an empty document. Call startDocument first.

errors.descHtml: indent contains a character that is not whitespace.

classes.summaryHtml: Reads and writes XML documents. parse reads a whole document into a tree of Core\Xml\Node objects. reader returns the nodes of a document one at a time and does not build a tree. writer builds a new document one node at a time, and escapes every text for you.

classes.name: Core\Xml\Node
classes.summary: One node of a document tree. `Core\Xml::parse` and `Core\Html::parse` return the document node, and you reach the other nodes through `children`. A node is an element, a text, a comment, a processing instruction or the document itself, and `kind` tells you which. Every string you read from a node is `tainted`, because it came from outside the program.

doc.shortHtml: The kind of a node in a parsed document. There are exactly five kinds. Core\Xml::parse, Core\Html::parse and Core\Xml\Reader all return nodes of these kinds, so code that checks the kind works the same with each of them.

Returns what kind of node this is: an element, a text, a comment, a processing instruction or the document. Compare it with a Core\Xml\Node::Kind case, for example to skip everything that is not an element.
doc.returnHtml: A Core\Xml\Node::Kind case. There are exactly five cases, so a match over them covers every node.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the name of this node. For an element, this is the tag name. For a processing instruction, it is the target, such as print in <?print fast?>. A text node, a comment and the document have no name, so they return an empty string.
doc.returnHtml: A tainted string. The name is written as in the document, with its prefix: for <x:a/> the result is x:a. To find the namespace of the prefix, use namespaceUri.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the namespace URI of this element. For <x:item>, the URI comes from the nearest xmlns:x declaration on the element or above it. For a name without a prefix, it comes from the nearest xmlns declaration. An inner declaration replaces an outer one. The prefix xml always has the URI http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace.
doc.returnHtml: A tainted string, or null. The result is null for a node that is not an element, for an element that no declaration covers, and for an element under xmlns="". The name does not change: name still returns x:item.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the text of this node. For a text node, this is its characters. For a comment, it is the comment's content, and for a processing instruction it is the part after the name. An element and the document return an empty string. Their text is in their text children.
doc.returnHtml: A tainted string. Entities such as & and character references such as b are expanded. A CDATA section gives the text written inside it.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the attributes of this element, in the order the document wrote them. For a node that is not an element, the array is empty.
doc.returnHtml: An array keyed by attribute name. The name is written as in the document, with its prefix, such as xml:lang. Entities such as & are expanded in the value. A tab or a line break written inside the value becomes a space, as XML requires. The values are tainted.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the children of this node, in the order of the document. For the document node, this is the root element and any comment or processing instruction beside it. For an element, it is everything between its start tag and its end tag. A text, a comment and a processing instruction have no children, so the array is empty.
doc.returnHtml: An array with one Core\Xml\Node per child. The spaces and line breaks between two elements are text nodes, and they are in the array too.

doc.shortHtml: Returns this node and everything inside it as XML text. Use it to write a document, or one part of it, back out after you read it. Every element is written with an end tag, so <e/> is written as <e></e>. The XML rules apply, also to a tree from Core\Html::parse.
doc.returnHtml: A tainted string, with no XML declaration at the start. In text, &, < and > are escaped. In an attribute value, ", a tab and a line break are escaped too. When you parse the result, you get the same tree again.

errors.descHtml: The tree contains something XML cannot write: a name that is not a valid XML name, a comment that contains -- or ends with -, a processing instruction that contains ?>, or a character XML does not allow. Only a tree from Core\Html::parse can contain these, because Core\Xml::parse does not accept them.

classes.summaryHtml: One node of a document tree. Core\Xml::parse and Core\Html::parse return the document node, and you reach the other nodes through children. A node is an element, a text, a comment, a processing instruction or the document itself, and kind tells you which. Every string you read from a node is tainted, because it came from outside the program.

classes.name: Core\Xml\Reader
classes.summary: Goes through an XML document one node at a time. `Core\Xml::reader` returns a reader. Each call to `read` returns the next node, and `null` at the end of the document. The reader does not build a tree, so a large document does not need a lot of memory. `depth` tells you how deeply the current node is nested.

doc.shortHtml: Reads the next node of the document and returns it. At the end of the document, it returns null. An element is returned when its opening tag is read. It has its name and its attributes, but no children. The nodes inside it are returned by the next calls to read. A closing tag is not a node, so use depth to see where an element ends.
doc.returnHtml: The next node: an element, a text, a comment or a processing instruction. The result is null at the end of the document. Every string you read from the node is tainted, because it came from outside the program.

errors.descHtml: The document is not well-formed at the place the reader has reached. Core\Xml::parse throws the same errors. The nodes before that place were already returned. The reader does not move past the error, so the next read throws the same error again.

doc.shortHtml: Returns how deeply the node that read returned last is nested. The root element has depth 0. A node inside the root element has depth 1, and each level adds one. A closing tag is not a node, so the depth is how you see where an element ends. When the depth is the same as or smaller than an earlier element's depth, that element is closed.
doc.returnHtml: A whole number. It is 0 before the first read, and 0 again after read returns null.

classes.summaryHtml: Goes through an XML document one node at a time. Core\Xml::reader returns a reader. Each call to read returns the next node, and null at the end of the document. The reader does not build a tree, so a large document does not need a lot of memory. depth tells you how deeply the current node is nested.

classes.name: Core\Xml\Writer
classes.summary: Builds a new XML document one node at a time. `Core\Xml::writer` returns a writer. `startDocument` begins the document, and `endDocument` returns it as a string. Between them, `startElement` and `endElement` open and close each element. The writer escapes every text and every attribute value for you, and it throws a `LogicError` for any call that would make the document invalid.

doc.shortHtml: Starts the document and writes the XML declaration <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>. Call it first, before any other method. A writer writes one document, so you call this once.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. After this call, you can write the root element.

errors.descHtml: The document is already started. The document is already finished with endDocument.

doc.shortHtml: Finishes the document and returns it as a string. Every element must be closed first. So the string this method returns is always a document that an XML parser can read.
doc.returnHtml: The whole document as a string. The string is not tainted, because the writer escaped every text and checked every name. After this call, every other method of the writer throws an error.

errors.descHtml: An element is still open. No root element was written. The document was not started with startDocument. The document is already finished.

doc.shortHtml: Opens an element, such as <order>. Everything you write until the matching endElement goes inside it. Call attribute right after this method to add attributes to the element.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The element's name, such as order or atom:link. It must be a valid XML name. The writer does not escape it.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The element is open, and the next calls write inside it.

errors.descHtml: The name is not a valid XML name. The root element is already written and closed. 1024 elements are already open inside each other. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Closes the element that startElement opened last. You do not pass a name, because the writer remembers which elements are open. So the end tags always match the start tags.
doc.returnHtml: Nothing. An empty element is written as <a/>. An element with something inside is closed with </a>.

errors.descHtml: No element is open. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Writes text inside the open element. The writer escapes it: & becomes &, < becomes < and > becomes >. A parser reads back exactly the text you wrote, so the text can never add an element or an attribute.

params.name: text
params.descHtml: The text to write. It can contain any character XML allows, including <, & and quotes. A tainted text is allowed, because the writer escapes it.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. After this call, the writer does not indent inside this element, because added whitespace would change the text.

errors.descHtml: No element is open. The text contains a control character that XML cannot write. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Adds one attribute to the element that startElement opened last. Call it right after startElement, before you write anything inside the element. The writer escapes the value, so a value can contain quotes, <, & and line breaks.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The attribute's name, such as id or xml:lang. It must be a valid XML name.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The attribute's value. When a parser reads the document, it gets back exactly this text. A tainted value is allowed, because the writer escapes it.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The attribute is written in the element's start tag.

errors.descHtml: Something was already written inside the element, or no element is open. The element already has an attribute with this name. The name is not a valid XML name. The value contains a control character that XML cannot write. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Writes an XML comment, such as <!-- note -->. You can write it before the root element, inside an element, or after the root element is closed.

params.name: text
params.descHtml: The comment's text. It is written unchanged, because XML cannot escape anything inside a comment. It cannot contain --, and it cannot end with -.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The comment is written at the place the writer has reached.

errors.descHtml: The text contains -- or ends with -. The text contains a control character that XML cannot write. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Writes text inside the open element as a CDATA section, such as <![CDATA[a < b]]>. The text is written unchanged. A parser reads it as the same text that content writes.

params.name: text
params.descHtml: The text to write. < and & are allowed and are not escaped. The text cannot contain ]]>, because that ends a CDATA section.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. After this call, the writer does not indent inside this element, like after content.

errors.descHtml: No element is open. The text contains ]]>. The text contains a control character that XML cannot write. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Writes a processing instruction, such as <?xml-stylesheet href="a.css"?>. It is a note for the program that reads the document. It has a target and data, and nothing goes inside it.

params.name: target
params.descHtml: The name of the program or purpose the instruction is for. It must be an XML name. It cannot be xml in any casing, because startDocument already writes that one. A tainted string does not compile here.

params.name: data
params.descHtml: The instruction's data. It is written unchanged, because XML cannot escape anything inside an instruction. It cannot contain ?>. When it is "", only the target is written. A tainted string does not compile here, because the program that reads the document follows the data.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The instruction is written at the place the writer has reached.

errors.descHtml: The target is not an XML name, or it is xml. The data contains ?>. The data contains a control character that XML cannot write. The document is not open.

doc.shortHtml: Writes a document type declaration, such as <!DOCTYPE html>, before the root element. It writes only the name. It does not write a link to a DTD file or any entity definitions. The declaration is for programs outside Novis. Core\Xml::parse and Core\Xml::reader throw an error for any document that contains <!DOCTYPE.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The name of the document type. It must be an XML name. Usually it is the name of the root element.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. The declaration is written before the root element.

errors.descHtml: The root element is already started. A declaration is already written. The name is not an XML name. The document is not open.

classes.summaryHtml: Builds a new XML document one node at a time. Core\Xml::writer returns a writer. startDocument begins the document, and endDocument returns it as a string. Between them, startElement and endElement open and close each element. The writer escapes every text and every attribute value for you, and it throws a LogicError for any call that would make the document invalid.

classes.name: Core\Zip
classes.summary: Reads zip archives. `entries` lists the names in an archive, `read` returns one file from it, and `extract` writes its files into a folder. Every archive is checked before any name or file is returned. An archive with an unsafe name, such as `../config.php`, throws a `ParseError`.

doc.shortHtml: Returns the names of the entries in an archive, in the order its central directory lists them. The whole archive is checked first. If one entry uses .., an absolute path or a symlink, it throws an error and lists nothing.

params.name: archive
params.descHtml: The bytes of the archive. Only its central directory is read. So the time to list an archive depends on the number of entries, not on the size of the archive.

doc.returnHtml: One tainted string per entry. A name is always tainted, whatever the type of the archive was. The name was written by whoever built the archive. An archive written directly in a test is no safer than a downloaded one.

errors.descHtml: $archive is not a valid zip archive, or one of its entries is unsafe. An entry is unsafe when it has an absolute path or a .. part, or is a symlink. It is also unsafe when it is nested in more than 64 folders, or repeats a name. A bad archive never throws an IOError. That error is for a failing disk.

members.name: read
members.signature: read(bytes $archive, string $name, uint $maxBytes = 67108864, uint $maxRatio = 1000): tainted bytes

doc.shortHtml: Returns the decompressed bytes of one entry. The output has a size limit that cannot be switched off.

params.name: archive
params.descHtml: The bytes of the archive. It is checked the same way as in entries. An unsafe entry anywhere in the archive makes this call throw too, whichever entry you read.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The entry to read. It is compared with the names in the archive exactly, and it is never treated as a path. A name that entries returned works as it is.

params.name: maxBytes
params.descHtml: The largest output this call may produce, in bytes. It can be lower than [limits] max_decompressed, but not higher. 0 means zero bytes, not unlimited.

params.name: maxRatio
params.descHtml: The largest output per byte of the compressed entry. This is the second part of the size limit, because a zip bomb is small before it is decompressed.

doc.returnHtml: All the bytes of the entry. The result is never cut short. An entry larger than either limit throws an error. The bytes are tainted, like the names, because somebody else wrote the archive.

errors.descHtml: Every case where entries throws. It is also thrown when no entry has that name, or the entry uses a compression method this class cannot read. Other causes are a broken compressed stream, a wrong CRC-32, or output above either limit.

doc.shortHtml: Writes the entries of an archive under $destination and returns how many files it wrote. The whole archive is checked before any byte is written. Each directory is created and then checked to be inside $destination, before anything is written into it.

params.name: archive
params.descHtml: The bytes of the archive. It is checked the same way as in entries. An unsafe entry anywhere in the archive makes this call throw before it writes anything.

params.name: destination
params.descHtml: The directory to write the files to. It is created if it does not exist. The call needs fs.write and also fs.read for it, because Novis reads the directories above a name to find where it points.

params.name: maxBytes
params.descHtml: The largest output this call may produce for the whole archive, in bytes. It is not a limit per entry. Many small entries can add up to an attack too. It can be lower than [limits] max_decompressed, but not higher.

params.name: maxRatio
params.descHtml: The largest output per byte of a compressed entry. This limit is per entry, because each entry is decompressed on its own.

doc.returnHtml: The number of files written. A directory entry is created, but it is not counted. So the number is the number of new files.

errors.descHtml: Every case where entries throws. It is also thrown for a wrong CRC-32, or for output above either limit, per entry or for the whole archive.
fs.read or fs.write is not granted for the destination. It is also thrown when a directory inside it points outside it. This happens when somebody creates a link while the files are written.

Creating or writing a file failed. A file with the name of an entry may already exist, because extract never overwrites a file. Or the disk failed. The safety checks of this class throw a ParseError or a RuntimeError instead.

classes.summaryHtml: Reads zip archives. entries lists the names in an archive, read returns one file from it, and extract writes its files into a folder. Every archive is checked before any name or file is returned. An archive with an unsafe name, such as ../config.php, throws a ParseError.
